> **Quick start:** `sipnab -I capture.pcap` to analyze a file, or `sudo sipnab` for live capture on the default interface. Add `-N` for non-interactive output.

Complete flag reference for sipnab. This page groups flags by function.

## Start here

A first run needs only a handful of these flags:

- [`-I`, `--input`](#capture) reads packets from a capture file, a directory of them, an archive of them, or a glob, instead of live capture. It reads stored vCon containers too.
- [`-d`, `--device`](#capture) names the network interface to capture on.
- [`-N`, `--no-tui`](#mode) turns on non-interactive mode, with no TUI. The batch and output flags require it.
- [`--report`](#output) generates a summary report after capture completes. Requires `-N`.
- [`--json`](#output) prints output as NDJSON, one JSON object per line. Requires `-N`.
- [`--filter`](#matching) takes a Filter DSL expression or a diagnostic alias name, such as `codec-asym` or `late-media`, and a [named filter](@/docs/filter-dsl.md#named-filters) as `@name`.

The **Since** column names the first sipnab release whose command line accepted the flag, under its current name or one of its aliases. `Unreleased` means no published release has the flag yet. Check what your own binary accepts with `sipnab --help`.

CLI flags always override config file values (see [config-reference.md](@/docs/config.md)).

- Boolean flags default to `off` (false) unless otherwise noted.
- For task-oriented recipes rather than a flag catalog, start with [examples.md](@/docs/cookbook.md).

## Common recipes

A few flag combinations to get productive fast.

- For the full task-oriented collection, see the [Cookbook](@/docs/cookbook.md). It covers triage, filtering, recording, security and HEP.
- For symptom-driven diagnostics, see [Troubleshooting](@/docs/troubleshooting.md).
- This page is otherwise a flag reference (grouped below).

### Debug a failed call

Start by listing every failed call in the pcap. The Call-IDs worth chasing come from this list.

```bash
sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --filter "state == 'Failed'"
```

With one of those Call-IDs in hand, print just that dialog's call flow.

- `--no-cli-print` is what makes it *just* that.
- On its own, `--call-report` appends the report to the whole capture's per-message dump.
- So without it, the report you came for arrives after every message in the file.

```bash
sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --call-report "abc123@host" --no-cli-print
```

When the finding belongs in a ticket, write the same report as Markdown to a file. Do not read it on the terminal.

- Keep `--no-cli-print` here too.
- Without it, `report.md` opens with hundreds of lines of raw SIP before its first heading.

```bash
sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --call-report "abc123@host" --markdown --no-cli-print > report.md
```

### Monitor live SIP quality

Watch live traffic for calls that are already degraded:

- MOS below 3.0, or
- audio flowing in only one direction.

```bash
sudo sipnab -N -d eth0 --filter "rtp.mos < 3.0 OR one_way == true"
```

Feed the same set of problem calls into a monitoring pipeline as NDJSON. Keep a copy on disk at the same time.

```bash
sudo sipnab -N -d eth0 --problems --json | tee /var/log/sipnab/problems.ndjson
```

Hand each quality drop to an external alerting script rather than reading it yourself.

- `--exec-rate-limit` bounds the invocations per second.
- So one bad trunk cannot fork a process per stream.

```bash
sudo sipnab -d eth0 --on-quality-exec "/usr/local/bin/pagerduty-alert.sh" \
  --quality-threshold 3.0 --exec-rate-limit 5
```

### Measure post-dial delay across calls

Find the calls whose setup took longer than three seconds. The output is NDJSON for whatever consumes it next.

```bash
sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --filter "pdd > 3.0" --json
```

The `--slow-setup` alias asks the same question against the run's own post-dial delay threshold.

- The threshold is 11 seconds, unless `--pdd-threshold` or `[diagnosis] post_dial_delay_secs` moves it.
- So a quick check needs no filter expression at all.

```bash
sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --slow-setup --report
```

### Security monitoring

Detect SIP scanning and append it in fail2ban's format to the log its jail reads.

- `--kill-scanner` is what detects.
- `--fail2ban` only chooses the format, so leaving it out leaves the log empty.

Every example below passes `-N`:

- `-N` runs the detectors and writes `--fail2ban` lines. The fail2ban output
  needs `-N`.
- The interactive TUI (the default when you leave `-N` off) runs the same
  detectors and shows their findings, but never sends a response to a
  scanner.
- `--cores N` refuses the detection flags with exit 2: the parallel reader
  runs no detectors. sipnab refuses `--stir-shaken` with them. Drop `--cores` to detect.

```bash
sudo sipnab -N -d eth0 --kill-scanner --fail2ban >> /var/log/sipnab/scanners.log
```

Before that log reaches a jail, run the same detectors over a capture of an ordinary hour. Read the list of addresses they would ban.

- On a carrier trunk it routinely names your own SBCs.
- The reason: the enumeration signature and a busy hunt group look alike.

```bash
sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --kill-scanner --fail2ban \
  | grep -oE 'src=[^ ]+' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
```

Audit a capture for digest credentials that went out where anyone could read them.

```bash
sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --digest-leak
```

Run the whole sweep at once: scanners, fraud heuristics, and registration floods. Alerts go to both syslog and structured JSON.

```bash
sudo sipnab -N -d eth0 --kill-scanner --fraud-detect --reg-flood \
  --alert syslog --alert json --syslog
```

### Export for Wireshark analysis

Print a display filter to paste into Wireshark after opening the capture.

```bash
sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --wireshark
```

Or print a `tshark` command that applies a display filter to the capture. Use this when the next step is a shell pipeline rather than the Wireshark GUI.

```bash
sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --tshark-filter 'sip.from.user == "1001"'
```

After the per-message lines it prints the command to run:

```text
tshark -r 'capture.pcap' -Y 'sip.from.user == "1001"' -V
```

### Export call audio as WAV

Audio export is a TUI workflow. See [Keybindings](@/docs/keybindings.md#rtp-streams).

### Pipe through jq for custom analysis

Count failures by response code. The dominant one is then obvious.

```bash
sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --filter "state == 'Failed'" --json \
  | jq -r 'select(.is_request == false) | .status_code' \
  | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
```

List every distinct User-Agent the capture saw. This finds the odd endpoint out.

```bash
sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --json \
  | jq -r '.ua // empty' | sort -u
```

### Bound, split, and multi-interface captures

Stop after a fixed packet count and summarize the capture.

```bash
sipnab -N -d eth0 -n 1000 --report
```

Roll to a new pcapng every 50 MiB. Then a long capture does not become one file too large to open.

```bash
sipnab -d eth0 -O /var/captures/sip.pcapng --pcapng --split filesize:50
```

Keep only the newest four of those files. Then a long capture fits a fixed amount of disk.

- `--split-keep` **deletes** the older files as rotation creates new ones.
- It deletes only the files this run wrote.

```bash
sipnab -d eth0 -O /var/captures/sip.pcapng --pcapng --split filesize:50 --split-keep 4
```

**The drop user creates the output files.** Run as root, sipnab does this:

- It opens the capture device.
- It drops privileges to `nobody` (or the `--user` you name) before it creates the `-O` file.
- It creates every `--split` file later still.
- Right after the drop, before it reads the first packet, it checks that the drop user can create these:
  - the `-O` file,
  - `--export-vcon-dir`,
  - `--vcon-out`,
  - `--redact-map`.

So a directory only root may write ends the run at startup with exit code `1`. One example is a directory made with a plain `sudo mkdir`:

```text
Failed to create output file '/var/captures/sip.pcapng': Permission denied (os error 13). sipnab dropped privileges to user 'nobody' before opening output; make the directory writable by that user (e.g. install -d -o nobody <dir>), pass --user <name> for a user that can write there, or --no-priv-drop.
```

There are three fixes:

- Give the directory to the drop user with `sudo install -d -o nobody /var/captures`.
- Pass `--user` naming an account that can already write it.
- Keep root for the whole run with `--no-priv-drop`.

> **`--split-keep` deletes capture files.** sipnab deletes nothing unless you
> pass the flag. It deletes nothing at `--split-keep 0`. The reason: a capture
> is very often the only copy of the evidence.
>
> - sipnab deletes only the files the running process created and named.
> - It never lists the directory. So a file left beside them stays where it is:
>   - a file from an earlier run, from another tool, or from you,
>   - however closely its name resembles a rotation.
>
> A run that dies mid-capture leaves behind whatever it had not yet deleted.
>
> - The next run starts its own list and never adopts those files.
> - sipnab names each file it deletes in the log.
> - It counts them in the closing summary.

Capture across every interface at once. Timestamp each message relative to the one before it.

- On Linux the `any` pseudo-device is what makes this every interface.
- `--multi-device` is for naming a specific list, as below.

```bash
sipnab -d any --delta-time
```

Capture on two named interfaces instead, one libpcap handle each.

```bash
sipnab -d eth0,eth1 --multi-device --delta-time
```

> **Tip:** Every output flag (`--json`, `--report`, `--fail2ban`, etc.) needs `-N`. Think of it as "non-interactive mode". It disables the TUI and writes to stdout instead.

## Capture

| Flag | Value | Default | Since | Description |
|------|-------|---------|-------|-------------|
| `-d`, `--device` | `<IFACE>` | platform default | 0.3.0 | Network interface to capture on. With no `-d`, no `-I` file and no `-L` HEP listener, sipnab picks a default that differs by platform — see the note below. Config: `[capture] device` |
| `-I`, `--input` | `<FILE\|DIR\|GLOB>` | -- | 0.3.0 | Read packets from a capture file, a directory of them, an archive of them, or a glob, instead of live capture. **Repeatable.** sipnab reads the files in capture order, never in filename order — see the note below. A `.tar`, `.tgz` or `.tar.gz` reads like a directory: see [Archives read like directories](#archives-read-like-directories). A stored vCon container (`*.vcon.json`, or any file whose first character other than whitespace is `{`) reads as the SIP messages it stores, marked `origin=vcon`, with no media. sipnab reports a schema finding and reads the container anyway, and skips one with no SIP it can read, naming the reason: see [Analyze a stored vCon](@/docs/vcon.md#analyze-a-stored-vcon) |
| `--recursive` | -- | off | 0.5.70 | Descend into subdirectories when `-I` names a directory |
| `--input-name` | `<GLOB>` | -- | 0.5.70 | Read only files whose *name* matches this pattern when `-I` names a directory or an archive. Applies at every depth under `--recursive`, and to an archive's members at every depth |
| `--vcon-key` | `<FILE>` | -- | 0.5.219 | Decrypt an encrypted vCon container (draft-ietf-vcon-vcon-core-04 section 5.3) with the RSA private key in this PEM file, then verify the signed form inside. Applies to every vCon reader: `-I`, the MCP `analyze_vcon` and `validate_vcon` tools, and `POST /v1/vcon/analyze` and `POST /v1/vcon/validate`. The file must be readable by its owner only. Without it sipnab refuses an encrypted container and names this flag. A signed container needs no key: sipnab verifies its signature. sipnab reads a gzip format container (section 6.2) with or without it. See [A signed, encrypted or compressed container](@/docs/vcon.md#a-signed-encrypted-or-compressed-container). Config: `[vcon_input] key` |
| `--vcon-signer-ca` | `<FILE\|system>` | -- | 0.5.219 | Read a signed or encrypted vCon container only when its signing certificate chains, through the intermediates in its `x5c`, to a CA certificate in this PEM file, with every certificate in the chain within its validity period. `system` uses the host's CA bundle; write `./system` for a file of that name. While this flag is in force, sipnab refuses an unsigned container: it has no signer to check. Config: `[vcon_input] signer_ca` |
| `--vcon-signer-sha256` | `<HEX>` | -- | 0.5.219 | Read a signed or encrypted vCon container only when its signing certificate has this SHA-256 fingerprint: 64 hex digits, plain or in colon-separated pairs, either case, as `openssl x509 -noout -fingerprint -sha256` prints it. While this flag is in force, sipnab refuses an unsigned container. Config: `[vcon_input] signer_sha256` |
| `--vcon-x5u-ca` | `<FILE\|system>` | -- | 0.5.219 | Fetch the certificate chain of a signed vCon container that names it only by an `x5u` URL (draft-ietf-vcon-vcon-core-04 section 5.2.2), over HTTPS, trusting the server only when it chains to a CA certificate in this PEM file; `system` uses the host's CA bundle. sipnab reads at most 256 KiB of the answer, waits at most 10 seconds, fetches each URL once per run, and refuses an `x5u` that is not `https://`. Without this flag sipnab fetches nothing, and refuses such a container naming this flag. sipnab verifies a signature that carries `x5c` with it, and does not fetch its `x5u`. Config: `[vcon_input] x5u_ca` |
| `-O`, `--output` | `<FILE>` | -- | 0.3.0 | Write captured packets to a pcap file. `--filter` chooses what sipnab shows and analyzes, not what this file holds: a BPF filter (the positional argument, such as `"udp port 5060"`) narrows the file. Run as root, sipnab creates this file, and every `--split` file, after it drops privileges, so the drop user (`nobody` unless `--user` names another) must be able to write the directory. sipnab checks this before it reads the first packet and exits `1` when the drop user cannot. See [the note above](#bound-split-and-multi-interface-captures) |
| `-B`, `--buffer` | `<MIB>` | `64` | 0.3.0 | Kernel capture buffer size in MiB (per device). See [Tuning capture](@/docs/tuning-capture.md). sipnab refuses `0` (no ring at all) with exit `2`, and `[capture] buffer = 0` with exit `1`. Config: `[capture] buffer` |
| `--buffer-budget` | `<MIB>` | `64` | 0.4.4 | Sets the size of the in-flight capture→processing queue. sipnab converts the budget to a packet count at an assumed 2048 bytes per packet, so `64` holds 32768 packets, and keeps the count between 10000 and 5000000: `0` and any value up to `19` give the 10000-packet floor. The limit counts packets, not bytes. A queued packet can be as large as the snapshot length, so with full 65535-byte packets the 64 MiB default can hold about 2 GiB; overrides `[capture] buffer_budget_mb`. Config: `[capture] buffer_budget_mb` |
| `--snaplen` | `<BYTES>` | `65535` | 0.3.0 | Snapshot length for packet capture (bytes). sipnab refuses `0` (no byte of any packet) with exit `2`, and `[capture] snaplen = 0` with exit `1`. Config: `[capture] snaplen` |
| `--capture-profile` | `signaling\|full` | -- | 0.5.109 | Picks a `--snaplen` for you: `signaling` is 1500 bytes, which keeps every SIP header whole and drops most of each RTP payload, and `full` is 65535. An explicit `--snaplen` overrides it. More: [Tuning capture](@/docs/tuning-capture.md#snapshot-length-snaplen-and-why-it-decides-your-ring-capacity). Config: `[capture] snaplen` |
| `-S`, `--limitlen` | `<BYTES>` | -- | 0.5.9 | Parse only the first N bytes of each packet. Caps what the SIP parser and matchers inspect, independent of `--snaplen` (capture length) and `--payload-limit` (display truncation). At least 1: sipnab refuses `0` |
| `--no-reassembly` | -- | off | 0.5.9 | Disable IP-fragment and TCP-segment reassembly; sipnab parses every packet standalone (inverse of segment reassembly). Useful for pure single-packet UDP scanning |
| `-x`, `--quiet-bad-parse` | -- | off | 0.5.10 | Suppress the per-packet "SIP parse error" diagnostic emitted when a SIP-looking packet fails to parse. sipnab drops the packet either way; this only silences the notice on a noisy link. sipnab logs the notice at debug level, so it shows only with `SIPNAB_LOG=debug` |
| `--portrange` | `<RANGE>` | `5060-5061` | 0.3.0 | SIP **signaling** port range. Media is never gated — RTP uses SDP-negotiated dynamic ports. The default is narrow and carriers routinely run SIP on 5070, 5080 and elsewhere, so widen it or analyze a fraction of the file — see the note below. HEP input (`-L`, `--hep-parse`) is never gated: the sender already chose what to send, and the ports in its HEP chunks are its claim, not something sipnab captured. Config: `[capture] portrange` |
| `--ws-portrange` | `<RANGE>` | `80, 443, 8080, 8443` | 0.5.99 | Ports carrying SIP-over-WebSocket ([RFC 7118](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7118.html)), as one inclusive `START-END` range in the same grammar as `--portrange`. Kamailio, OpenSIPS and Janus each default to a WSS port outside the shipped set, and behind a reverse proxy sipnab sees the port the proxy forwards to: name that port here, or sipnab reads none of that signaling. A range **replaces** the shipped set, exactly as `--portrange` replaces the default signaling ports. sipnab counts the SIP-over-WebSocket it declines to unwrap and names the ports it arrived on. The range governs plain WebSocket only: sipnab reads a WebSocket frame it decrypts out of TLS with `--keylog` on any port and labels it WSS. It joins a frame split across TLS records, several frames in one record, and a message fragmented across frames, up to 65,536 bytes per message, and reads an HTTP upgrade and its `101` answer split across TLS records, up to 8,192 bytes. A frame, message or upgrade it cannot finish or decode counts in the NOT DECODED line. Config: `[capture] ws_ports` |
| `--multi-device` | -- | off | 0.3.0 | Open one capture per interface named in a comma-separated `-d` list, e.g. `-d eth0,docker0 --multi-device`. It does **not** enumerate interfaces for you: with a single `-d` (or none) it falls back to an ordinary single capture. On Linux the zero-argument default already sniffs every interface via the `any` pseudo-device |
| `--no-rtp` | -- | off | 0.3.0 | Disable RTP capture and analysis. Config: `[capture] no_rtp` |
| `--rtp` | -- | off | 0.5.204 | Capture and analyze RTP even when `[capture] no_rtp = true`. The last of `--no-rtp` / `--rtp` typed wins. Config: `[capture] no_rtp` |
| `-p`, `--no-promisc` | -- | off | 0.5.8 | Do not put the interface into promiscuous mode. Promisc is on by default for a named device; the `any` pseudo-device is never promiscuous. Config: `[capture] promisc` |
| `--bpf-file` | `<FILE>` | -- | 0.3.0 | Read the BPF capture filter from a file. It takes precedence over the positional filter and replaces `[capture] bpf_filter`, and like them it applies to `-I` capture files as well as live capture. Config: `[capture] bpf_filter` |
| `--capture-tunnels` | `[<PORTS>]` | off | 0.5.80 | Also capture **all** traffic on the UDP tunnel ports, so SIP inside GTP-U, VXLAN or GENEVE reaches sipnab. Bare flag means `2152,4789,6081`; pass a list for non-standard ports (`--capture-tunnels=8472`). Off by default: it takes every packet on those ports, which on a mobile core is the entire user plane, because a BPF filter cannot reach the inner port behind a GTP-U extension-header chain. Ignored when you supply your own filter |
| `-n`, `--count` | `<N>` | -- | 0.3.0 | Stop after receiving N packets (counts every packet received, including any a HEP listener later drops by allowlist, rate limit, or auth). At least 1: sipnab refuses `0` |
| `--duration` | `<DURATION>` | -- | 0.3.0 | Stop after duration (e.g., `30s`, `5m`, `1h`). A bare number is seconds. Must be greater than zero: sipnab refuses `0`, `0s`, `0m` and `0h` with exit `2` |
| `--autostop` | `<CONDITION>` | -- | 0.3.0 | Autostop condition: `filesize:N` stops after N MiB of output, `duration:N` after N seconds. `filesize` counts MiB, the unit `--split filesize` and `-B/--buffer` also use |
| `--split` | `<CONDITION>` | -- | 0.3.0 | Split output files (e.g., `filesize:50` for 50 MiB chunks) |
| `--split-keep` | `<N>` | -- | 0.5.100 | Keep only the newest N split files: sipnab **deletes** the older ones as `--split` rotates, turning `-O` into a ring buffer. Off unless you pass it, and off at `0`. sipnab deletes only the files the running process created and named, so a file left by an earlier run, another tool, or you survives however closely its name resembles a rotation. See [the warning above](#bound-split-and-multi-interface-captures) |
| `--replay` | -- | off | 0.3.0 | Replay packets from a pcap file at original timing |
| `--pcapng` | -- | off | 0.3.0 | Use pcapng format for output files. [pcapng Metadata](#pcapng-metadata) covers the metadata sipnab writes into pcapng output |
| `<BPF_FILTER>...` | positional | -- | 0.3.0 | BPF capture filter expression (trailing positional args), handed to libpcap as typed. Not the display filter (`--filter`). Replaces the filter sipnab would otherwise generate from `--portrange`. `--bpf-file` takes precedence, and either one replaces `[capture] bpf_filter`. The filter applies to `-I` capture files as well as live capture. When `[capture] bpf_filter` filters a file run, sipnab prints a warning naming the key, so a file whose calls fall outside the filter does not look empty. Unlike `sngrep` and `sipgrep`, sipnab takes no match expression here; match SIP text with `-e`. A filter typed here that does not compile says so, and sipnab refuses a lone argument that names an existing file, naming the `-I` it was missing. Config: `[capture] bpf_filter` |

> **The auto-generated filter looks through VLAN, QinQ, PPPoE and MPLS.**
> With no filter of your own on a live capture, sipnab builds one from
> `--portrange`.
>
> - It also matches SIP inside these, on Ethernet and on Linux cooked captures:
>   - one VLAN tag,
>   - QinQ,
>   - PPPoE Session,
>   - one or two MPLS labels.
> - A bare `portrange` would match none of that traffic.
> - See
>   [How the generated filter reaches encapsulated SIP](@/docs/encapsulations.md#how-the-generated-filter-reaches-encapsulated-sip)
>   for what it covers and its two limits.
>
> **The auto-generated filter admits the media too.** RTP travels on whatever
> ports SDP negotiated.
>
> - So the filter admits UDP on any port whose first payload byte marks RTP
>   version 2. This covers IPv4 and IPv6 without extension headers.
> - Media inside a VLAN tag or a tunnel is not admitted. Name it in a filter of
>   your own.
> - With `--no-rtp` the filter stays signaling-only. Nothing would read the
>   media.
> - With `--hep-listen` as well as `-d`, the interface takes the media only.
>   - The HEP mirror already delivers the signaling.
>   - Taking it off the wire too would deliver every message twice.
>
> **UDP tunnels are opt-in.** GTP-U, VXLAN and GENEVE are not covered by
> default, and sipnab says so at startup.
>
> - BPF cannot parse a variable-length GTP-U extension-header chain to reach
>   the inner port.
> - So the only way to cover them is to capture everything on the port. See
>   `--capture-tunnels`.
>
> **A filter you supply is never rewritten.** It goes to `pcap_compile`
> exactly as typed. If it looks encapsulation-blind, sipnab says so once. It
> still uses your expression.

> **What you get when you omit `-d`.** The default is not the same everywhere,
> and the difference decides whether you see loopback traffic:
>
> | Platform | Default | Scope |
> |---|---|---|
> | Linux | the `any` pseudo-device | **every interface at once**, loopback included |
> | macOS / BSD | libpcap's default device, from the routing table; otherwise the first non-loopback interface | **one interface** |
>
> On Linux:
>
> - A SIP proxy often talks to itself over loopback. So capturing only `eth0`
>   silently misses it.
> - Pass `-d any` to say so explicitly.
> - Promiscuous mode does not apply to `any`. So `--no-promisc` changes
>   nothing there.
>
> On macOS you get a *single* interface.
>
> - If SIP is not on the one libpcap picked, you see nothing.
> - The capture then looks merely quiet.
> - Name `-d` explicitly.

> **`-I` and `-d` are alternatives, not companions.** sipnab accepts both, and the FILE wins.
>
> - sipnab reads the file and never opens the interface.
> - The output looks like a normal run.
> - sipnab warns on stderr when you do this.
> - To switch a file command to live capture, **remove `-I`** rather than adding `-d` beside it.

> **`--portrange` decides how much of the file you analyze.** The default,
> `5060-5061`, is narrow.
>
> - SIP on other ports is ordinary. Carriers and SBCs use 5070, 5080 and
>   others routinely.
> - A capture from a real trunk commonly carries a large share of its
>   signaling outside the default.
>
> Reading a file, sipnab skips any SIP message whose source **and**
> destination ports both fall outside the range. A skipped message is in no
> count, dialog or output, so check for skips before you trust a total.
>
> The run says how many it skipped on stderr, with the busiest port:
>
> ```text
> NOT ANALYZED: 7 further SIP message(s) were seen on ports outside --portrange and are in none of the totals above. Busiest: 5060 (7). Re-run with --portrange 1-65535 to include them.
> ```
>
> `--report` includes the same fact:
>
> ```text
> INCOMPLETE RUN — this report does not describe the whole capture:
>   - 7 SIP message(s) were seen on ports outside --portrange and were not analyzed; re-run with --portrange 1-65535 to include them
> ```
>
> Both came from `sipnab -N -I sip_call.pcap --portrange 1-2 --report`, a
> capture whose SIP is all on port 5060.
>
> `--portrange 1-65535` analyzes everything the capture holds. Reach for it
> first on an unfamiliar capture. Narrow it once you know what is in there.
>
> **Live capture is different, and worse.**
>
> - With no explicit BPF filter, sipnab compiles the range into the filter.
> - So the kernel drops the traffic before sipnab sees it.
> - Nothing downstream, this counter included, can report what went missing.
> - Set the range correctly *before* the capture, because no rerun recovers
>   it.

> **`NOT DECODED` is the other line to read before the totals.**
>
> - `--portrange` is about SIP sipnab chose not to analyze.
> - This line is about frames it could not read at all:
>   - an unsupported link type,
>   - an EtherType carrying no IP,
>   - an IP protocol that is no transport,
>   - a truncated frame,
>   - a decode error.
> - Such a frame counts as a packet (it arrived). It reaches no message, dialog
>   or stream.
> - So on its own, the summary reports the same thing in two cases: the
>   capture held no SIP, or sipnab understood none of it:
>
> ```text
> NOT DECODED: 3 of 3 frame(s) (100.0%) produced nothing and are in none of
> the counts above. Reasons: unsupported link type 147 (3). NOTHING IN THIS
> CAPTURE WAS READ — every frame failed to decode, so the totals above describe
> no traffic whatsoever and a zero among them is not evidence of absence.
> ```
>
> Every reason carries the number that identifies it. That number is what you
> act on.
>
> - `unsupported link type 147` names the file's pcap link type, here
>   `LINKTYPE_USER0`, which sipnab does not decode.
> - Convert the capture with `editcap -T ether in.pcap out.pcap` when its
>   frames are Ethernet underneath, or open an issue naming the number.
>
> A small count is normal. ARP is undecodable by definition and appears on any
> Ethernet capture. So read the share, not the count.
>
> When the share is high, sipnab additionally refuses to state
> "No SIP traffic found" as a finding. It has no basis for one. The same breakdown appears in
> two more places:
>
> - as a `NOT DECODED (capture-wide)` section in `--report`,
> - as `sipnab_capture_undecodable_frames_total{reason}` plus
>   `sipnab_capture_undecoded_fraction` on `/metrics`.
>
> [`docs/troubleshooting.md`](https://github.com/NormB/sipnab/blob/main/docs/troubleshooting.md) tables what each reason means and what to do about
> it.

**Examples**
- `sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --sandbox best-effort --report` — analyze a capture with the filesystem bounded to the input and the crash directory. On a kernel without Landlock this warns and analyzes anyway, which is the point of `best-effort`
- `sudo sipnab -N -d eth0 -O /var/captures/live.pcap --sandbox required` — refuse to capture at all unless the ruleset installed. Use this where an unsandboxed capture is worse than none. The run exits non-zero and names the reason rather than starting
- `sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --seccomp log` — read a capture with every system call recorded. The filter refuses nothing, so the analysis matches a run without the flag. What you get is the record of which calls a file-reading run makes
- `sudo sipnab -N -d eth0 --count 5000 --seccomp log && auditctl -s` — record the calls a LIVE capture makes, bounded by `--count` so the log cannot run away, then check where the records went. A connected audit daemon has them in `ausearch -m SECCOMP`. A pid of 0 means they are in `dmesg`
- `sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --rtp --report` — analyze the media too when your config file sets `[capture] no_rtp = true`
- `sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --no-rtp --rtp --report` — the last of the pair wins, so this run analyzes RTP
- `sipnab -N -I capture.pcap -e INVITE udp port 5060` — the `sngrep` habit `sngrep INVITE udp port 5060`, written for sipnab: the match expression goes after `-e` and the words after the options are the capture filter
- `sipnab -N -I 0192d6a4-1b2c-8d3e-9f40-5a6b7c8d9e0f.vcon.json --vcon-key recipient.key --json-dialogs` — analyze an encrypted vCon sipnab wrote: decrypt it with the recipient's private key, verify its signature, and print its dialogs
- `sipnab --mcp -N -I capture.pcap --vcon-key /etc/sipnab/vcon-recipient.key` — serve the MCP tools with a key, so `analyze_vcon` and `validate_vcon` read encrypted containers an agent hands over
- `sipnab -N -I signed.vcon.json --vcon-signer-ca signing-ca.pem --report` — analyze a signed vCon only when the CA in `signing-ca.pem` issued its signing certificate
- `sipnab -N -I sealed/ --vcon-key recipient.key --vcon-signer-ca system --json-dialogs` — read a directory of encrypted vCons, each only when a CA in the host's CA bundle issued its signer
- `openssl x509 -in signer.pem -noout -fingerprint -sha256` — print the fingerprint `--vcon-signer-sha256` takes, from the signing certificate. For the signing certificate in the next example it prints `sha256 Fingerprint=4A:27:CF:DC:D8:87:A5:E5:A9:B5:DE:7E:27:37:C2:48:28:2B:86:44:8A:B3:60:6F:42:99:B2:E2:26:FC:0F:19`; pass the part after `=`. `sha256sum signer.pem` hashes the PEM text and gives a different value
- `sipnab -N -I signed.vcon.json --vcon-signer-sha256 4A:27:CF:DC:D8:87:A5:E5:A9:B5:DE:7E:27:37:C2:48:28:2B:86:44:8A:B3:60:6F:42:99:B2:E2:26:FC:0F:19 --json-dialogs` — analyze a signed vCon only when one known certificate signed it
- `sipnab -N -I sealed.vcon.json --vcon-key recipient.key --vcon-signer-ca signing-ca.pem --vcon-signer-sha256 4a27cfdcd887a5e5a9b5de7e2737c248282b86448ab3606f4299b2e226fc0f19 --report` — require both: the signing certificate chains to `signing-ca.pem` and has this fingerprint
- `sipnab -N -I signed.vcon.json --vcon-x5u-ca system --json-dialogs` — analyze a signed vCon whose signature names its certificate chain only by an `x5u` URL: fetch the chain over HTTPS from a server the host's CA bundle trusts
- `sipnab -N -I signed.vcon.json --vcon-x5u-ca pki-ca.pem --vcon-signer-ca signing-ca.pem --report` — fetch the `x5u` chain from a server the CA in `pki-ca.pem` issued, and read the vCon only when its signer chains to `signing-ca.pem`

- `sudo sipnab --device eth0 --output capture.pcap --portrange 5060-5080 --count 10000` — record up to 10000 packets from eth0 into a pcap, watching a widened SIP port range
- `sudo sipnab --device eth0 --buffer 16 --buffer-budget 128 --snaplen 2048 --quiet-bad-parse` — live-capture a busy link with bigger kernel and queue buffers, a capped snapshot length, and parse-error notices silenced (the CLI matcher -x)
- `sudo sipnab -N -d eth0,eth1 --multi-device --output capture.pcap --autostop filesize:100` — capture on two named interfaces at once, headlessly, stopping once the output file reaches 100 MiB. `--multi-device` needs the list. Without one it is a no-op
- `sipnab -N --input capture.pcap --replay --no-rtp` — replay a pcap at its original timing with RTP capture and analysis disabled
- `sudo sipnab -N -d eth0 --capture-profile signaling --output signaling.pcap` — record signaling on a busy link: 1500 bytes keeps every SIP header whole while dropping the bulk of each RTP packet, which is where the ring pressure comes from. Check `sipnab_capture_snapped_frames_total` afterwards to see how many frames arrived short
- `sudo sipnab -N -d eth0 --capture-profile signaling --snaplen 4096` — the explicit number wins over the profile, for a trunk carrying INVITEs too large even for one MTU (deep `Record-Route` sets, ISUP encapsulation). Use `--capture-profile full` instead when you need `--retain-audio`, WAV export or a faithful `-O` re-emit, all of which need RTP payload
- `sipnab -N --input /var/captures/ --json-dialogs --no-cli-print` — read every capture in a directory as one timeline, so a call split across the ring buffer resolves to one dialog instead of two fragments
- `sipnab -N --input /var/captures/ --recursive --input-name '*.pcap.gz' --json-dialogs --no-cli-print` — descend into per-day subdirectories and read only the compressed archives
- `sipnab -N --input 'captures/tg.pcap[0-4]' --report` — analyze the first five members of a ring buffer with a glob sipnab expands itself, no shell needed
- `sipnab -N --input session.tgz --report` — analyze every capture in an archive as one timeline without unpacking it, each member not read named with the reason
- `sipnab -N --input a.pcap --input b.pcap --json-dialogs --no-cli-print` — read two named captures as a single set, ordered by their packets
- `sipnab -N --input /var/captures/ --input-name 'edge1-*' --recursive --json` — pick one host's captures out of a tree holding several
- `sipnab -N --input capture.pcap --limitlen 512 --no-reassembly --quiet-bad-parse` — scan a pcap quickly: parse only the first 512 bytes of each packet, every packet standalone (no reassembly), without parse-error noise
- `sudo sipnab --device eth0 --bpf-file sip.bpf --no-promisc --duration 5m` — capture for 5 minutes using a BPF filter read from sip.bpf, without putting the interface into promiscuous mode (the CLI matcher -p)
- `sudo sipnab -N --device eth0 --capture-tunnels --buffer 64 --duration 5m` — capture SIP traveling inside GTP-U, VXLAN or GENEVE as well as the encapsulations the auto-filter already covers. This takes **every** packet on ports 2152, 4789 and 6081, so the same command widens the kernel buffer. Check the drop counters in the summary before trusting a long run
- `sudo sipnab -N --device eth0 --capture-tunnels=8472 --portrange 5060-5080 --report` — cover a Linux VXLAN fabric on its pre-IANA port 8472 instead of the three defaults, across a widened signaling range
- `sudo sipnab --device eth0 --portrange 5060-5090 --buffer 8 --buffer-budget 256 --duration 1h` — monitor an hour of traffic across a wide SIP port range with enlarged capture buffers
- `sipnab -N --input capture.pcap --replay --limitlen 1500 --no-rtp` — replay signaling only from a pcap, parsing at most 1500 bytes of each packet
- `sudo sipnab --device eth0 --bpf-file sip.bpf --no-promisc --snaplen 9000 --count 500` — stop after 500 packets that pass the sip.bpf filter, non-promiscuous, with the snapshot length sized for jumbo frames
- `sudo sipnab -N --device eth0 --output capture.pcap --autostop duration:60 --no-reassembly` — write a one-minute capture that treats every packet standalone (IP-fragment and TCP-segment reassembly off)
- `sipnab -N --input webrtc.pcap --ws-portrange 8081-8081 --portrange 1-65535 --json-dialogs --no-cli-print` — a WSS listener behind a reverse proxy that forwards to 8081: without the range the entire WebRTC signaling leg is invisible, and sipnab reports how many messages it skipped and on which port
- `sudo sipnab -d eth0 --ws-portrange 1-65535 --portrange 1-65535` — unwrap SIP-over-WebSocket wherever it appears on a box whose WSS port you do not know yet, then read the skip line to learn which ports were carrying it


### Read a ring buffer or split capture as one capture

A call's INVITE may be in one file of a rotated capture and its BYE in the
next. Read the whole set in one run, so each call appears once, complete.

Name the files with a glob, a directory, or several `-I` flags. Quote a glob so
sipnab expands it rather than the shell:

```bash
sipnab -N -I 'ring/tg.pcap*' --json-dialogs --no-cli-print
```

sipnab orders the files by the timestamp of each file's first packet, never by
name. A `tcpdump -C 100 -W 10` ring buffer overwrites its oldest file in place,
so its numeric suffixes do not follow time. The first log line names the file
sipnab reads first:

```text
INFO sipnab::app::bootstrap: Reading 2 capture files in timestamp order (first: 'ring/tg.pcap1')
```

- sipnab recognizes a capture by its contents, not its extension. A file named
  `tg.pcap0`, or one with no extension, opens.
- It decompresses gzip files as it reads them, so a directory holding both
  `.pcap` and `.pcap.gz` files needs nothing extra.
- A file you name with `-I` that sipnab cannot read stops the run with an
  error. sipnab skips, with a warning, a file it finds by expanding a directory
  or glob and cannot read.

Reading the files one run at a time instead splits each call that crosses a
file boundary into two incomplete dialogs: one that never ends, and a BYE with
no INVITE.

### Archives read like directories

Point `-I` at a `.tar`, a `.tgz`, a `.tar.gz` or a `.zip`, and sipnab reads it
the way it reads a directory. See [Archives](#archives) for password-protected
ones.

- Every capture inside joins the set, in capture order, alongside anything else
  `-I` named.
- Nobody has to unpack it first.
- The answer matches what reading the unpacked directory gives.

The rules:

- **Layers nest.** These unwrap on the way to the capture, up to four layers
  deep:
  - a gzip-compressed member such as `ring-3.pcap.gz`,
  - a tar inside a `.tgz`,
  - or both.

  sipnab identifies each layer by its first bytes, never by its name. So a
  gzip file named `c.pcap` still opens.
- **sipnab accounts for every member.** A member that is not a capture gets a
  `Skipping` line naming it and the reason. The reasons are:
  - empty,
  - not a capture (with its first four bytes),
  - a link,
  - a device node,
  - a sparse file,
  - a format sipnab does not unwrap, such as 7-Zip, `zstd`, `xz` or `bzip2`.

  The closing `-I resolved to` line counts them.

  A member may have a link type sipnab does not decode, such as an LTE MAC log.
  - It gets a line naming it.
  - Its frames count as not decoded.
  - A BPF filter that cannot compile against that link type skips the member.
    It does not end the run.
- **Names come from the archive, paths never do.**
  - sipnab writes each member to a file it names itself, in a private directory
    under `$TMPDIR`.
  - It deletes that directory when the run ends.
  - A member called `../../etc/x` lands in that directory like any other.
  - Output, logs and frame pointers name a member `<archive>/<member>`. For
    example: `session.tgz/ring/a.pcap#12`.
  - `--show-frame` reads that member straight back out of the archive.
- **Inflation stops at a ceiling.**
  - Every byte any gzip layer produces counts against `--max-gunzip-bytes`.
    sipnab sums the count across the layers of one input.
  - One archive may hold at most 10,000 entries.
  - An archive cut short, or stopped at a ceiling, keeps what arrived. It
    marks the run incomplete:
    - exit status `1`,
    - `archives.cut_short` in the `sipnab_run` record.
- **`--input-name` filters members** by file name, the same way it filters a
  directory's files. On a file you name directly with `-I`, such as a single
  `call.pcap.gz`, a pattern that matches the file's name reads it, and one that
  does not stops the run with exit `1`:

  ```text
  -I/--input: -I 'call.pcap.gz' names a file directly, which --input-name '*.pcap' does not match; --input-name filters only files found in a directory or by a glob. Drop one of the two.
  ```
- **Decryption works on members exactly as on plain files.** Each of these
  decrypts a member the same way:
  - `--keylog`,
  - the secrets a pcapng embeds,
  - SDES keys in the SDP,
  - `--dtls-keylog`.

  It does not matter whether the member arrived plain, gzip-compressed, in a
  tar, in a `.tgz`, or gzip-compressed inside a `.tgz`.

A run may die without cleaning up, from a crash or `kill -9`.

- It leaves its directory behind, holding a lock that died with it.
- The next run that unpacks an archive removes it.

## Archives

Captures often travel as password-protected ZIP files. They carry subscriber
identities, numbers and credentials.

- Unpacking one by hand leaves a decrypted copy on disk. That defeats the
  password.
- Point `-I` at the ZIP instead. sipnab then:
  - opens it,
  - reads the captures inside,
  - deletes its own owner-only copy of each member when the run ends.
- A ZIP reads like a `.tgz`. So everything in
  [Archives read like directories](#archives-read-like-directories) applies to
  it.
- A ZIP nested in a tar, or a tar in a ZIP, unwraps too.

Builds with the `archive` feature read ZIP and 7z files. These include it:

- the `full` build,
- every release binary, the static musl tarballs and the `-noaudio` packages
  among them.

| Flag | Value | Default | Since | Description |
|------|-------|---------|-------|-------------|
| `--archive-password-file` | `<FILE>` | -- | 0.5.187 | Read archive passwords from a file, one per line. sipnab strips only the line ending: spaces belong to the password. sipnab refuses a file you own that other users can read (`chmod 600` it), the rule ssh applies to a private key, and accepts a file another user owns, such as a Kubernetes secret mount. `/dev/fd/3` and `<(pass show pcaps)` work |
| `--archive-password-command` | `<CMD>` | -- | 0.5.187 | Run a command and use the first line it prints, like `restic --password-command`. sipnab runs it without a shell and passes its stderr through, so a secret manager can prompt. A non-zero exit fails the run, and sipnab never shows the command's output. The command gets 120 seconds and 64 KiB of output |
| `--archive-password-stdin` | -- | off | 0.5.187 | Read an archive password from the first line of stdin, like `docker login --password-stdin` |
| `--archive-password` | `<PASSWORD>` | -- | 0.5.187 | An archive password on the command line. **Insecure**, and sipnab warns on every use: other local users can read it in `ps`, and your shell saves it in its history |
| `--archive-password-encoding` | `<ENC>` | all | 0.5.187 | Try passwords in one encoding only: `utf-8`, `cp437`, `cp850` or `cp1252` |
| `--no-password-prompt` | -- | off | 0.5.187 | Never ask for an archive password on the terminal |

**Where a password comes from, best first.** sipnab tries every source you
configure, in this order, before it gives up on a member:

- `--archive-password-file`, for scripts and services.
- `--archive-password-command`.
- `--archive-password-stdin`.
- The systemd credential `archive-password`.
  - When `$CREDENTIALS_DIRECTORY/archive-password` exists, sipnab reads it like
    a password file.
  - So `LoadCredential=archive-password:/etc/sipnab/pcaps.pw` or
    `LoadCredentialEncrypted=` in the unit is all it takes.
  - Writing `--archive-password-file %d/archive-password` in the unit works
    too.
- The `SIPNAB_ARCHIVE_PASSWORD` environment variable. It ranks below every
  source above because a process's environment leaks:
  - child processes inherit it,
  - systemd and OWASP both advise against secrets there.
- `--archive-password`, which warns on every use.
- The prompt. When no configured password opens a member, sipnab asks on the
  terminal, the way ssh and sudo do: `Password for evidence.zip (member voip/call3.pcap, attempt 1 of 3):`.
  - It reads `/dev/tty`, not stdin. So it still asks with stdin redirected.
  - It echoes nothing.
  - Each archive gets three attempts.
  - An empty entry, or Ctrl-D, skips that archive's locked members.
  - Ctrl-U clears the line.
  - Ctrl-C stops the run.
  - sipnab restores the terminal on every one of those paths.
  - Sometimes it never asks and never waits. Locked members then count as
    `encrypted_no_password`. This happens:
    - with no terminal, as in cron, CI or a detached agent,
    - or with `--no-password-prompt`.
  - A TUI run asks here for the archives `-I` names, before it draws.
  - A capture opened inside the TUI asks in its own window, described in
    [Archive password popup](@/docs/keybindings.md#archive-password-popup).

**How sipnab tries them.**

- The password that opened one member of an archive goes first for that
  archive's other members.
- It never goes to another archive unless you configured it.
- ZIP never records which encoding its creator typed the password in. So
  sipnab also tries a non-ASCII password in these forms:
  - its NFC and NFD forms,
  - the CP437, CP850 and CP1252 code pages that `unzip` and 7-Zip fall back
    to.
- All of those spellings count as one attempt.
- Passwords may be up to 4096 bytes. sipnab refuses a longer one whole rather
  than cutting it short.

**What it reads.**

- ZIP members stored or deflated:
  - unencrypted,
  - encrypted with WinZip AES (128, 192 or 256-bit),
  - or encrypted with the legacy ZipCrypto.
- 7z archives compressed with LZMA or LZMA2:
  - unencrypted or AES-256,
  - with or without an encrypted member list.
- A 7z password covers the whole archive. The format stores it as UTF-16 text.
  So sipnab tries its NFC and NFD forms but no code pages.
- A 7z sets how much work deriving its key takes.
  - sipnab refuses one asking for more than 7-Zip's own ceiling of 2^24
    rounds, as `bound_exceeded (7z key derivation)`.

sipnab reads ZipCrypto and warns once per archive that it protects nothing.

- The `bkcrack` tool recovers its keys from 12 known bytes.
- A capture's first bytes are predictable.
- A wrong password fails the format's own check.
- One wrong password in 256 slips past ZipCrypto's check byte. For that one, the
  member's CRC fails instead, and sipnab moves on to the next candidate.

**What it reports.** Each member sipnab does not read gets a `Skipping` line
with the reason. The reason is one of these:

- `encrypted, and no password was supplied`,
- `encrypted, and no password supplied opens it`,
- a format it cannot decrypt.

You may name an archive with `-I` and sipnab may read nothing from it.

- That fails the run with exit status `1`.
- It names each member with its reason code, such as
  `evidence.zip/call3.pcap: encrypted_no_password`.
- If some members open, the run succeeds. The closing `-I resolved to` line
  counts the rest.

**Where the password never goes.** No log line at any level contains it. No
error message, output format or export contains it either.

- A run that holds a password turns core dumps off.
- `--allow-coredump` warns that a dump would contain it.

**Exports carry the data out unencrypted.**

- These each warn once that they write that data unencrypted, when they write
  from a member decrypted out of a password archive:
  - `-O`,
  - `--strip-secrets`,
  - `--write-annotated`.
- The section comment of a `--write-annotated` copy says so too. It names no
  password.

**Examples**

- `sipnab -N -I evidence.zip --archive-password-file ~/.config/sipnab/pcaps.pw --report` — read a password-protected ZIP with the password in an owner-only file
- `sipnab -N -I evidence.zip --archive-password-file <(pass show pcaps/lab) --json-dialogs --no-cli-print` — take the password straight from a password manager through a pipe, so it never touches the disk
- `sipnab -N -I evidence.zip --archive-password-command 'pass show pcaps/lab' --report` — let sipnab run the password manager itself
- `printf '%s\n' "$PCAP_PW" | sipnab -N -I evidence.zip --archive-password-stdin --report` — pass a password a CI job holds in a masked variable
- `sipnab -N -I evidence.zip --archive-password-file pw.txt --archive-password-encoding cp437 --report` — try only the DOS code page, for an archive you know an old Windows tool made
- `sipnab -N -I evidence.zip --archive-password-stdin --archive-password-encoding cp1252 --json-dialogs --no-cli-print < pw.txt` — read the password from a redirected file and try only the Windows code page
- `sipnab -N -I 'captures/*.zip' --archive-password-command 'op read op://lab/pcaps/password' --json-dialogs --no-cli-print` — open every ZIP a glob finds with one password from 1Password's CLI
- `sipnab -N -I evidence.zip --archive-password 'correct horse' --report` — a throwaway lab archive only: the password lands in `ps` and your shell history, and sipnab warns
- `sipnab -N -I lab.zip --archive-password "$LAB_PW" --report` — the same trade-off from a variable, which still shows in `ps`; prefer `--archive-password-stdin`
- `sipnab -N -I evidence.zip --report` — no password configured: sipnab asks on the terminal for each locked archive, three tries each
- `sipnab -N -I evidence.zip --no-password-prompt --json-dialogs --no-cli-print` — in a script that must never wait on a keyboard: sipnab skips and counts the locked members instead
- `sipnab -N -I 'drop/*.zip' --archive-password-file pw.txt --no-password-prompt --report` — try the configured passwords and nothing else, even from a terminal

## Mode

| Flag | Value | Default | Since | Description |
|------|-------|---------|-------|-------------|
| `-N`, `--no-tui` | -- | off | 0.3.0 | Non-interactive mode (no TUI). Required for batch/output flags |
| `-c`, `--calls-only` | -- | off | 0.3.0 | Show only calls: dialogs an INVITE started. The dialog outputs apply it (`--json-dialogs`, `--report`, the per-message printout), and the TUI opens with only INVITE checked in its filter dialog. It leaves out OPTIONS, REGISTER, SUBSCRIBE and other dialogs. Like `--filter`, it does not narrow what `-O` writes |
| `-t`, `--telephone-event` | -- | off | 0.3.0 | Decode telephone-event (DTMF) RTP payloads and log each event at `info`, digit value masked as `x` |
| `--dtmf-cleartext` | -- | off | 0.5.82 | Log each DTMF digit VALUE on a second line, at `debug`, after the masked `info` line. Needs `-t`: without it nothing decodes the events and sipnab logs nothing. Publishes PINs and card numbers |
| `-q`, `--quiet` | -- | off | 0.3.0 | Suppress informational output; only show results |

**Examples**

- `sipnab --no-tui -I capture.pcap --calls-only` — analyze a pcap headlessly, showing only calls (dialogs an INVITE started), without OPTIONS pings, registrations or subscriptions
- `sudo sipnab --no-tui -d eth0 --telephone-event` — headless live capture that decodes DTMF and logs each event with its duration and SSRC, digit value masked
- `sipnab --no-tui -I capture.pcap --calls-only --telephone-event` — read a capture headlessly, report only calls, and log how many DTMF events each one carried
- `sipnab --no-tui -I lab.pcap --telephone-event --dtmf-cleartext` — read a capture you own and disclose the digit values. Also set `SIPNAB_LOG=debug`, or the run prints nothing but the mask
- `sudo sipnab --no-tui -d eth0 --telephone-event --dtmf-cleartext 2>dtmf.log` — capture live and steer the cleartext digits into a file whose permissions you control instead of a shared terminal or journald. Again needs `SIPNAB_LOG=debug`

**Read this before using `--dtmf-cleartext`.** DTMF digits keyed after answer
include:

- PINs,
- calling-card numbers,
- account numbers,
- credit-card numbers with their CVVs.

[RFC 4733](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4733.html) carries them in the clear no matter how well the signaling layer
protected the call. So `-t` alone logs everything you diagnose with, with the
digit value replaced by `x`:

- that an event arrived,
- its duration,
- its SSRC,
- its timestamp.

`DTMF digit='x' duration=200ms ssrc=0xdeadbeef`

`--dtmf-cleartext` adds a second line carrying the value. It is not a display
setting, and it needs `-t`: without `-t` nothing decodes the events, so neither
line appears.

- It puts a caller's PIN wherever this run's log goes:
  - your terminal,
  - a redirected file,
  - journald,
  - every aggregator downstream of journald.
- Turning it on takes two deliberate acts. sipnab writes the cleartext line at
  `debug` while the masked line stays at `info`. So:
  - pass the flag **and**
  - raise the level.
- Either one alone shows you nothing but the mask. Both, in one copyable line:

```bash
SIPNAB_LOG=debug sipnab --no-tui -I lab.pcap --telephone-event --dtmf-cleartext 2>dtmf.log
```

Each event then logs two lines, the masked one and the cleartext one:

```text
INFO sipnab::app::batch: DTMF digit='x' duration=120ms ssrc=0x5711bf84
DEBUG sipnab::app::batch: DTMF cleartext digit='6' duration=120ms ssrc=0x5711bf84
```

**Where the events go.** sipnab writes one masked line per decoded event and
keeps a count. No report, JSON field or MCP tool carries the digits. One output
does: a vCon written by a `[[vcon.rule]]` with `dtmf_events = true` records each
key press as `keydown` and `keyup` events whose `button` is the digit (see
[What the Dialog Object says about the call](@/docs/vcon.md#what-the-dialog-object-says-about-the-call)). `--redact` removes them.

To see the log lines:

- Run with `-N`. A TUI session shows none of them, because TUI mode sets the log
  level to `error` so log lines do not overwrite the screen.
- Leave out `--quiet`. It sets the level to `warn` and hides them.
- `SIPNAB_LOG=info` overrides the TUI level. Redirect stderr to a file when you
  use it, or the lines draw over the TUI.


## Matching

| Flag | Value | Default | Since | Description |
|------|-------|---------|-------|-------------|
| `-e`, `--match` | `<PATTERN>` | -- | 0.5.6 | SIP payload match-expression (the positional match expression). Regex tested against the whole raw message; once any message in a dialog matches, sipnab shows the rest of that dialog too (dialog-following). In the TUI, the call list holds only dialogs one of whose messages matched, and every later message of each; the REST API and MCP server a TUI run starts read the same dialogs. Honors `-i`/`-v`/`-w`/`--single-line`. Independent of the trailing `<BPF_FILTER>` positional |
| `-i`, `--ignore-case` | -- | off | 0.3.0 | Case-insensitive matching for header filters and patterns |
| `-v`, `--invert` | -- | off | 0.3.0 | Invert the match: select messages that do NOT match. Dialog-following still applies, so once sipnab selects a message of a dialog, every later message of that dialog prints, including ones that match |
| `-w`, `--word` | -- | off | 0.3.0 | Match whole words only |
| `--single-line` | -- | off | 0.3.0 | Prevent `.` from matching newlines in payload regexes; does not unfold headers |
| `--from` | `<PATTERN>` | -- | 0.3.0 | Filter by SIP From header (regex pattern). Config: `[filter] from` |
| `--to` | `<PATTERN>` | -- | 0.3.0 | Filter by SIP To header (regex pattern). Config: `[filter] to` |
| `--contact` | `<PATTERN>` | -- | 0.3.0 | Filter by SIP Contact header (regex pattern) |
| `--ua` | `<PATTERN>` | -- | 0.3.0 | Filter by User-Agent header (regex pattern) |
| `--filter` | `<EXPR>` | -- | 0.3.0 | Filter DSL expression OR a diagnostic alias name (`codec-asym`, `late-media`, etc.) — see [filter-dsl.md](@/docs/filter-dsl.md). A value may be bare or quoted: `method == INVITE` and `method == 'INVITE'` are the same filter. The expression may use a [named filter](@/docs/filter-dsl.md#named-filters) from `[filters]` as `@name`. Config: `[filter] expression` |
| `--since` | `<RFC3339>` | -- | 0.5.214 | Keep only dialogs whose first message is at or after this instant (`2026-10-09T10:00:00Z`). The window is half-open, `[--since, --until)`: see [Scope a run to a time window](#scope-a-run-to-a-time-window). ANDed with `--filter`. Needs `-N` |
| `--until` | `<RFC3339>` | -- | 0.5.214 | Keep only dialogs whose first message is before this instant; a dialog at exactly `--until` belongs to the next window. Must be after `--since`. ANDed with `--filter`. Needs `-N` |

**Examples**

- `sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --match "alice@example.com" --ignore-case` — show every dialog that mentions alice@example.com, case-insensitively (dialog-following payload match)
- `sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --match "486 Busy Here" --word --single-line` — whole-word match for 486 rejections, preventing `.` from spanning header lines
- `sudo sipnab -d eth0 --match "REGISTER" --invert` — live view of everything except REGISTER traffic (inverted match)
- `sudo sipnab -d eth0 --ua "friendly-scanner" --contact "203\.0\.113\." --ignore-case` — flag scanner traffic live: a known scanner User-Agent (any case) with a Contact pointing into 203.0.113.0/24
- `sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --ua "sipcli" --contact "192\.0\.2\." --single-line` — filter a pcap by User-Agent and a Contact in 192.0.2.0/24, restricting payload regex dots to a single line
- `sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --match "OPTIONS" --word --invert` — suppress keep-alive noise: show messages that do not contain the whole word OPTIONS
- `sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --report --since 2026-10-09T10:00:00Z --until 2026-10-09T11:00:00Z` — report only the calls that started between 10:00 and 11:00 UTC


### Scope a run to a time window

`--since` and `--until` keep the dialogs whose first message falls in the
half-open window `[--since, --until)`.

- A dialog at exactly `--since` is in.
- A dialog at exactly `--until` is in the next window.
- So adjacent windows never count a call twice.
- Either bound alone leaves the other side open.
- Values are [RFC 3339](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3339.html) instants. sipnab converts an offset other than `Z` to UTC.

The window is the one every surface applies, under three spellings:

| Surface | Spelling |
|---|---|
| CLI | `--since <RFC3339>` / `--until <RFC3339>` |
| REST | `GET /v1/dialogs?after=<RFC3339>&before=<RFC3339>` |
| MCP | `search_by_time` with `start` / `end` |
| Filter DSL | `time >= '<RFC3339>' AND time < '<RFC3339>'` |

The CLI cannot use REST's names. `-A`/`--after` already sets the context lines
printed after a match.

The window joins `--filter` and the diagnostic alias flags in one filter. So
these all see the same dialogs:

- `--report`,
- `--json-dialogs`,
- `--analyze`,
- the per-message stream,
- `--export-vcon-when`.

`--call-report` and `--export-vcon` name one call by Call-ID and are not
narrowed.

A window may hold none of the capture's dialogs. The run then exits 0 with
empty listings, and says so on stderr, naming the window and the span the
capture's dialogs cover:

```text
--since/--until: no dialog's first message falls in [2030-01-01T00:00:00Z, unbounded); this capture's dialogs begin between 2023-11-14T22:13:20Z and 2023-11-14T22:13:20Z
```

These exit 2:

- an `--until` that is not after `--since`,
- a value that is not RFC 3339.

```text
--until 2023-11-14T22:13:20Z is not after --since 2023-11-14T23:00:00Z: the window [--since, --until) would hold no instant
```

The flags need `-N`. In the TUI, set the time range in the call list's filter
dialog.

**Examples**

- `sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --json-dialogs --no-cli-print --since 2026-10-09T10:00:00Z --until 2026-10-09T11:00:00Z` — one JSON line per call that started between 10:00 and 11:00 UTC
- `sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --report --filter "state == 'Failed'" --since 2026-10-09T10:00:00Z` — the failed calls that started at or after 10:00 UTC

## Name resolution

| Flag | Value | Default | Since | Description |
|------|-------|---------|-------|-------------|
| `--resolve` | -- | off | 0.4.3 | Turn name resolution on (manual mappings + `/etc/hosts`). In the TUI, press `n` to cycle Off / Static / DNS; in headless `-O --pcapng` export it embeds a Name Resolution Block. Config: `[names] enabled` |
| `--no-resolve` | -- | off | 0.5.204 | Show addresses, not names, whatever else would turn name resolution on: `[names] enabled`, `--names`, `--reverse-dns`, `[names] hosts_file` or `[names.manual]`. Also stops reverse-DNS lookups. The last of `--resolve` / `--no-resolve` typed wins. Config: `[names] enabled` |
| `--reverse-dns` | -- | off | 0.4.3 | Also use reverse DNS (PTR) lookups. Implies `--resolve`. Emits DNS queries for captured IPs. Config: `[names] reverse_dns` |
| `--no-reverse-dns` | -- | off | 0.5.204 | Do not make reverse-DNS lookups even when `[names] reverse_dns = true`. The last of `--reverse-dns` / `--no-reverse-dns` typed wins. Config: `[names] reverse_dns` |
| `--dns-cache-entries` | `<N>` | `4096` | 0.5.100 | Reverse-DNS results held at once. Past the cap sipnab drops the oldest entry, so a capture touching more hosts than this -- a carrier edge, a peering point, or any long `--reverse-dns` window -- keeps re-looking-up addresses it already resolved. Nothing reports that: a dropped lookup only shows as an address displayed unresolved, so the symptom is names that flicker. The worker queue's depth follows this figure; sipnab derives it rather than taking a second number. Config: `[names] dns_cache_entries` |
| `--names` | `<FILE>` | -- | 0.4.3 | Preload IP → name mappings from an `/etc/hosts`-format file. Repeatable. Config: `[names] hosts_file` |

See the [Name Resolution](@/docs/keybindings.md#name-resolution) keys for in-TUI naming (`N`) and persistence.

**Examples**
- `sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --no-reverse-dns` — make no DNS queries when your config file sets `[names] reverse_dns = true`
- `sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --reverse-dns --no-reverse-dns` — the last of the pair wins, so sipnab makes no lookups
- `sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --no-resolve` — show raw addresses when your config file turns names on, through `[names] enabled`, a hosts file or `[names.manual]`
- `sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --resolve --no-resolve` — the last of the pair wins, so addresses print as addresses

- `sudo sipnab -d eth0 --resolve --names /etc/sipnab/hosts.map` — live capture with name resolution from a static hosts-format mapping file
- `sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --resolve --names /etc/sipnab/hosts.map --names ~/.config/sipnab/lab-names -O named.pcapng --pcapng --no-cli-print` — write a copy of an offline pcap whose Name Resolution Block carries the names from two mapping files and `/etc/hosts`; Wireshark and `tshark -q -z hosts` show them. When both files name one address, the later file wins. A headless run prints addresses, not names: the names go only into the pcapng file
- `sudo sipnab -d eth0 --reverse-dns` — live capture that also resolves captured IPs via reverse DNS (PTR) lookups
- `sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --reverse-dns --names ~/.config/sipnab/lab-names -O named.pcapng --pcapng --no-cli-print` — write a copy of an offline pcap whose Name Resolution Block carries names from reverse DNS and a local mapping file
- `sudo sipnab -N -d eth0 --reverse-dns --dns-cache-entries 65536` — a peering point or carrier edge, where a capture touches far more than four thousand hosts: the wider cache stops sipnab re-resolving addresses it already knows, and the worker queue widens with it
- `sipnab -N -I lab.pcap --reverse-dns --dns-cache-entries 256 -O lab-named.pcapng --pcapng --no-cli-print` — the opposite, for a small lab capture on a memory-tight box, where a few hundred entries cover every host in the file


## pcapng metadata

| Flag | Value | Default | Since | Description |
|------|-------|---------|-------|-------------|
| `--strip-secrets` | `<OUTPUT>` | -- | 0.4.3 | With `-I <input>`, write a copy of the input pcapng to `<OUTPUT>` with all Decryption Secrets Blocks removed (the `editcap --discard-all-secrets` analog), then exit. sipnab never touches the input and writes the output atomically. |
| `--show-frame` | `<POINTER>` | -- | 0.5.77 | Resolve a frame pointer from a previous run, print that frame, then exit. Takes `<source>#<ordinal>` or `<source>#<ordinal>@<digest>` — the form the `frame` field of `--json-dialogs`, `--report`, the REST API and MCP carries. With a digest, sipnab checks the bytes against it and refuses a capture that changed after sipnab minted the pointer, writing nothing to stdout. Without one, sipnab prints the frame and marks it `UNVERIFIED`. |

Note: with resolution active, sipnab saves name mappings into a pcapng Name
Resolution Block.

- This happens on both the TUI save path and the headless `-O --pcapng` export
  (whenever `--resolve`/`--names` apply).
- Headless pcapng exports also describe themselves:
  - the Section Header Block records the producing application
    (`sipnab <version>`) and OS,
  - the Interface Description Block records the capture source as the
    interface name.
- Opening a pcapng reads embedded NRB names and DSB TLS secrets back. sipnab
  decrypts with them.
- See [the design doc](https://github.com/NormB/sipnab/blob/main/docs/design/pcapng-metadata.md).

**Examples**

- `sipnab --show-frame 'capture.pcap#41@6f3a1c02b8d4e795'` — print the frame a dialog opened in, verifying the capture has not changed since
- `sipnab --show-frame 'capture.pcap#41'` — same frame, printed as `UNVERIFIED` because the short form carries nothing to check against
- `sipnab -N -I capture.pcapng --strip-secrets clean.pcapng` — write a sanitized copy of a pcapng with every Decryption Secrets Block removed
- `sipnab -N -I tls-call.pcapng --strip-secrets tls-call-clean.pcapng` — strip embedded TLS secrets from a decrypted-session capture before sharing it in a support ticket


## Operator notes

A note is a remark a person writes about one SIP message. It travels to the
person who opens the capture next.

- sipnab writes each note into a pcapng packet comment. Wireshark shows it
  beside the frame.
- sipnab never reads a packet comment back. A note is output, never part of
  the analysis.

| Flag | Value | Default | Since | Description |
|------|-------|---------|-------|-------------|
| `--notes` | `<FILE>` | -- | 0.5.185 | A JSON Lines file of notes, one `{"frame": "<pointer>", "note": "<text>"}` per line. With `--write-annotated`, the notes to write into the copy; take each pointer from the `frame` field of `--json`. In the TUI, the session's notes file: sipnab loads it at start when it exists, and the save dialog's NOTES format writes there (`C` on a message types a note; see [keybindings](@/docs/keybindings.md#call-flow)). In any other run sipnab refuses the flag, because nothing would read it. sipnab refuses a note over 4096 bytes, or one holding a control character other than newline and tab, an SDES `inline:` key, a TLS key-log line or a digest `response=` value, and one bad line refuses the whole file. The format is in [output formats](@/docs/output-formats.md#operator-notes-file). |
| `--write-annotated` | `<OUTPUT>` | -- | 0.5.185 | With `-I <capture>` and `--notes`, write a pcapng copy of that one capture to `<OUTPUT>` with each note as a packet comment on the frame it names, then exit. sipnab never touches the input. Every note must name its frame with a digest (`#<ordinal>@<digest>`), and the frame's bytes must still match it: when the capture changed after someone wrote the note, sipnab refuses, exits 1, and writes nothing. The copy carries the original frames byte for byte, drops decryption secrets, name resolution blocks and the input's own comments, and says so in its section comment. sipnab refuses a `.pcap` or `.cap` output, because classic pcap has no field for a comment. |

**Examples**

- `sipnab -N -I call.pcap --notes call.notes.jsonl --write-annotated call-annotated.pcapng` — hand a carrier the call with your notes on the frames they are about, readable in Wireshark
- `sipnab -N -I ticket-4711.pcapng --notes ticket-4711.notes.jsonl --write-annotated ticket-4711-for-vendor.pcapng` — annotate a copy of a pcapng from a ticket without touching the original, which keeps its decryption secrets and the copy does not
- `sipnab -I call.pcap --notes call.notes.jsonl` — open the call in the TUI with the notes you saved last time, and save new ones back to the same file


## Diagnostic aliases

Shortcut flags that expand to predefined filter DSL expressions. See [filter-dsl.md](@/docs/filter-dsl.md#named-aliases) for the exact expansion of each alias.

| Flag | Value | Default | Since | Description |
|------|-------|---------|-------|-------------|
| `--problems` | -- | off | 0.3.0 | Show calls matching any diagnostic signal: failed state, one-way audio, RTP loss past `--loss-bad-pct` (5% by default), jitter past `--jitter-bad-ms` (50 ms by default), NAT mismatch, more than 3 retransmits, post-dial delay past `--pdd-threshold` (11 s by default), codec/ptime/payload/duration asymmetry, or late media. Every one of those thresholds tracks the run's own setting, so a network that tuned `[diagnosis]` or `[quality]` to its own SLA gets an alias that agrees with the rest of the run — see [Named Aliases](@/docs/filter-dsl.md#named-aliases) for the exact expansion. Orphaned RTP is **not** among them: an orphaned stream belongs to no dialog, so it cannot select one. Find it in the "Orphaned Streams" section of `--report`, or `/v1/streams?orphaned=true` |
| `--slow-setup` | -- | off | 0.3.0 | Show calls whose post-dial delay passes `--pdd-threshold` (11 seconds by default, from `[diagnosis] post_dial_delay_secs`) |
| `--short-calls` | -- | off | 0.3.0 | Show completed calls shorter than `--fraud-short-call` (3 seconds by default, from `[security] fraud_short_call_secs`) |
| `--one-way` | -- | off | 0.3.0 | Show calls with potential one-way audio issues |
| `--nat-issues` | -- | off | 0.3.0 | Show calls whose RTP arrived from an address no SDP advertised (NAT-rewritten media source) |

Multiple diagnostic flags combine with OR.

- Adding `--filter` ANDs its expression with that selection.
- For example, `--problems --filter "from.user == '1001'"` selects only problem
  calls from user 1001.

**Examples**

- `sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --short-calls --one-way` — flag completed calls under 3 seconds and calls with suspected one-way audio in a capture
- `sudo sipnab -d eth0 -N --one-way --nat-issues` — live-monitor for one-way audio and NAT-rewritten media sources
- `sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --short-calls --report` — summarize short completed calls from a capture in a post-run report


## Output

| Flag | Value | Default | Since | Description |
|------|-------|---------|-------|-------------|
| `--json` | -- | off | 0.3.0 | Output as NDJSON (one JSON object per line, schema in [output-formats.md](@/docs/output-formats.md)). Requires `-N` |
| `--json-pretty` | -- | off | 0.3.0 | Output each message as pretty-printed multi-line JSON (use `--json` for line-oriented NDJSON). Requires `-N` |
| `--json-dialogs` | -- | off | 0.5.68 | NDJSON, one object per **dialog**, emitted after capture (needs `-N`; pair with `--no-cli-print` to get only the objects). `--json` is per message: a dialog filter such as `state == 'Failed'` selects dialogs and then emits every message of them, provisional responses included. This is the per-call shape, carrying `final_status_code` and `final_status_reason` so a failed call says which code failed it — those two are the final answer to the dialog's INVITE, or to the `REGISTER`/`OPTIONS`/`SUBSCRIBE`/`PUBLISH` that opened a dialog without one, and are `null` while it has none. |
| `--plugin` | `<PATH>` | -- | 0.5.69 | Load a WASM plugin that contributes its own dialog detections; repeatable. Findings appear under `plugin_findings`. Requires the `plugins` Cargo feature (**not** in the default set). A plugin runs with no imports — no filesystem, network or clock — but still sees each message's headers, so loading one is a trust decision. See [wasm-plugin-api.md](https://github.com/NormB/sipnab/blob/main/docs/design/wasm-plugin-api.md) |
| `--report` | -- | off | 0.3.0 | Generate summary report after capture completes. Requires `-N`. When the inputs include stored vCon containers, the report adds one row per container, read or skipped with the reason, and their totals; with `--json` or `--json-pretty`, as one JSON object under the key `sipnab_vcon_containers`. See [Read many containers at once](@/docs/vcon.md#read-many-containers-at-once) |
| `--call-report` | `<CALL-ID>` | -- | 0.3.0 | Generate a detailed report for a specific Call-ID. Implies non-interactive |
| `--export-vcon` | `<CALL-ID>` | -- | 0.5.125 | Export one dialog as an observer vCon container ([`draft-ietf-vcon-vcon-core`](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-vcon-vcon-core/), syntax `0.4.0`): unsigned, with each party's `name` taken only from a `From` or `To` display name and marked `validation: "none"`, with the audio this run retained inline up to `--vcon-max-inline-media`, and with what the capture missed attached. Goes to stdout unless `--vcon-out` names a file, and then silences the per-message stream so the container stays parseable. Implies non-interactive. On a live capture (`-d` or `--hep-listen`), sipnab writes the container when that call ends, about ten seconds after its last message, while the capture runs. A stopped live run writes nothing, so stopping sipnab leaves no call data behind. With `-I`, sipnab writes it at the end of the run. A live run refuses `--redact` and `--redact-map`, which only write at the end of a run; use them with `-I`. Needs the `vcon` Cargo feature, which `full` has and the default set does not. More: [Export a call as a vCon](@/docs/vcon.md) |
| `--export-vcon-when` | `<EXPR>` | -- | 0.5.127 | Emit a vCon for every dialog matching this filter expression, one container per dialog, into `--export-vcon-dir`. `EXPR` is the language `--filter` already speaks ([`docs/filter-dsl.md`](https://github.com/NormB/sipnab/blob/main/docs/filter-dsl.md)), so `state == 'Failed'` and `response_code >= 400 and rtp.codec == 'PCMU'` work without new syntax. sipnab parses the expression before the capture opens, so a malformed one fails the run rather than leaving an empty directory. Conflicts with `--export-vcon`, which answers the same question for one named call. Implies non-interactive, and unlike `--export-vcon` it leaves stdout alone, because the containers go to a directory. On a live capture (`-d` or `--hep-listen`), sipnab writes each matching call's container while the capture runs, about ten seconds after the call ends. A stopped live run writes nothing more, so stopping sipnab leaves no call data behind. With `-I`, sipnab writes every container at the end of the run. A live run refuses `--redact`, `--redact-map` and `--content-deny-tombstone`, which only write at the end of a run; use them with `-I`. Needs the `vcon` Cargo feature |
| `--export-vcon-dir` | `<DIR>` | -- | 0.5.127 | Directory for the containers `--export-vcon-when` produces, created if absent. Each file takes its Call-ID as a name, with every character outside `A-Za-z0-9._-` becoming `_` and the whole truncated. Requires `--export-vcon-when` |
| `--vcon-max-inline-media` | `<MIB>` | `5` | 0.5.128 | Largest inline media body a vCon may carry, in MiB. Raise it when you know the store that reads your containers accepts larger ones: some stores answer success for a container above their own limit and then drop its payload. `0` refuses every inline body without turning the exporter off, and the refusal still appears in the completeness caveat. Batch export, the REST server and the MCP server all read this one value. Needs the `vcon` Cargo feature |
| `--content-deny-header` | `<NAME>` | -- | 0.5.127 | Suppress content for any dialog carrying this header. No default: sipnab suppresses nothing until you name a header. The header's PRESENCE suppresses and its value plays no part, so `Privacy: none` suppresses exactly as `Privacy: id` does. Matched case-insensitively, as SIP header names are ([RFC 3261](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3261.html) 7.3.1). **Deny only**: no header makes sipnab keep content it would otherwise leave out. Needs the `vcon` Cargo feature |
| `--content-deny-tombstone` | -- | off | 0.5.128 | Write an identity-only container for each dialog `--content-deny-header` suppressed, instead of nothing. Requires `--content-deny-header`. The container carries the dialog's identity and a `redacted` object declaring `type` alone, because no fuller version of the container exists anywhere to point at. It carries no message trace, no media and no bodies. Off by default. A tombstone reveals that the call EXISTED, so leave it off when the header means "this call must leave no trace". Needs the `vcon` Cargo feature |
| `--vcon-out` | `<PATH>` | stdout | 0.5.125 | Write the `--export-vcon` container to this path instead of stdout. Requires `--export-vcon`. Refuses a path that names a capture this run reads, or that lies inside a directory this run reads, before opening any writer. A write that fails exits non-zero. Leaves the per-message stream alone, since the container no longer shares stdout with it. Pair with `--no-cli-print` for a silent run |
| `--vcon-digest` | -- | off | 0.5.128 | Print a SHA-256 of every container `--export-vcon-when` writes into `--export-vcon-dir`, in `sha256sum` format, on stdout while the progress summary stays on stderr. Each line names the bare file name, so `sha256sum -c` run inside that directory verifies it. It prints nothing for `--export-vcon`, with or without `--vcon-out`. Implies `--no-cli-print`, so no message line shares stdout with the digests. Prints to stdout, so it needs `-N` and `--mcp` refuses it. Needs the `vcon` Cargo feature |
| `--redact` | -- | off | 0.5.130 | Replace identities, addresses, hostnames and correlation identifiers in an exported vCon with keyed pseudonyms. Every identity becomes a keyed token that is equal exactly when the original was equal, and every address goes through a prefix-preserving map, so a reader can still tell that forty failures came from one subscriber, or that media went to a subnet the SDP never advertised. sipnab deletes digest credentials and inline audio rather than tokenizing them. Rewrites the serialized container only: the TUI, the reports and every in-process analysis keep the real values. Refused when the run exports no container. Needs the `vcon` Cargo feature |
| `--redact-key-file` | `<FILE>` | fresh key | 0.5.130 | Read the redaction secret from this file instead of drawing a fresh one from the operating system. Without it no token joins against any other export and nothing can reverse them; supply a file when the same subscriber must carry the same token across exports. The whole file is the secret, trailing newline included. Requires `--redact` |
| `--redact-keep-prefix` | `<N>` | `0` | 0.5.130 | Keep this many leading digits of a number verbatim, so route and NPA analysis survives. Every retained digit is a digit of a real subscriber number in the clear. A country code is one to three digits and an NANP area code is three, so choose the count for your numbering plan. Requires `--redact` |
| `--redact-map` | `<FILE>` | -- | 0.5.130 | Write the token-to-original table to this file, mode `0600`, set at creation rather than by a `chmod` afterwards. It reverses every pseudonym the run produced, so it is as sensitive as the capture it came from. Refuses to write over an existing file. Requires `--redact` |
| `--markdown` | -- | off | 0.3.0 | Format report output as Markdown |
