| `--stun` | -- | off | 0.5.112 | Report the STUN and TURN activity in the capture, and what it achieved: one row per transaction (for example Binding, Allocate, Refresh, CreatePermission and ChannelBind) naming the method, how many requests it took, whether anything answered, and the reflexive or relayed address the server reported back. An unanswered Binding Request means the client never learned its public address, so it advertised its private one in its SDP and media to it does not arrive. A TURN allocations section appears when a relay is in the capture, with the lifetime that decides when each one lapses. Columns for the relayed address, the ICE role and a FAILED `FINGERPRINT` appear only when the capture holds one. On a capture holding ICE connectivity checks an ICE section names the candidate pair the agents nominated, which is the path the media took, and any pair where both agents claimed the same role or answered `487 Role Conflict`. Where a relay carried media, the allocations section says which channel carried which SSRC, so a reader can trace a relayed stream in the stream list back to the allocation that carried it. Silent when the capture holds no STUN and no TURN. Requires `-N` |
| `--json-stun` | -- | off | 0.5.112 | NDJSON, one object per STUN/TURN transaction and per TURN allocation, emitted after capture. Each carries a `record` field (`transaction`, `turn_allocation` or `ice`) so a consumer never infers the kind from which keys are present; an allocation also carries the derived `lapsed` and the `channels` that attribute relayed media to it, and the single `ice` record carries the checks, the nominated pairs and any role conflicts. The machine-readable form of `--stun`. Requires `-N` |
| `--analyze` | -- | off | 0.5.112 | Analyze the capture and print every problem in it, worst first — one ranked list instead of one dialog at a time. It aggregates the diagnosis sipnab already computes (one-way audio, media that never arrived, an SDP address STUN contradicts, ICMP unreachables, failed and unacknowledged calls, codec and framing asymmetry) plus capture-level evidence, counted exactly and evidenced with Call-IDs, addresses, timestamps and packet counts. It derives nothing new. What sipnab did NOT read — undecodable frames, SIP a port gate discarded, records a retention cap dropped — appears at the top, because those make every count below them a floor, and a capture that did not fully decode never gets a clean verdict. Requires `-N` |
| `--json-analyze` | -- | off | 0.5.112 | The `--analyze` result as one JSON object, emitted after capture: the findings, plus the frames read and the dialogs examined, so a clean capture still prints an object. Requires `-N` |
| `--yang-analyze` | -- | off | 0.5.185 | The `--analyze` result [RFC 7951](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7951.html)-encoded: the same analysis `--json-analyze` prints, as one JSON document that validates against the `sipnab-diagnosis` YANG module. 64-bit integers are strings, names use hyphens, and each finding carries its `rank`. Asked for with `--json-analyze`, both come from one analysis. Requires `-N` |
| `--print-yang-module` | -- | off | 0.5.185 | Print the `sipnab-diagnosis` YANG 1.1 module and exit: the model the [RFC 7951](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7951.html) export of the capture analysis validates against, byte for byte the file committed under `yang/`. Needs no capture, config or privileges |
| `--hexdump` | -- | off | 0.3.0 | Include hex dump of SIP payloads. Requires `-N` |
| `--delta-time` | -- | off | 0.3.0 | Show delta time between consecutive messages. Config: `[display] delta_time` |
| `--no-delta-time` | -- | off | 0.5.204 | Show absolute times even when `[display] delta_time = true`. The last of `--delta-time` / `--no-delta-time` typed wins. Config: `[display] delta_time` |
| `-A`, `--after` | `<N>` | -- | 0.3.0 | Show N messages after each match (like `grep -A`) |
| `--show-empty` (`--full`) | -- | off | 0.3.0 | Show the full header block of bodyless messages (responses, OPTIONS, REGISTER, ACK, BYE); by default they show only the summary line |
| `--proto-number` | -- | off | 0.5.10 | Annotate the transport tag with the IANA IP protocol number, e.g. `UDP(17)` / `TCP(6)`. Long-only because `-N` is `--no-tui` here; TLS, WS and WSS report their TCP carrier's number (6) |
| `--line-buffer` | -- | off | 0.3.0 | Flush output after each line (useful for piping) |
| `--color` | `<WHEN>` | `auto` | 0.3.0 | Color output mode: `auto`, `always`, `never`. Config: `[display] color` |
| `--from-to-mode` | `<MODE>` | `default` | 0.4.4 | Default TUI From/To column display: `default` (user else host:port), `host-port`, `user`, `user-host-port`. Cycle at runtime with `u`. Overrides `[display] from_to`. Config: `[display] from_to` |
| `--payload-limit` | `<BYTES>` | -- | 0.3.0 | Maximum payload bytes the per-message text printout shows for each message, with `--show-empty` and `--hexdump` too. It does not shorten `--json`, `--json-pretty` or `-T`/`--text-dump` output. Config: `[display] payload_limit` |
| `-T`, `--text-dump` | -- | off | 0.3.0 | Dump raw SIP message text (like the CLI matcher `-T`) |
| `--no-cli-print` | -- | off | 0.3.2 | Suppress per-message CLI output (useful with `--report` / `--call-report` so only the post-capture summary reaches stdout) |
| `--wireshark` | -- | off | 0.3.0 | Print a display filter for the current capture to paste into Wireshark; use with `-N` |
| `--tshark-filter` | `<EXPR>` | -- | 0.3.0 | Generate a tshark-compatible display filter string |
| `--fail2ban` | -- | off | 0.3.0 | Switch the per-message stream to fail2ban-readable log lines. Requires `-N`. It selects a **format**, not a detection: only two events ever reach it, and each needs its own detector armed beside it — `--kill-scanner` (with `--kill-ua` to add User-Agents it matches) produces `scanner_detected`, `--reg-flood` produces `reg_flood`. On its own it emits nothing, and warns on stderr about the coming silence, because an empty jail log reads as "nothing attacked me". Detections carried by HEP input (`--hep-listen`, `--hep-parse`) never reach it without `--hep-allow-kill`: the inner addresses are the sender's claim, a jail line would ban whatever address the sender chose, and the run says so once at startup |
| `--lint` | -- | off | 0.5.84 | Run the RFC conformance linter over every dialog and print each finding with its rule identifier and the RFC section it reads from. The linter compares what the capture holds against what the cited section calls for, so a finding names a section rather than an opinion. Informational on its own: it changes what gets printed and never the exit code. Pair it with `--lint-fail-on` to make a pipeline stop. Prints to stdout, so it needs `-N` and `--mcp` refuses it. The rule catalog is in [sip-lint-rules.md](@/docs/sip-lint-rules.md), and over MCP as `explain_rule` |
| `--lint-fail-on` | `<SEVERITY>` | -- | 0.5.84 | Exit `3` when the linter reports a finding at or above this severity: `info`, `notice`, `warning` (or `warn`), or `error`. Any other value exits `2` and names the four. Needs `--lint`. A pipeline can tell a runtime failure (1) and a wrong invocation (2) apart from a non-conformant capture (3). `info`, the lowest severity, trips on any finding |
| `--group-by` | `<FIELD>` | -- | 0.3.0 | Group output by field (e.g., `call-id`, `from`, `method`) |
| `--max-groups` | `<N>` | `100000` | 0.5.97 | Distinct `--group-by` keys one run retains. Past it sipnab refuses new keys and warns that the output is incomplete. `-l`/`--limit` bounds tracked dialogs, not this buffer. Requires `--group-by`. Config: `[limits] max_groups` |
| `--max-grouped-messages` | `<N>` | `200000` | 0.5.97 | Messages `--group-by` buffers across every group. sipnab holds them in memory until the capture ends, because the last packet may belong to the first group. Requires `--group-by`. Config: `[limits] max_grouped_messages` |
| `--node-name` | `<NAME>` | hostname | 0.5.81 | Name this box reports as, in `capture_identity.node` on every MCP and REST answer about the loaded capture. The exceptions are MCP `capture_health`, the `hep_senders` tool and its REST route, a `yang-json` report body, and a vCon container served as the body of `GET /v1/dialogs/{call_id}/vcon`; [MCP across an estate](@/docs/mcp-estate.md#check-what-federation-cannot-prove) and [the REST reference](@/docs/api.md#which-capture-these-counts-came-from) list each answer. Lets an agent querying several servers at once tell which one saw a given fact. Distinct from the capture instance, which changes when a different capture loads; the node name stays the same. **The default puts your hostname on the wire.** Clipped to 64 characters. sipnab refuses an empty value (exit 2). Config: `[capture] node_name` |

**Examples**
- `sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --no-delta-time` — print absolute times when your config file sets `[display] delta_time = true`
- `sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --delta-time --no-delta-time` — the last of the pair wins, so times print absolute

- `sipnab -N -I calls.pcap --lint --no-cli-print` — run the RFC conformance linter over every dialog in a capture and print each finding with the rule identifier and the RFC section it reads from. Informational: it leaves the exit code alone
- `sipnab -N -I calls.pcap --export-vcon-when "state == 'Failed'" --export-vcon-dir out --redact --redact-keep-prefix 4 --no-cli-print` — hand a vendor every failed call with keyed tokens standing in for the subscriber numbers and the area code intact, so they can still see which route the failures came from
- `sipnab -N -I calls.pcap --export-vcon call-1 --vcon-out out.vcon --redact --redact-key-file team.key --redact-map out.map --no-cli-print` — a stable key, so today's tokens join against last week's, and the reversal table written beside the container at `0600`
- `sipnab -N -I calls.pcap --export-vcon-when "state == 'Completed'" --export-vcon-dir out --redact --redact-keep-prefix 3 --redact-map out.map --no-cli-print` — export every completed call, keep the NANP area code readable so a route analysis still works, and write the reversal table beside the export. Three digits is a choice about a real subscriber number, not a default sipnab can make for you: a country code is one to three digits and a national destination code is anything
- `sipnab -N -I calls.pcap --export-vcon-when "state == 'Failed'" --export-vcon-dir out --redact --redact-key-file team.key --redact-keep-prefix 0 --no-cli-print` — the shape to send outside the team, here for every failed call. A shared key still joins a subscriber across exports, no digits survive in the clear, and with no `--redact-map` written nothing anywhere reverses the tokens
- `sipnab -N -I calls.pcap --lint --lint-fail-on error --no-cli-print` — the CI gate. Exits 3 when any finding is at or above `error`, so a pipeline stops on a non-conformant capture. Exit 3 is not 1 or 2, so a failing gate is distinguishable from a failing tool and from a bad invocation
- `sipnab -N -I calls.pcap --lint --lint-fail-on warning --no-cli-print` — a stricter gate: stop on warnings as well as errors, for a pipeline that treats interop degradation as a build failure rather than a note
- `sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --json-dialogs --no-cli-print --plugin ./short-calls.wasm` — run a custom detection over every dialog and emit its findings beside sipnab's own
- `sudo sipnab -d eth0 -N --json-dialogs --no-cli-print --plugin ./site-rules.wasm --plugin ./fraud.wasm` — stack two site-specific detections over live traffic. Each plugin is sandboxed and a failure in one never stops the capture
- `sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --stun --no-cli-print` — read what NAT traversal actually achieved: which probes drew an answer, what public address came back, and which drew nothing. A capture holding only failed STUN is not an empty capture, it is the cause of a one-way-audio complaint
- `sipnab -N -I relay.pcap --stun --markdown --no-cli-print` — the same tables as Markdown, for pasting into a ticket. On a capture that went through a TURN relay this adds the allocations section, where a `LAPSED` status means the relay tore the allocation down while media was still crossing it
- `sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --json-stun --no-cli-print | jq 'select(.record == "transaction" and .responded_at == null)'` — every transaction nothing answered, as JSON
- `sipnab -N -I relay.pcap --json-stun --no-cli-print | jq 'select(.lapsed == true)'` — the relay allocations that ran out under live media, which no SIP message anywhere reports
- `sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --analyze --no-cli-print` — one ranked list of everything wrong with the file, worst first, with the evidence for each finding
- `sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --analyze --filter "state == 'Failed'" --no-cli-print` — narrow the DIALOG findings to failed calls. The capture-level evidence (undecodable frames, discarded ports, dropped records) is deliberately not narrowed, because it bounds every count in the report
- `sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --json-analyze --no-cli-print | jq '.findings[] | select(.severity == "critical")'` — the critical findings only, for a pipeline
- `sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --json-analyze --no-cli-print | jq '.complete'` — whether the capture decoded fully. `false` means every count in the analysis is a floor, so do not trust a clean-looking verdict
- `sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --yang-analyze --no-cli-print > analysis.json` — the capture analysis as a YANG instance document. `yanglint -t data sipnab-diagnosis@2026-10-09.yang analysis.json` validates it
- `sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --json-analyze --yang-analyze --no-cli-print` — both encodings of ONE analysis, one line each: the same findings, the same counts, the same `rank` order
- `sipnab --print-yang-module > sipnab-diagnosis@2026-10-09.yang` — save the YANG module this build's RFC 7951 export validates against, under the file name [RFC 7950](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7950.html) gives it, for `yanglint` or `pyang`
- `sipnab --print-yang-module | pyang -f tree` — the shape of the capture analysis as a YANG tree: every node, its type, and which are lists
- `sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --json-dialogs --no-cli-print --quiet | jq -c 'select(.state == "Failed")'` — one line per failed call, each carrying the code that failed it, instead of every message of every failed dialog
- `sudo sipnab -d eth0 -N --json-dialogs --no-cli-print --line-buffer > calls.ndjson` — record one summary object per call from live traffic, flushed per line for a downstream collector
- `sudo sipnab -N -d eth0 --node-name sbc-edge-1 --mcp --mcp-transport http` — one node of a federated setup, naming itself so an agent can attribute each answer to this box rather than another
- `sudo sipnab -N -d eth0 --node-name pbx-core-2 --report` — override the hostname on a box whose real name should not travel, while still labeling the capture
- `sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --json-pretty > messages.json` — export every SIP message from a capture as pretty-printed JSON, each payload whole
- `sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --show-empty --payload-limit 200` — print every message with its headers, each payload cut at 200 bytes
- `sudo sipnab -d eth0 -N --json-pretty --group-by method --line-buffer > live.json` — stream live SIP traffic as pretty-printed JSON grouped by method, flushing after each line for downstream tooling
- `sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --text-dump --hexdump --proto-number --color never` — dump raw SIP text with hex payloads and IANA protocol numbers, uncolored for log archiving
- `sudo sipnab -d eth0 -N --match REGISTER --after 2 --text-dump --line-buffer --color always` — follow live REGISTER traffic in real time, printing raw text plus 2 messages of context after each match
- `sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --show-empty --delta-time --hexdump --group-by call-id` — review a capture with per-message delta times, empty-bodied messages included, and hex dumps grouped per call
- `sudo sipnab -d eth0 -N --match OPTIONS --after 5 --show-empty --proto-number --payload-limit 256` — inspect OPTIONS keepalives with 5 messages of trailing context, empty bodies shown, and display capped at 256 payload bytes
- `sudo sipnab -N -d eth0 --from-to-mode host-port --wireshark` — capture live with host:port From/To columns and print a Wireshark display filter when capture ends
- `sipnab -I capture.pcap --from-to-mode user-host-port` — browse an existing capture in the TUI with full user@host:port From/To columns
- `sipnab -N -I busy-day.pcap --group-by call-id --max-groups 250000 --no-cli-print` — group a capture holding more calls than the shipped 100000-key cap, instead of taking the first hundred thousand and a warning naming how many keys sipnab turned away
- `sipnab -N -I busy-day.pcap --group-by from --max-grouped-messages 2000000 --json` — regroup a large capture by caller with room for every message, keeping the output one valid JSON object per line
- `sipnab -N -I untrusted.pcap --group-by call-id --max-groups 500 --max-grouped-messages 5000 --no-cli-print` — group a capture from outside your network under a tight pair of caps, so an attacker-chosen Call-ID cannot buy more memory than you allowed
- `sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --export-vcon '1-1966@10.0.2.20' > call.vcon` -- hand one observed dialog to a conversation-data pipeline as a vCon. The container names sipnab as an observer party and records what this capture missed
- `sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --export-vcon '1-1966@10.0.2.20' --vcon-out ./call.vcon --no-cli-print` -- the same container to a file, with the run otherwise silent. Use this form in a script: a path sipnab cannot write fails the run with a non-zero exit
- `sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --export-vcon-when "state == 'Failed'" --export-vcon-dir ./failed/ --content-deny-header X-No-Record` -- the same failures, minus any call whose signaling carries an `X-No-Record` header
- `sipnab -N -I ./captures --export-vcon-when 'duration > 30' --export-vcon-dir ./long/ --content-deny-header Privacy` -- leave out every call carrying a `Privacy` header, whatever its value: `Privacy: none` suppresses exactly as `Privacy: id` does
- `sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --export-vcon-when "state == 'Failed'" --export-vcon-dir ./failed/` -- one container per failed dialog, without naming each Call-ID. A capture where nothing failed writes nothing and says so on stderr
- `sipnab -N -I ./captures --export-vcon-when "duration > 30 and rtp.codec == 'PCMU'" --export-vcon-dir ./long-g711/ --no-cli-print` -- the predicate is the filter language, so the conditions that narrow a report also choose which calls get a container
- `sipnab -N -I ./captures --export-vcon '1-1966@10.0.2.20' --vcon-out ./captures/1-1966.vcon` -- refused before anything opens a writer: `--vcon-out` may not name a path inside a directory this run reads, the same rule `-O` follows
- `sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --export-vcon '1-1966@10.0.2.20' | jq -r '.analysis[0].body.capture_completeness.note'` -- read the completeness note before the contents. The analysis `body` declares `encoding: "json"`, so `jq` indexes into it directly. The note says what sipnab read and what it dropped, from this run's own counters
- `sipnab -N -I ./captures --export-vcon-when 'duration > 30' --export-vcon-dir ./long/ --vcon-max-inline-media 64` -- carry audio up to 64 MiB per container, for a store you know accepts containers that large
- `sipnab -N -I ./captures --export-vcon-when 'response_code >= 200' --export-vcon-dir ./calls/ --vcon-max-inline-media 0 --retain-audio` -- keep the containers and inline none of the audio. Each container's completeness caveat records that sipnab refused the audio
- `sipnab -N -I ./captures --export-vcon-when "state == 'Failed'" --export-vcon-dir ./failed/ --content-deny-header X-No-Record --content-deny-tombstone` -- write an identity-only container for each denied dialog instead of nothing, so a consumer can tell a withheld call from one that never happened. It carries no message trace, no media and no bodies, and declares `redacted` with `type` alone
- `sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --export-vcon-when 'duration > 0' --export-vcon-dir ./out/ --content-deny-header Privacy --content-deny-tombstone` -- write a tombstone for every call carrying a `Privacy` header. A tombstone reveals that the call existed; leave the flag off when the header means the call must leave no trace
- `sipnab -N -I ./captures --export-vcon-when 'duration > 30' --export-vcon-dir ./long/ --vcon-digest > SHA256SUMS` -- record what sipnab wrote. The digests go to stdout in `sha256sum` format and the progress summary stays on stderr, so the redirect captures only the digests
- `sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --export-vcon-when 'duration > 0' --export-vcon-dir ./out/ --vcon-digest | tee ./out/SHA256SUMS` -- keep the digests beside the containers they describe. Each line names the bare file name, so the directory verifies wherever it is later moved
- `cd ./long/ && sha256sum -c ../SHA256SUMS` -- verify the containers later with the standard tool. The digest covers the bytes sipnab wrote, not the copy a store holds after it adds its own fields
- `sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --tshark-filter 'sip.Method == "INVITE"'` — print a tshark-compatible display filter for the INVITE traffic in a capture. sipnab hands the expression to tshark's `-Y` verbatim, so it takes WIRESHARK display-filter syntax rather than sipnab's `--filter` DSL: `sip.Method`, not `method`. Quote the whole expression in single quotes so the inner double quotes survive the shell


## Queries

A query flag answers one question about the capture after sipnab has read
it, then exits. Each one:

- counts only the dialogs the run's filter admits: `--filter`, the
  [diagnostic aliases](#diagnostic-aliases) and `--since`/`--until`;
- makes the run headless, as `--call-report` does, so `-N` is optional;
- prints a table, or the same table in Markdown under `--markdown`;
- under `--json`, prints one JSON object on the last line of stdout, with the
  shape the matching REST route returns. `--json-pretty` prints the same
  object indented.

Add `--no-cli-print` to leave out the per-message lines, and `--quiet` to leave
out the end-of-run summary on stderr.

| Flag | Value | Default | Since | Description |
|------|-------|---------|-------|-------------|
| `--timeline` | `[=<SECONDS>]` | `60` | 0.5.230 | Print how many dialogs opened in each interval of this many seconds, oldest first. Intervals align to the epoch, and an empty interval shows a count of zero. `--json` prints the shape of `GET /v1/timeline`. `0` exits 2. A span of more than 100,000 intervals exits 1 |
| `--count-by` | `<DIMENSION>` | | 0.5.230 | Count the dialogs by one dimension, largest first: `state`, `response_code`, `method`, `from.user`, `to.user`, `ua`, `src.ip`, `dst.ip` or `rtp.codec`. `--json` prints the shape of `GET /v1/aggregate`. Any other dimension exits 2 |
| `--rates-by` | `<DIMENSION>` | | 0.5.230 | Print the carrier metrics of each value of one dimension: ASR, NER, ACD, post-dial delay, the tenth-percentile MOS and the retransmit rate. Takes every `--count-by` dimension, plus `to_domain`, `hour` and `next_hop`. `--json` prints the shape of `GET /v1/dialogs/rates`. Any other dimension exits 2 |
| `--talkers` | `<BY>` | | 0.5.230 | Rank the busiest participants, most dialogs first: by sending address (`ip`), `User-Agent` or `Server` banner (`ua`), or the dialed number's leading digits (`prefix`). `--json` prints the shape of `GET /v1/talkers`. Any other value exits 2 |
| `--prefix-digits` | `<N>` | `4` | 0.5.230 | How many leading digits `--talkers prefix` ranks by. Needs `--talkers`; only `prefix` reads it. `0` exits 2 |
| `--call-tree` | `<CALL-ID>` | | 0.5.231 | Print every leg of one call as a tree across B2BUA, SBC and PBX hops, with the strategy that matched each leg. `--json` prints the shape of `GET /v1/dialogs/{call_id}/tree`. A Call-ID the run did not track exits 1 |
| `--correlate` | `<CALL-ID>` | | 0.5.231 | Print the other legs of one call and the strategy that matched each: an identifier the legs share, or a timing guess. `--json` prints the shape of `GET /v1/dialogs/{call_id}/correlated`. A Call-ID the run did not track exits 1 |
| `--compare-dialogs` | `<CALL-ID-A> <CALL-ID-B>` | | 0.5.231 | Put two calls side by side: state, final response code, message count and methods, with the fields that differ marked, and each call's diagnosis hints. `--json` prints the shape of `GET /v1/dialogs/compare`. A Call-ID the run did not track exits 1 |
| `--endpoint-ip` | `<IP>` | | 0.5.231 | Print everything one address did: dialogs by method and state, messages sent and received, call outcomes, registration, banners, the signaling stack, media, and the most recent dialogs. `--json` prints the shape of `GET /v1/endpoints`. An address that does not parse exits 2 |
| `--endpoint-user` | `<USER>` | | 0.5.231 | Print everything one SIP user did, matched against the user part of each dialog's From and To: the `--endpoint-ip` rollup without the message counts. `--json` prints the shape of `GET /v1/endpoints`. Not with `--endpoint-ip` |
| `--export-audio` | `<CALL-ID>` | | 0.5.231 | Write one call's decoded RTP audio to a WAV file, and print the export summary. Holds the call's audio payload for the run, as `--retain-audio` does. A Call-ID the capture does not hold, a call with nothing to decode, or an existing file exits 1 |
| `--export-audio-out` | `<FILE>` | the Call-ID with `.wav` | 0.5.231 | The file `--export-audio` writes. It must not exist. Needs `--export-audio` |
| `--vcon-validate` | `<FILE>` | | 0.5.231 | Check a vCon container file against sipnab's vendored schema and print the verdict and every finding. Exits 0 when valid and 3 when invalid, and 1 when sipnab cannot read or check the file. Needs no `-I`. `--json` prints the shape of `POST /v1/vcon/validate`. Needs the `vcon` feature |
| `--compare-captures` | `<A> <B>` | | 0.5.231 | Compare two capture files: for each dimension, the dialogs per value in A (the baseline) and B, and the change, largest movement first. Needs no `-I`. `--json` prints the shape of `GET /v1/captures/compare`. The same file twice exits 2; a file that yields no dialogs exits 1 |
| `--compare-dimensions` | `<DIMENSIONS>` | `state,response_code` | 0.5.231 | The dimensions `--compare-captures` diffs, comma-separated, from the `--count-by` set. Any other exits 2. Needs `--compare-captures` |
| `--find-in-files` | `<PATH>...` | | 0.5.231 | Find which capture files hold the dialogs the run's filter selects (`--filter`, a diagnostic alias, `--since`/`--until`). A directory stands for the capture files directly in it. Exits 0 when it read every file and 1 when it could not; with no filter it exits 2. `--json` prints the `sweep` the MCP tool `find_in_captures` reports |
| `--expect` | `<FILE>` | | 0.5.231 | Judge the capture against the rules of an expectation suite (`sipnab.expect.toml`), print each rule's verdict, and exit with the suite's: `0` every rule that ran passed, `1` a rule failed, `2` no rule ran. A suite sipnab cannot read, or one holding a rule the evaluator refuses, exits 2 before sipnab reads the capture. `--json` prints the report the MCP tool `evaluate_expectations` returns |
| `--relay-holdings` | -- | | 0.5.231 | Ask the relay named by `--rtpengine-control` which calls it holds right now, print their Call-IDs, and exit. Asking transmits one `list` request, so it needs a live source (`-d` or `-L`): on `-I` it asks nothing and exits 2. It runs before the capture opens and answers nothing else. Exits 0 with the list, and 1 when the relay did not answer (`unreachable`), declined (`refused`) or sent a reply sipnab cannot trust (`suspect`). `--json` prints the body of `GET /v1/relay/holdings`, those classifications included. See [Ask the relay which calls it holds](#ask-the-relay-which-calls-it-holds). Feature: `native` |
| `--relay-holdings-max` | `<CALLS>` | `32` | 0.5.231 | The most Call-IDs `--relay-holdings` asks the relay for, REST's `max_calls`. When the relay returns that many it may hold more, and the answer says so (`truncated` under `--json`). Needs `--relay-holdings`; `0` exits 2 |
| `--top` | `<N>` | `50` | 0.5.230 | How many rows `--count-by`, `--rates-by` or `--talkers` keeps, or `--compare-captures` keeps per dimension, or how many recent dialogs `--endpoint-ip` or `--endpoint-user` lists. One line sums or counts the rest, as `other_count` or `truncated` does under `--json`. Needs one of those flags; `0` exits 2 |

### Call volume over time

Count the calls that opened in each five-second interval:

```sh
sipnab -I tests/pcap-samples/sip-problem-call.pcap --timeline=5 --no-cli-print --quiet
```

```text
Call volume: 3 buckets of 5 s, 5 dialogs
Start                      Dialogs
----------------------------------
2023-11-14T22:13:20+00:00  2
2023-11-14T22:13:25+00:00  2
2023-11-14T22:13:30+00:00  1
```

Give the width after `=`. A bare `--timeline` uses 60-second intervals. An
interval with no call in it shows a count of zero, so a gap in traffic shows
as a row of zeros.

One histogram holds at most 100,000 intervals. When the calls span more
intervals of the width than that, sipnab prints no histogram, writes on stderr
how many intervals the span needs and a width that fits, and exits 1. Run it
again with that width or a wider one.

Count only the failed calls:

```sh
sipnab -I tests/pcap-samples/sip-problem-call.pcap --timeline=5 --no-cli-print --quiet --filter 'state == Failed'
```

```text
Call volume: 3 buckets of 5 s, 4 dialogs
Start                      Dialogs
----------------------------------
2023-11-14T22:13:20+00:00  1
2023-11-14T22:13:25+00:00  2
2023-11-14T22:13:30+00:00  1
```

Read the answer as JSON. `capture_identity` names the run that produced it,
so it differs from run to run. `jq` drops it here:

```sh
sipnab -I tests/pcap-samples/sip-problem-call.pcap --timeline --json --no-cli-print --quiet | jq -c 'del(.capture_identity)'
```

```json
{"schema_version":1,"buckets":[{"start":"2023-11-14T22:13:00+00:00","bucket_seconds":60,"dialogs":5}],"returned":1,"bucket_seconds":60}
```

The REST route `GET /v1/timeline?bucket_seconds=60` and the MCP tool
`timeline` answer the same question about a loaded capture.

### Dialogs by one dimension

Count the calls in a capture by their state:

```sh
sipnab -I tests/pcap-samples/sip-problem-call.pcap --count-by state --no-cli-print --quiet
```

```text
Dialogs by state: 2 values, 5 dialogs
Value      Dialogs
------------------
Failed     4
Completed  1
```

The values are largest first, and values with the same count are in
alphabetical order. A dialog with no value for the dimension counts under
`(none)`.

Keep only the first values with `--top`. The last line sums the rest:

```sh
sipnab -I tests/pcap-samples/sip-problem-call.pcap --count-by response_code --top 2 --no-cli-print --quiet
```

```text
Dialogs by response_code: 5 values, 5 dialogs
Value  Dialogs
--------------
200    1
404    1
Other: 3 dialogs in 3 values past --top 2
```

Count one dimension at a time. To count a subset of the calls, narrow the run
with `--filter` instead of adding a second dimension. Count who the failed calls
were for, keeping three:

```sh
sipnab -I tests/pcap-samples/sip-problem-call.pcap --count-by to.user --filter 'state == Failed' --top 3 --no-cli-print --quiet
```

```text
Dialogs by to.user: 4 values, 4 dialogs
Value  Dialogs
--------------
dave   1
frank  1
heidi  1
Other: 1 dialog in 1 value past --top 3
```

Read the answer as JSON. `jq` drops `capture_identity`, which names the run:

```sh
sipnab -I tests/pcap-samples/sip-problem-call.pcap --count-by state --json --no-cli-print --quiet | jq -c 'del(.capture_identity)'
```

```json
{"schema_version":1,"group_by":"state","buckets":[{"value":"Failed","count":4},{"value":"Completed","count":1}],"other_count":0,"distinct_values":2,"total_matched":5}
```

The REST route `GET /v1/aggregate?by=state` and the MCP tool
`aggregate_dialogs` answer the same question about a loaded capture.

### Carrier metrics by one dimension

Print the answer-seizure ratio (ASR), network effectiveness ratio (NER),
average call duration (ACD), post-dial delay (PDD), the tenth-percentile MOS and
the retransmit rate for each call state:

```sh
sipnab -I tests/pcap-samples/sip-problem-call.pcap --rates-by state --no-cli-print --quiet
```

```text
Carrier metrics by state: 2 values, 5 dialogs
Value      Dialogs  asr  ner  acd   pdd_p50  pdd_p95  mos_p10  retransmit_rate
------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Failed     4        0    50   -     -        -        -        0
Completed  1        100  100  17.9  850      850      -        0
Units: asr percent, ner percent, acd seconds, pdd_p50 milliseconds, pdd_p95 milliseconds, mos_p10 mos, retransmit_rate retransmissions per dialog
-: the group's population could not support the figure; --json names why in not_grounded
```

- `asr` and `ner` are percentages of the INVITEs that reached a final
  response. NER also credits the outcomes the far end decided, such as busy
  and decline, so it can be higher than ASR.
- `acd` is the mean conversation time of the calls answered and torn down
  inside the capture.
- `-` means the group holds no call to compute the figure from. Here the far
  end answered none of the failed calls, so that group has no ACD.

`--rates-by` takes every `--count-by` dimension, plus `to_domain`, `hour` and
`next_hop`. `--top` keeps the largest groups and sums the rest:

```sh
sipnab -I tests/pcap-samples/sip-problem-call.pcap --rates-by response_code --top 2 --no-cli-print --quiet
```

```text
Carrier metrics by response_code: 5 values, 5 dialogs
Value  Dialogs  asr  ner  acd   pdd_p50  pdd_p95  mos_p10  retransmit_rate
--------------------------------------------------------------------------
200    1        100  100  17.9  850      850      -        0
404    1        0    0    -     -        -        -        0
Other: 3 dialogs in 3 values past --top 2
Units: asr percent, ner percent, acd seconds, pdd_p50 milliseconds, pdd_p95 milliseconds, mos_p10 mos, retransmit_rate retransmissions per dialog
-: the group's population could not support the figure; --json names why in not_grounded
```

Under `--json`, each group carries its population, and `not_grounded` says why
each `null` figure is missing:

```sh
sipnab -I tests/pcap-samples/sip-problem-call.pcap --rates-by state --json --no-cli-print --quiet | jq -c '.groups[] | {value, asr: .metrics.asr, ner: .metrics.ner, acd_why: .not_grounded.acd}'
```

```json
{"value":"Failed","asr":0.0,"ner":50.0,"acd_why":"no call in this group was both answered and torn down inside the capture, so no conversation was timed"}
{"value":"Completed","asr":100.0,"ner":100.0,"acd_why":null}
```

The REST route `GET /v1/dialogs/rates?by=state` and the MCP tool
`group_dialogs` answer the same question about a loaded capture.

### The busiest talkers

Rank the addresses that sent the most dialogs, keeping three:

```sh
sipnab -I tests/pcap-samples/sip-problem-call.pcap --talkers ip --top 3 --no-cli-print --quiet
```

```text
Talkers by ip: 10 talkers, 5 dialogs
Talker      Dialogs  Messages  INVITEs  Answered  Failed  Share%
----------------------------------------------------------------
192.0.2.20  1        4         1        1         0       20
192.0.2.10  1        3         1        1         0       20
192.0.2.30  1        2         1        0         1       20
Other: 7 talkers past --top 3
```

Among talkers with the same number of dialogs, the one with more messages comes
first, then the lower key.
`Share%` is the share of the counted dialogs each talker took part in. A
dialog counts for every participant, so the shares can add up to more than
100.

Rank the dialed numbers by their first five digits:

```sh
sipnab -I tests/pcap-samples/Asterisk_ZFONE_XLITE.pcap --talkers prefix --prefix-digits 5 --no-cli-print --quiet
```

```text
Talkers by prefix: 2 talkers, 5 dialogs
Talker  Dialogs  Messages  INVITEs  Answered  Failed  Share%
------------------------------------------------------------
10009   3        10        0        0         0       60
10008   2        17        1        1         0       40
```

`prefix` uses four digits when `--prefix-digits` is not given. Four digits put
both numbers under one prefix:

```sh
sipnab -I tests/pcap-samples/Asterisk_ZFONE_XLITE.pcap --talkers prefix --prefix-digits 4 --no-cli-print --quiet
```

```text
Talkers by prefix: 1 talker, 5 dialogs
Talker  Dialogs  Messages  INVITEs  Answered  Failed  Share%
------------------------------------------------------------
1000    5        27        1        1         0       100
```

Rank the software by its `User-Agent` or `Server` banner:

```sh
sipnab -I tests/pcap-samples/Asterisk_ZFONE_XLITE.pcap --talkers ua --no-cli-print --quiet
```

```text
Talkers by ua: 2 talkers, 5 dialogs
Talker                            Dialogs  Messages  INVITEs  Answered  Failed  Share%
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
X-Lite 4 release 4.0 stamp 58832  4        9         1        1         0       80
Asterisk PBX 1.6.0.6              2        4         1        1         0       40
```

The REST route `GET /v1/talkers?by=ip` and the MCP tool `top_talkers` answer
the same question about a loaded capture.

### Every leg of one call

A call through a B2BUA, an SBC or a PBX is several dialogs, one per hop. Name
one of them to see the others as a tree:

```sh
sipnab -I tests/pcap-samples/b2bua-asterisk.pcapng --call-tree b2bua-caller-synth@203.0.113.1 --no-cli-print --quiet
```

```text
Call tree from b2bua-caller-synth@203.0.113.1: 2 legs, depth 1, 28 messages, 1 timing guess
Leg                                   Strategy          Score  Match  Followed
------------------------------------------------------------------------------
b2bua-caller-synth@203.0.113.1        root              -      -      yes
  b2bua-leg-synth@203.0.113.101:5060  timing_heuristic  50     guess  no
```

- Each hop indents the leg two more spaces.
- `Match` is `identifier` when the legs share an identifier (`X-Call-ID`,
  `Session-ID`, the SDP origin, P-Charging-Vector or a Via branch), and
  `guess` when only their timing ties them.
- `Followed` is `no` on a guess: sipnab lists the leg but does not look for
  that leg's own matches, so one wrong guess does not pull in unrelated calls.

The Call-ID must match exactly, and `--report` lists the ones the run holds. Under
`--json`, each leg names its parent and depth:

```sh
sipnab -I tests/pcap-samples/b2bua-asterisk.pcapng --call-tree b2bua-caller-synth@203.0.113.1 --json --no-cli-print --quiet | jq -c '.legs[] | {call_id, depth, strategy, followed}'
```

```json
{"call_id":"b2bua-caller-synth@203.0.113.1","depth":0,"strategy":null,"followed":true}
{"call_id":"b2bua-leg-synth@203.0.113.101:5060","depth":1,"strategy":"timing_heuristic","followed":false}
```

The REST route `GET /v1/dialogs/{call_id}/tree` and the MCP tool
`get_call_tree` walk the same tree.

### The other legs of one call

List the calls sipnab ties to one call, and how:

```sh
sipnab -I tests/pcap-samples/sip-rtp-g711.pcap --correlate 1-1966@10.0.2.20 --no-cli-print --quiet
```

```text
Legs correlated with 1-1966@10.0.2.20: 1 leg
Leg               Strategy    Score  Match       Gap ms
-------------------------------------------------------
1-1968@10.0.2.20  sdp_origin  90     identifier  -
```

The two calls carry the same SDP origin, an identifier, so the score is high.
When no identifier ties two legs and only their timing does, the match is a
guess, `Gap ms` shows how far apart the two calls began, and the answer says
so:

```sh
sipnab -I tests/pcap-samples/b2bua-asterisk.pcapng --correlate b2bua-caller-synth@203.0.113.1 --no-cli-print --quiet
```

```text
Legs correlated with b2bua-caller-synth@203.0.113.1: 1 leg
Leg                                 Strategy          Score  Match  Gap ms
--------------------------------------------------------------------------
b2bua-leg-synth@203.0.113.101:5060  timing_heuristic  50     guess  3
Every leg here is a timing guess: no identifier ties it to this call.
```

A call that no other leg ties to prints no rows and exits 0. A Call-ID the run
did not track exits 1. `--call-tree` follows these matches leg by leg. The
REST route `GET /v1/dialogs/{call_id}/correlated` and the MCP tool
`find_correlated` answer for one leg as this flag does.

### Two calls side by side

Compare a call that failed with another, to see what they have in common:

```sh
sipnab -I tests/pcap-samples/sip-problem-call.pcap --compare-dialogs busy-3a2b1c@192.0.2.30 unavail-4e5f60@192.0.2.50 --no-cli-print --quiet
```

```text
Comparing busy-3a2b1c@192.0.2.30 (A) with unavail-4e5f60@192.0.2.50 (B): 1 field differs
Field              A           B           Differs
--------------------------------------------------
state              Failed      Failed      
final_status_code  486         503         differs
msg_count          4           4           
methods            ACK,INVITE  ACK,INVITE  
Hints for A: Call failed: 486 Busy Here.
Hints for B: Call failed: 503 Service Unavailable.
```

Give the two Call-IDs after the flag, each matched exactly. sipnab compares the
four fields in the table, and `differs` marks the ones that are not the same.
It lists the hints for each call without comparing them.

Under `--json`, `differences` names the fields that differ:

```sh
sipnab -I tests/pcap-samples/sip-problem-call.pcap --compare-dialogs completed-9f8e7d@192.0.2.10 busy-3a2b1c@192.0.2.30 --json --no-cli-print --quiet | jq -c '{differences, a: .a.final_status_code, b: .b.final_status_code}'
```

```json
{"differences":["state","final_status_code","msg_count","methods"],"a":200,"b":486}
```

The REST route `GET /v1/dialogs/compare`, given the two Call-IDs as `a` and `b`,
and the MCP tool `compare_dialogs` compare the same fields.

### Everything one endpoint did

Name an address to see what it did in the capture, keeping its three most
recent dialogs:

```sh
sipnab -I tests/pcap-samples/Asterisk_ZFONE_XLITE.pcap --endpoint-ip 192.168.10.2 --top 3 --no-cli-print --quiet
```

```text
Endpoint ip 192.168.10.2: 5 dialogs
Dialogs by method: INVITE 1, OPTIONS 1, REGISTER 1, SUBSCRIBE 2
Dialogs by state: Completed 2, Registered 1, Terminated 2
Messages: 14 sent, 13 received
Calls: 1 INVITE, 1 with a final response, 0 failed (0%); final responses: 200 x1
Registration: 1 dialog, 1 succeeded, 0 failed, 0 authentication loops
Banners: User-Agent Asterisk PBX 1.6.0.6 (4)
Signaling stack: chan_sip, 2 of 3 observations agree, from 4 requests
Media: 1 stream (0 orphaned), 2 packets, 0 lost, max jitter 0.03 ms, codecs PCMU
Most recent dialogs (3 of 5):
Call-ID                                       Method     State       Final  Started
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
ZDYzOWVlNjEwM2NjZTBjNzliNmM1ZTNiOGZjNWFhN2E.  INVITE     Completed   200    2010-09-27T07:12:58.755873+00:00
MDA3MzcwMWQxNmNhNTBmMTZiNGNkY2JjYjZkNzViZTM.  SUBSCRIBE  Terminated  404    2010-09-27T07:12:50.010873+00:00
OGY5ZTk4MzFkYzZhM2FlYjNjNTA3ZTM2ZWY0YzI1ODA.  SUBSCRIBE  Terminated  404    2010-09-27T07:12:50.003249+00:00
```

- `Messages` counts what the address sent and what other hosts sent to it.
- `Banners` are the `User-Agent` and `Server` values it sent.
- `Signaling stack` names the SIP library its requests look built by, and how
  many of three observations (the Via branch, the From tag and the Call-ID)
  agree.
- The counts cover every dialog the address took part in. `--filter` does not
  narrow them, and `--top` bounds only the list of recent dialogs.

Name a SIP user instead, matched against the user part of each dialog's From
and To:

```sh
sipnab -I tests/pcap-samples/Asterisk_ZFONE_XLITE.pcap --endpoint-user 10009 --top 2 --no-cli-print --quiet
```

```text
Endpoint user 10009: 5 dialogs
Dialogs by method: INVITE 1, OPTIONS 1, REGISTER 1, SUBSCRIBE 2
Dialogs by state: Completed 2, Registered 1, Terminated 2
Calls: 1 INVITE, 1 with a final response, 0 failed (0%); final responses: 200 x1
Registration: 1 dialog, 1 succeeded, 0 failed, 0 authentication loops
Banners: none
Signaling stack: not inferred
Media: 3 streams (0 orphaned), 997 packets, 370 lost, max jitter 0.56 ms, codecs PCMU
Most recent dialogs (2 of 5):
Call-ID                                       Method     State       Final  Started
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
ZDYzOWVlNjEwM2NjZTBjNzliNmM1ZTNiOGZjNWFhN2E.  INVITE     Completed   200    2010-09-27T07:12:58.755873+00:00
MDA3MzcwMWQxNmNhNTBmMTZiNGNkY2JjYjZkNzViZTM.  SUBSCRIBE  Terminated  404    2010-09-27T07:12:50.010873+00:00
```

A user has no message counts, because messages belong to an address. Under
`--json`, the answer has the fields `GET /v1/endpoints` returns:

```sh
sipnab -I tests/pcap-samples/Asterisk_ZFONE_XLITE.pcap --endpoint-ip 192.168.10.2 --json --no-cli-print --quiet | jq -c '{dialogs, messages_sent, messages_received, calls: .calls.invites}'
```

```json
{"dialogs":5,"messages_sent":14,"messages_received":13,"calls":1}
```

```sh
sipnab -I tests/pcap-samples/Asterisk_ZFONE_XLITE.pcap --endpoint-user 10009 --json --no-cli-print --quiet | jq -c '{dialogs, by_method, codecs: .streams.codecs}'
```

```json
{"dialogs":5,"by_method":{"INVITE":1,"OPTIONS":1,"REGISTER":1,"SUBSCRIBE":2},"codecs":["PCMU"]}
```

The REST route `GET /v1/endpoints`, given `ip` or `user`, and the MCP tool
`describe_endpoint` describe the same endpoint.

### One call's audio as a WAV file

Write the decoded audio of one call to a file:

```sh
sipnab -I tests/pcap-samples/sip-rtp-g711.pcap --export-audio 1-1966@10.0.2.20 --no-cli-print --quiet
```

```text
Exported 8.5s of mu-law audio (425 frames, PCMU/8000Hz) to 1-1966_10.0.2.20.wav — PARTIAL: media in only ONE direction reached this capture; no stream going the other way was observed. That may be a one-way call, or a capture point that only sees one leg -- this file cannot tell you which.
```

- The file is in the current directory, named after the Call-ID with every
  character other than a letter, a digit, `-`, `_` or `.` replaced by `_`.
- One stream makes a mono file and two make a stereo one.
- The summary says when the file holds less than the call. Here the capture
  saw the audio in one direction only, so the summary says `PARTIAL`. The
  file carries the same note inside it.
- sipnab does not keep audio unless asked. `--export-audio` asks, for this run,
  as `--retain-audio` does.

Name the file with `--export-audio-out`:

```sh
sipnab -I tests/pcap-samples/sip-rtp-g711.pcap --export-audio 1-1966@10.0.2.20 --export-audio-out call.wav --no-cli-print --quiet
```

```text
Exported 8.5s of mu-law audio (425 frames, PCMU/8000Hz) to call.wav — PARTIAL: media in only ONE direction reached this capture; no stream going the other way was observed. That may be a one-way call, or a capture point that only sees one leg -- this file cannot tell you which.
```

sipnab never replaces an existing file: if the file is there, the run exits 1
and leaves it as it was. Under `--json`, the answer names the file and what it
holds:

```sh
sipnab -I tests/pcap-samples/sip-rtp-g711.pcap --export-audio 1-1966@10.0.2.20 --export-audio-out call.wav --json --no-cli-print --quiet
```

```json
{"schema_version":1,"path":"call.wav","summary":"Exported 8.5s of mu-law audio (425 frames, PCMU/8000Hz) to call.wav — PARTIAL: media in only ONE direction reached this capture; no stream going the other way was observed. That may be a one-way call, or a capture point that only sees one leg -- this file cannot tell you which.","partial":true,"dialog_seen":true,"duration_secs":8.5,"sample_rate":8000,"channels":1,"bytes":136516}
```

`partial` and `dialog_seen` are the two facts the REST route
`GET /v1/dialogs/{call_id}/audio` sends as headers beside the same WAV bytes.
The MCP tool `export_audio` writes the same file into its file root.

### Check a vCon file against the schema

Check that a vCon container conforms to the draft-ietf-vcon-vcon-core-04 schema
sipnab ships:

```sh
sipnab --vcon-validate tests/fixtures/vcon/sip-rtp-g711-1966.vcon.json
```

```text
tests/fixtures/vcon/sip-rtp-g711-1966.vcon.json: valid against https://ietf.org/vcon/schemas/unsigned-vcon.json
```

`--vcon-validate` reads the file and exits. It needs no capture, so give no
`-I`. For a signed or encrypted container, sipnab checks the unsigned vCon
inside.

The exit status is the verdict, so a CI step can stop on a container that does
not conform:

- `0`: the container is valid.
- `3`: the container is invalid. sipnab prints one row per finding: the JSON
  Pointer to the value, the schema keyword that refused it, and why.
- `1`: sipnab could not check it: the file is missing, it is not JSON, it is
  JSON but not an object, or a `critical` extension forbids reading it.

Under `--json`, the answer is the one `POST /v1/vcon/validate` returns:

```sh
sipnab --vcon-validate tests/fixtures/vcon/sip-rtp-g711-1966.vcon.json --json
```

```json
{"schema_version":2,"verdict":"valid","schema_id":"https://ietf.org/vcon/schemas/unsigned-vcon.json","schema_path":"tests/schemas/vcon.schema.json","errors":[]}
```

The MCP tool `validate_vcon` runs the same check on a container an agent
passes it.

### Compare two captures

Hold one capture against another, such as today's against yesterday's, and see
what moved:

```sh
sipnab --compare-captures tests/pcap-samples/sip-problem-call.pcap tests/pcap-samples/sip-rtp-g711.pcap
```

```text
A: tests/pcap-samples/sip-problem-call.pcap, 23 packets, 5 dialogs, 0 streams
B: tests/pcap-samples/sip-rtp-g711.pcap, 852 packets, 2 dialogs, 2 streams

By state:
Value      A  B  Change
-----------------------
Failed     4  0  -4
InCall     0  1  +1
Completed  1  1  0

By response_code:
Value  A  B  Change
-------------------
200    1  2  +1
404    1  0  -1
486    1  0  -1
503    1  0  -1
603    1  0  -1

'tests/pcap-samples/sip-problem-call.pcap' (5 dialogs) is the baseline; 'tests/pcap-samples/sip-rtp-g711.pcap' (2 dialogs) is held against it, so delta is b minus a.
```

- The first file, A, is the baseline. `Change` is B minus A, so a negative
  change means the value became rarer.
- Each dimension lists the values that moved most first.
- sipnab reads both files and exits. It needs no capture, so give no `-I`.

Choose the dimensions with `--compare-dimensions`, and keep fewer values with
`--top`. An `(other)` row sums the values past the cut:

```sh
sipnab --compare-captures tests/pcap-samples/sip-problem-call.pcap tests/pcap-samples/sip-rtp-g711.pcap --compare-dimensions method,ua --top 1
```

```text
A: tests/pcap-samples/sip-problem-call.pcap, 23 packets, 5 dialogs, 0 streams
B: tests/pcap-samples/sip-rtp-g711.pcap, 852 packets, 2 dialogs, 2 streams

By method:
Value   A  B  Change
--------------------
INVITE  5  2  -3

By ua:
Value    A  B  Change
---------------------
(none)   5  0  -5
(other)  0  2  +2

'tests/pcap-samples/sip-problem-call.pcap' (5 dialogs) is the baseline; 'tests/pcap-samples/sip-rtp-g711.pcap' (2 dialogs) is held against it, so delta is b minus a.
```

`(none)` counts the dialogs with no value for the dimension. Here no call in A
carried a `User-Agent`. Compare the codecs the two captures carried:

```sh
sipnab --compare-captures tests/pcap-samples/sip-problem-call.pcap tests/pcap-samples/sip-rtp-g711.pcap --compare-dimensions rtp.codec
```

```text
A: tests/pcap-samples/sip-problem-call.pcap, 23 packets, 5 dialogs, 0 streams
B: tests/pcap-samples/sip-rtp-g711.pcap, 852 packets, 2 dialogs, 2 streams

By rtp.codec:
Value   A  B  Change
--------------------
(none)  5  0  -5
PCMA    0  1  +1
PCMU    0  1  +1

'tests/pcap-samples/sip-problem-call.pcap' (5 dialogs) is the baseline; 'tests/pcap-samples/sip-rtp-g711.pcap' (2 dialogs) is held against it, so delta is b minus a.
```

Under `--json`, the answer is the one `GET /v1/captures/compare` returns. List
the values that moved in each dimension:

```sh
sipnab --compare-captures tests/pcap-samples/sip-problem-call.pcap tests/pcap-samples/sip-rtp-g711.pcap --json | jq -c '[.dimensions[] | {dimension, moved: [.buckets[] | select(.delta != 0) | .value]}]'
```

```json
[{"dimension":"state","moved":["Failed","InCall"]},{"dimension":"response_code","moved":["200","404","486","503","603"]}]
```

The REST route reads its two files from `--api-file-root`, and its summary adds
that neither file is the capture the server holds. The MCP tool
`compare_captures` runs the same comparison.

### Find the files that hold a call

Find which of several captures hold failed calls:

```sh
sipnab --find-in-files tests/pcap-samples/sip-problem-call.pcap tests/pcap-samples/sip-rtp-g711.pcap tests/pcap-samples/sip-auth-failure.pcapng --problems
```

```text
Found in 3 of 3 files; every file was read.
File                     Dialogs  First Call-ID
----------------------------------------------------------------------
sip-problem-call.pcap    4        busy-3a2b1c@192.0.2.30
sip-rtp-g711.pcap        2        1-1966@10.0.2.20
sip-auth-failure.pcapng  1        auth-fail-register-synth@203.0.113.1
```

- The filter is the one a run with the same flags applies: `--filter`, a
  diagnostic alias such as `--problems`, and `--since`/`--until`.
- Each row is a file with a match, how many of its dialogs matched, and the
  first matching Call-ID.
- sipnab reads the files and exits. It needs no capture, so give no `-I`.

Name a directory to search the capture files directly in it. Here the search is
for one Call-ID:

```sh
sipnab --find-in-files tests/pcap-samples --filter 'call_id == "busy-3a2b1c@192.0.2.30"'
```

```text
Found in 1 of 36 files; not complete: 34 of 36 read, so a file not read may hold a match.
File                   Dialogs  First Call-ID
------------------------------------------------------
sip-problem-call.pcap  1        busy-3a2b1c@192.0.2.30
Not read: c07-sip-r2.cap: Failed to open pcap file 'tests/pcap-samples/c07-sip-r2.cap': libpcap error: unknown file format
Not read: rtsp-packets.cap: Failed to open pcap file 'tests/pcap-samples/rtsp-packets.cap': libpcap error: unknown file format
```

The two `.cap` files are in a format sipnab does not read, so the answer says
it could not read every file, and the run exits 1. When a search is not
complete, a call it did not find may still be in a file it did not read.

Under `--json`, `complete` says whether sipnab read every file:

```sh
sipnab --find-in-files tests/pcap-samples/sip-problem-call.pcap tests/pcap-samples/sip-rtp-g711.pcap --filter 'state == Failed' --json | jq -c '{complete, files: [.matches[] | {filename, dialogs_matched}]}'
```

```json
{"complete":true,"files":[{"filename":"sip-problem-call.pcap","dialogs_matched":4}]}
```

The MCP tool `find_in_captures` runs the same search over its file root.

### Fail a build on what a capture shows

Write the thresholds the traffic must meet in a suite file, and let the exit
status fail the CI step that runs it. Each rule names a metric (`count`,
`asr`, `lint_errors`, or a MOS percentile such as `mos_p10`), a comparison,
and a threshold, and may narrow itself with a `filter:` scope:

```sh
sipnab -I tests/pcap-samples/sip-problem-call.pcap --expect tests/fixtures/expect/sip-problem-call.expect.toml --no-cli-print --quiet
```

```text
Expectations: fail, 1 of 3 rules passed, 2 failed
Rule                  Metric  Op  Threshold  Observed  Sample  Verdict
----------------------------------------------------------------------
calls captured        count   >=  5          5         5       pass
answer-seizure ratio  asr     >=  50         20        5       fail
no busy answers       count   ==  0          1         5       fail
answer-seizure ratio: 20 is NOT >= 50 over 5 seizure(s)
no busy answers: 1 is NOT == 0 over 5 dialog(s)
```

The run exits with the suite's verdict:

- `0`: every rule that ran passed.
- `1`: at least one rule failed, as here.
- `2`: no rule ran, because every rule's population was below the
  `min_sample` it declared. A suite that checked nothing does not pass.

sipnab reads and checks the suite before it reads the capture, so a misspelled
metric or a filter that does not parse stops the run at once with exit `2`. The
rules judge every dialog of the capture: each rule's `scope` narrows it, and
`--filter` does not. For `lint_errors` rules, `--lint-suppress-file` applies.

Under `--json`, the answer is the report the MCP tool `evaluate_expectations`
returns, and `exit_code` is the run's exit status:

```sh
sipnab -I tests/pcap-samples/sip-problem-call.pcap --expect tests/fixtures/expect/sip-problem-call.expect.toml --json --no-cli-print --quiet | jq -c '{verdict, exit_code, failed: [.results[] | select(.verdict == "fail") | .name]}'
```

```json
{"verdict":"fail","exit_code":1,"failed":["answer-seizure ratio","no busy answers"]}
```

### Ask the relay which calls it holds

During an incident, ask the media relay which calls it is carrying right now,
without starting a capture. sipnab sends the relay named by
`--rtpengine-control` one `list` request, prints the Call-IDs it answers with,
and exits:

```sh
sudo sipnab -d eth0 --rtpengine-control 127.0.0.1:22222 --relay-holdings
```

```text
Holdings of relay (rtpengine at 127.0.0.1:22222), asked 2026-10-25T08:10:20.740734142+00:00
3 calls held.
Call-ID
--------------------------------
a84b4c76e66710@192.0.2.10
3848276298220188511@198.51.100.7
1-4242@192.0.2.10
```

Asking transmits, so sipnab asks only from a live source: an interface
(`-d`) or a HEP listener (`-L`). On a run that reads a file it asks nothing,
says why, and exits `2`. sipnab answers before it opens the capture, so the
run reads no packet and answers no other query flag.

The relay returns at most 32 Call-IDs unless you ask for a different number.
When it returns as many as you asked for, it may hold more, and the answer
says so:

```sh
sudo sipnab -d eth0 --rtpengine-control 127.0.0.1:22222 --relay-holdings --relay-holdings-max 2
```

```text
Holdings of relay (rtpengine at 127.0.0.1:22222), asked 2026-10-25T08:12:28.613317624+00:00
2 calls returned, as many as asked for, so the relay may hold more.
Call-ID
--------------------------------
a84b4c76e66710@192.0.2.10
3848276298220188511@198.51.100.7
```

On a busy relay, raise the limit. A HEP listener is a live source too, so a
host that only receives HEP can ask:

```sh
sipnab -L 0.0.0.0:9060 --rtpengine-control 127.0.0.1:22222 --relay-holdings --relay-holdings-max 500
```

rtpengine answers over UDP, and a large list may not fit in one datagram.

Under `--json`, the answer is the body `GET /v1/relay/holdings` returns:

```sh
sudo sipnab -d eth0 --rtpengine-control 127.0.0.1:22222 --relay-holdings --json
```

```json
{"call_ids":["a84b4c76e66710@192.0.2.10","3848276298220188511@198.51.100.7","1-4242@192.0.2.10"],"kind":"calls","obtained_at":"2026-10-25T08:10:20.788134229+00:00","origin":"asked","outcome":"ok","relay":"relay (rtpengine at 127.0.0.1:22222)","truncated":false}
```

A relay that sends no answer is not a relay that holds no calls. sipnab
prints the reason on stderr and exits `1`. Under `--json` the answer names the
classification instead of a list:

```text
--relay-holdings: unreachable: relay (rtpengine at 127.0.0.1:22222) did not answer (no reply from 127.0.0.1:22222 within 2s); asked, nothing came back
```

```json
{"detail":"relay (rtpengine at 127.0.0.1:22222) did not answer (no reply from 127.0.0.1:22222 within 2s); asked, nothing came back","outcome":"unreachable","responsibility":"relay_or_network"}
```

## Dialog

| Flag | Value | Default | Since | Description |
|------|-------|---------|-------|-------------|
| `-l`, `--limit` | `<N>` | `100000` | 0.3.0 | Maximum dialogs held in TOTAL over the run. **Not a concurrency limit** — nothing removes a completed dialog, so this bound scales with uptime rather than load: a box carrying five concurrent calls still evicts once 100,000 have completed, oldest first. Lower it for untrusted/high-volume capture. Config: `[limits] dialog_limit` |
| `-R`, `--rotate` | -- | **on** | 0.3.0 | Evict the oldest dialog at `--limit` capacity (LRU). On by default; pass it to state the default explicitly |
| `--no-rotate` | -- | off | 0.4.5 | Disable rotation: drop *new* dialogs at capacity instead of evicting the oldest (inverts the safe default) |
| `--dialog-track` | `<METHOD>` | `call-id` | 0.3.0 | Group messages by `call-id` (one unit per dialog) or `branch` (one per SIP transaction) |
| `--leg-correlation-window` | `<MS>` | `2000` | 0.5.100 | How far apart one call's two legs may start and still correlate on TIMING alone. sipnab falls back to this timing match when a B2BUA has rewritten every identifier the other correlation strategies compare. Two seconds suits a PBX that places the outbound leg at once; widen it for one that does an LNP or ENUM lookup, or walks an LCR list, first. Each correlation reports the strategy that matched. Config: `[sip] leg_correlation_window_ms` |
| `--active-idle-window` | `<SECS>` | `3600` | 0.5.100 | Seconds a dialog may go untouched and still count toward the active-dialog and active-call gauges every surface publishes. One hour is twice the default `Session-Expires` of [RFC 4028](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4028.html). Raise it where calls stay on hold longer than that, such as a contact center; a call whose BYE never arrived then also keeps counting for longer. Config: `[sip] active_idle_window_secs` |
| `--no-dialog` | -- | off | 0.3.0 | Disable dialog tracking entirely (message-only mode) |
| `--tag` | `<TAG>` | -- | 0.3.0 | Add this label to every dialog the run records, in the dialog's `tags` (`--json-dialogs`, `GET /v1/dialogs`, `GET /v1/dialogs/:call_id`, and MCP `list_dialogs` and `get_dialog`). It labels; it does not filter. |

> **`branch` counts transactions, not calls.**
>
> - RFC 3261 gives the ACK to a 2xx a new branch ([RFC 3261 section 17.1.1.3](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3261.html#section-17.1.1.3)). It gives the BYE another.
> - So one ordinary call appears as three or more units.
> - That is the transaction view working as intended.
> - Use it when a capture reuses one Call-ID across many transactions, such as
>   load generators or proxies under test.
> - Note that `--limit` then counts transactions too.

**Examples**

- `sipnab -N -I loadtest.pcapng --dialog-track branch --report` — per-transaction view of a load-generator capture that reuses one Call-ID
- `sipnab -N -I loadtest.pcapng --dialog-track call-id --report` — same capture as dialogs (the default), for a per-call view
- `sudo sipnab -d eth0 --limit 5000 --rotate` — monitor a busy proxy with a tight 5000-dialog memory bound, explicitly evicting the oldest dialog at capacity
- `sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --limit 20000 --no-rotate` — analyze a capture, dropping new dialogs (instead of evicting old ones) past 20000 tracked
- `sipnab -N -I day.pcap --limit 1000 --rotate --report` — report on the last 1000 calls of a long capture: each new call past 1000 evicts the oldest
- `sipnab -N -I day.pcap --limit 1000 --no-rotate --report` — report on the first 1000 calls of a long capture: sipnab drops the calls past 1000 and counts them
- `sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --tag site-a --json-dialogs` — label every dialog from this capture `site-a`, so a store that merges several captures can tell them apart: each dialog line carries `"tags":["site-a"]`
- `sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --tag site-a --api 127.0.0.1:8080` — serve the capture over REST with every dialog labeled `site-a`, so `GET /v1/dialogs/:call_id` shows which site the call came from
- `sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --no-dialog` — scan a capture message-by-message with dialog tracking disabled entirely
- `sudo sipnab -d eth0 -N --no-dialog` — watch raw live SIP messages on an interface without keeping any per-dialog state
- `sipnab -N -I sbc.pcap --leg-correlation-window 8000 --mcp` — correlate the two legs of a call across a B2BUA that dips an ENUM or LNP database before placing the outbound leg, which the shipped two seconds cannot reach
- `sipnab -N -I gateway.pcap --leg-correlation-window 500 --report` — a PBX that places the outbound leg immediately, where a tighter window stops a busy server's unrelated calls turning into one
- `sudo sipnab -N -d eth0 --metrics 127.0.0.1:9090 --active-idle-window 14400` — a contact center parking callers on hold for hours: at the shipped hour the active-call gauge stops counting them, and four hours covers the queue
- `sudo sipnab -N -d eth0 --metrics 127.0.0.1:9090 --active-idle-window 300` — a trunk where every call refreshes on a short session timer, so five minutes of silence already means the BYE went missing and counting it longer only inflates the gauge


## RTP

| Flag | Value | Default | Since | Description |
|------|-------|---------|-------|-------------|
| `--max-streams` | `<N>` | `50000` | 0.3.0 | Maximum number of RTP streams to track simultaneously. At least 1: sipnab refuses `0`. Config: `[limits] max_streams` |
| `--max-lost-sequences` | `<N>` | `1000` | 0.5.97 | Lost RTP sequence numbers retained per stream, for the Packet Loss Map and the burst/gap analysis. The default is about a minute of a call losing 1 % at 50 packets a second, so on a half-hour call the map shows the tail and marks itself truncated. The burst/gap window widens with it, and each retained loss costs two bytes per stream. Config: `[limits] max_lost_sequences` |
| `--quality-interval` | `<SECONDS>` | `5` | 0.5.160 | Seconds between RTP quality snapshots — the resolution of the per-stream quality trend, which carries a MOS, an R-factor and an `acceptable`/`degraded`/`not_scorable` verdict per interval. The shipped five seconds averages away any burst shorter than itself, so three half-second dropouts read as a mild five-second average. The trend still covers an hour of call time whatever this is, so one second retains 3600 snapshots per stream instead of 720: resolution costs memory, never history. Accepts 1 to 300. Config: `[limits] quality_interval_secs` |
| `--quality-threshold` | `<MOS>` | `3.0` | 0.3.0 | MOS quality threshold for alerts (1.0-5.0 scale) |
| `--g729-tables` | `<PATH>` | -- | 0.5.222 | The G.729 codebook table file, for decoding G.729 audio in WAV exports, vCon recordings, the live audio route and the dead-air measurement. sipnab ships no ITU-T table values: [`sipnab g729 install`](@/docs/g729.md) builds this file from the ITU-T G.729 software package. Absent, sipnab reads `[g729] tables`, else `g729-tables.bin` in the directory of the user config file (`$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/sipnab`, else `~/.config/sipnab`). sipnab reads a path given here as it is: when no file is there, sipnab leaves G.729 streams out of the audio and the export says `G.729 not decoded: codebook tables not installed; run sipnab g729 install`. Feature: `g729`. Config: `[g729] tables` |
| `--rtpengine-control` | `<ADDR>` | -- | 0.5.124 | Ask an rtpengine relay which calls it currently has up, so a capture that started mid-call can still name the dialog behind a stream. **Off unless you give an address**, and the address is never inferred from captured traffic. sipnab sends only rtpengine's read-only `list` and `query` commands, so it cannot change a relay's behavior. **Not a poller**: it asks at startup, before the capture opens, and again only when a stream turns up that nothing explains, never on a timer. sipnab asks about each relay-side socket at most once for the run, under a per-run ceiling on control transactions. **On `-I <file>` it sends nothing**: sipnab warns that a live relay would describe the calls up today rather than the calls in the capture, still decodes any relay control traffic the capture holds, and analyzes the file. Feature: `native` |
| `--rtpproxy-control` | `<ADDR:PORT>` | -- | 0.5.196 | Read rtpproxy's control traffic on this UDP socket and name the call each relayed stream belongs to, even on the relay's own machine where no SIP passes. The SIP proxy's command names the call and rtpproxy's reply names the port it opened; sipnab pairs the two by the cookie they share. Recording streams (`R`, `C`) are never named as the call's media. **Name the socket; sipnab assumes none**: rtpproxy's default control socket is a UNIX socket, which a capture cannot see, so give it a UDP one with `-s udp:ADDR:PORT` (22222 when you leave out the port) and pass the same address and port here. sipnab reads only datagrams to and from exactly that socket, because they carry no credential. **Passive**: sipnab never sends rtpproxy anything, and rtpproxy has no command that lists its sessions, so sipnab names a call already up when the capture starts from its next command. Works on live captures and on files, and applies to a capture opened inside the TUI. Feature: `native` |
| `--relay-stats` | -- | -- | 0.5.169 | Ask the relay named by `--rtpengine-control` for its OWN statistics -- packets relayed, sessions, its own loss and jitter -- and print them. They are `relay_reported`: a claim from the box, not a measurement sipnab made, and the header says so. **Same live source `--rtpengine-control` needs**, because asking transmits; on `-I <file>` it prints why it declines to ask rather than asking, and with no `--rtpengine-control` it says to name one. Feature: `native` |
| `--relay-stats-call` | `<CALL-ID>` | -- | 0.5.169 | Ask the relay named by `--rtpengine-control` for its own counters about ONE call, by Call-ID: per-stream and per-SSRC packet and byte counts, RTP and RTCP totals, as the relay counts them (`relay_reported`). A relay not holding the call answers in its own words, which sipnab reports rather than inventing a not-found. Same live-source gate as `--relay-stats`. Feature: `native` |
| `--relay-stats-list` | -- | -- | 0.5.169 | List which statistics the relay named by `--rtpengine-control` knows, rather than their values. The key set is version-specific, so "what can I ask for?" is a real question; sipnab asks the relay rather than reading a built-in table, and the header names how it got the set (for rtpengine, the relay listed them in a `statistics` reply). Same live-source gate as `--relay-stats`, because listing asks the relay and asking transmits. Feature: `native` |
| `--relay-stats-interval` | `<SECONDS>` | -- | 0.5.170 | Poll the relay named by `--rtpengine-control` for its statistics every SECONDS, for as long as the capture runs. Nothing polls by default. One transaction per interval, the next beginning only once the previous returns, so a slow relay slows the cadence rather than stacking requests. Each polled reading says it was `polled` and names the interval. CLI only (a poll is a standing instruction to transmit; the REST/MCP caller does not own the host). Same live-source gate as `--relay-stats`. Range 1--3600. A headless run prints each reading to stdout, so `-N` with `--mcp` refuses it. Feature: `native` |
| `--relay-compare` | `<CALL-ID>` | -- | 0.5.169 | Compare the relay's own RTP packet count for one call against what sipnab measured on the wire. It shows the relay's `totals.RTP.packets` for the call (`relay_reported`) beside sipnab's own count of the RTP packets it captured for it (`sipnab_measured`), both labeled, with a word verdict (`match` or `differ`) and a direction-aware note. The two count different sockets over different windows, so an ordinary gap is not a relay fault: if sipnab counted fewer the note names the undercount causes (a mirror-port drop, a mid-call restart) and points at `capture_health`; if sipnab counted more it names the usual cause -- a capture that sees both sides of the relay hairpin counts each packet twice, so a point upstream and downstream reads about twice the relay's count. It never sums the counts. Runs after capture, when sipnab's tally is final; sipnab reports a call the relay does not hold, or one it captured no RTP for, distinctly rather than comparing it against a made-up zero. Same live-source gate as `--relay-stats`. Feature: `native` |

**Examples**

- `sudo sipnab -d eth0 --quality-threshold 3.5 --max-streams 10000` — monitor live RTP with MOS alerts below 3.5. sipnab reports stream statistics once, at end of capture. There is no periodic interval report
- `sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --max-streams 100000` — batch-analyze RTP streams with a raised stream cap. The statistics arrive once, when the capture ends
- `sipnab -N -I long-call.pcap --max-lost-sequences 100000 --json-dialogs --no-cli-print` — keep every loss from a half-hour call that an operator escalated, so the Packet Loss Map covers the whole call and the burst count is the real one rather than the tail's
- `sudo sipnab -d eth0 --max-lost-sequences 200` — watch a busy trunk on a small box, holding a fifth of the shipped loss history per stream. The map still shows where loss is landing right now and marks itself truncated
- `sipnab -N -I g729-call.pcap --retain-audio --g729-tables /srv/sipnab/g729-tables.bin --export-vcon 'a84b4c76e66710@pc33.example.com' > call.vcon` — export a G.729 call's audio into a vCon, reading the tables from a file copied in from another host
- `sipnab -N -I dead-air.pcap --quality-interval 1 --json-dialogs --no-cli-print` — one snapshot a second on the call somebody complained about, so a half-second dropout appears as its own degraded interval instead of disappearing into a five-second mean
- `sudo sipnab -d eth0 --quality-interval 30 --max-streams 20000` — the other direction, on a busy trunk where twenty thousand streams each holding 720 snapshots is memory better spent elsewhere. Thirty seconds still covers the retained hour, in 120 entries per stream
- `sudo sipnab -N -d eth0 --rtpengine-control 127.0.0.1:22222` — start capturing on a proxy that shares a host with rtpengine, and ask the relay once, at startup, which calls are already up. Streams whose offer happened before sipnab started get a Call-ID, where otherwise sipnab would report them as orphans
- `sudo sipnab -N -d eth0 --rtpengine-control 192.0.2.50:22222 --max-streams 10000` — the relay on its own host: same question, over the network to its ng control port. sipnab sends only `list` and `query`, and asks again only when a stream turns up that the signaling does not explain — each socket once, under a ceiling it reports when it reaches
- `sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --rtpengine-control 127.0.0.1:22222` — sends nothing to the relay: sipnab warns that a file run never transmits, then analyzes the capture and exits `0`
- `sudo sipnab -N -d eth0 --rtpengine-control 127.0.0.1:22222 --relay-stats` — capture live and print the relay's own counters at startup: packets relayed, sessions held, its own loss. The header marks them `relay_reported`, because the relay reports on itself rather than sipnab measuring the wire
- `sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --relay-stats --rtpengine-control 127.0.0.1:22222` — asks nothing on a file run. sipnab logs `--relay-stats will not ask a relay on a run that reads a file`, analyzes the capture, and exits `0`
- `sudo sipnab -N -d eth0 --rtpengine-control 127.0.0.1:22222 --relay-stats-call 1-7@203.0.113.9` — the relay's own packet and byte counts for one call, by Call-ID, `relay_reported`. A header names the call and the moment asked
- `sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --relay-stats-call 1-7@203.0.113.9 --rtpengine-control 127.0.0.1:22222` — asks nothing on a file run, and logs the same `--relay-stats will not ask a relay` line as the relay-wide form
- `sudo sipnab -N -d eth0 --rtpengine-control 127.0.0.1:22222 --relay-stats-list` — ask the relay which statistics it knows, listed by name and not by value, so a caller learns what it can ask for before a request fails on a name this build does not have. The header says the relay listed them, rather than sipnab guessing from a table
- `sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --relay-stats-list --rtpengine-control 127.0.0.1:22222` — asks nothing on a file run, and logs the same `--relay-stats will not ask a relay` line
- `sudo sipnab -N -d eth0 --rtpengine-control 127.0.0.1:22222 --relay-compare 1-7@203.0.113.9` — after capture, put the relay's own RTP packet count for the call beside sipnab's measured count, each labeled with its tier, with a `match`/`differ` verdict and a note explaining that an ordinary gap is not a relay fault. It shows both counts and never sums them
- `sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --relay-compare 1-7@203.0.113.9 --rtpengine-control 127.0.0.1:22222` — compares nothing on a file run: sipnab logs `--relay-compare will not ask a relay on a run that reads a file` and exits `0`
- `sudo sipnab -N -d eth0 --rtpengine-control 127.0.0.1:22222 --relay-stats-interval 30` — capture live and ask the relay for its own counters every thirty seconds, each reading marked `polled` with the interval so it reads as a timer's output rather than a one-shot answer. Stop it with Ctrl-C. Nothing keeps transmitting after the process ends
- `sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --relay-stats-interval 30 --rtpengine-control 127.0.0.1:22222` — polls nothing on a file run: sipnab logs `--relay-stats-interval will not poll a relay on a run that reads a file` and exits `0`
- `sudo sipnab -N -d eth0 --rtpengine-control 127.0.0.1:22222 --relay-stats --json` — the same relay counters as one JSON object instead of the table, each value carrying its tier and refusals listed separately with the relay's code. Both forms read the same data, so `--json` and the table cannot disagree about a number
- `sipnab -N -I relay.pcap --rtpproxy-control 192.0.2.40:7722 --report` — read a capture taken on an rtpproxy relay whose control socket is `udp:192.0.2.40:7722`. Each stream on a port rtpproxy opened gets the Call-ID from the SIP proxy's command, and the report lists those calls as named by a media relay instead of reporting their media as orphaned
- `sudo sipnab -N -d eth0 --rtpproxy-control 127.0.0.1:22222` — capture live beside an rtpproxy started with `-s udp:127.0.0.1`, which listens on 22222. sipnab only reads the control traffic and never sends rtpproxy anything


## Diagnosis thresholds

The numbers the signaling and media checks compare against.

- Each decides whether a call that is working gets reported as broken.
- So the defaults are standards figures for the general case. Your own network
  beats them.
- Every flag has a config key under `[diagnosis]`, and the flag wins.

| Flag | Value | Default | Since | Description |
|------|-------|---------|-------|-------------|
| `--pdd-threshold` | `<SECS>` | `11.0` | 0.5.96 | Post-dial delay over which sipnab reports a call as slow. The default is the ITU-T E.721 Table 2 target that 95 percent of international connections must meet, because a capture does not say which kind of call it holds. Tighten it to 8.0 for toll or 6.0 for local traffic. Must be a finite number greater than 0: sipnab refuses `0`, a negative number, `nan` and `inf`. Config: `[diagnosis] post_dial_delay_secs` |
| `--ack-timeout` | `<SECS>` | `32.0` | 0.5.96 | Seconds a `2xx` may go unacknowledged before the missing `ACK` counts as a fault rather than as a capture that stopped early. The default is RFC 3261 Timer H. Must be a finite number greater than 0: sipnab refuses `0`, a negative number, `nan` and `inf`. Config: `[diagnosis] ack_timeout_secs` |
| `--no-final-response-timeout` | `<SECS>` | `180.0` | 0.5.96 | Seconds an `INVITE` may sit without a final response before the silence gets reported. The default is RFC 3261 Timer C. Below it, every call still ringing when the capture stopped gets reported. Must be a finite number greater than 0: sipnab refuses `0`, a negative number, `nan` and `inf`. Config: `[diagnosis] no_final_response_secs` |
