| `--duration-asymmetry-pct` | `<PCT>` | `5.0` | 0.5.96 | Percentage difference between the two legs' durations that counts as asymmetric. Greater than 0 and at most 100: sipnab refuses `0`, a negative number, a number over 100, `nan` and `inf`. Config: `[diagnosis] duration_asymmetry_pct` |
| `--duration-asymmetry-secs` | `<SECS>` | `2.0` | 0.5.96 | Absolute difference between the two legs' durations that counts as asymmetric. A call has to clear both this and the percentage, so raising either one alone quiets the detection. Must be a finite number greater than 0: sipnab refuses `0`, a negative number, `nan` and `inf`. Config: `[diagnosis] duration_asymmetry_secs` |
| `--late-media-ms` | `<MS>` | `500` | 0.5.96 | Milliseconds after the `200 OK` that media may start before it gets reported as late. A whole number of at least 1: sipnab refuses `0` and a negative number. Config: `[diagnosis] late_media_ms` |
| `--cn-suppression-ratio` | `<RATIO>` | `0.3` | 0.5.99 | Share of a call's packets, as a fraction of 1, that must be comfort noise before sipnab accepts comfort noise as the explanation for one-directional media. **The one threshold here that withholds a finding instead of raising one**, so it fails as silence: a VoLTE or mobile trunk running aggressive voice-activity detection routinely passes 30 percent comfort noise, and above the ratio sipnab never reports one-way audio on that trunk. Must be greater than 0 and 1 or less. Config: `[diagnosis] cn_suppression_ratio` |

**Examples**

- `sipnab -N -I calls.pcap --json-dialogs --pdd-threshold 6 --no-cli-print` — judge a capture you know is local traffic against E.721's local target rather than the international one the default assumes
- `sipnab -N -I trunk.pcap --json-dialogs --late-media-ms 150 --duration-asymmetry-secs 0.5 --no-cli-print` — a tight media audit for a trunk where a 150 ms media gap is already a clipped first syllable
- `sipnab -N -I sat-trunk.pcap --json-dialogs --pdd-threshold 15 --late-media-ms 900 --no-cli-print` — the other direction, for a satellite path where the shipped figures report every healthy call as slow
- `sipnab -N -I proxy.pcap --json-dialogs --ack-timeout 8 --no-final-response-timeout 30 --no-cli-print` — a proxy tap where the interesting window is far shorter than the RFC 3261 timers, so a stalled transaction shows up while the capture is still running
- `sipnab -N -I trunk.pcap --json-dialogs --ack-timeout 64 --no-final-response-timeout 300 --no-cli-print` — a lossy trunk where the RFC timers themselves fire too early, so only a genuinely dead transaction gets reported
- `sipnab -N -I b2bua.pcap --json-dialogs --duration-asymmetry-pct 25 --duration-asymmetry-secs 5 --no-cli-print` — a B2BUA capture where the legs never tear down together, so only a large gap is worth a line
- `sipnab -N -I b2bua.pcap --json-dialogs --duration-asymmetry-pct 1 --duration-asymmetry-secs 0.2 --no-cli-print` — the strict form of the same audit, for hunting a leg that drops media a fraction early
- `sipnab -N -I volte-trunk.pcap --json-dialogs --cn-suppression-ratio 0.8 --no-cli-print` — a mobile trunk whose voice-activity detection sends comfort noise on well over 30 percent of packets: at the shipped ratio sipnab treats that as the explanation for a one-directional flow and reports no one-way audio on any call
- `sipnab -N -I pbx.pcap --json-dialogs --cn-suppression-ratio 0.05 --no-cli-print` — the opposite, for a LAN PBX where a call carrying any comfort noise at all is still expected to be bidirectional


## Quality color bands

Where the quality color column turns yellow, and where it turns red.

- This is a different question from the diagnosis thresholds above.
- Those decide whether a working call counts as broken.
- These decide only what catches an operator's eye during triage.
- Every flag has a config key under `[quality]`, and the flag wins.

The shipped figures suit a general-purpose trunk. The right values belong to
the network you are watching.

- 30 ms of jitter is already a fault on a LAN PBX.
- 1 percent loss is unremarkable on an international one.
- A column tuned for neither is wrong in both directions.

These bands paint the TUI.

- A `-N` run prints the measurements themselves rather than a color.
- So sipnab validates a band set on a non-interactive run and then never
  consults it.

| Flag | Value | Default | Since | Description |
|------|-------|---------|-------|-------------|
| `--jitter-warn-ms` | `<MS>` | `30.0` | 0.5.97 | Jitter at or above which the column turns yellow. Config: `[quality] jitter_warn_ms` |
| `--jitter-bad-ms` | `<MS>` | `50.0` | 0.5.97 | Jitter at or above which the column turns red. Config: `[quality] jitter_bad_ms` |
| `--loss-warn-pct` | `<PCT>` | `1.0` | 0.5.97 | Loss at or above which the column turns yellow. `0` is a legitimate setting: it means any loss at all is worth a color. Config: `[quality] loss_warn_pct` |
| `--loss-bad-pct` | `<PCT>` | `5.0` | 0.5.97 | Loss at or above which the column turns red. Config: `[quality] loss_bad_pct` |
| `--mos-warn` | `<MOS>` | `4.0` | 0.5.97 | MOS below which the column turns yellow. MOS bands run downward, so this must sit at or above `--mos-bad`. Config: `[quality] mos_warn` |
| `--mos-bad` | `<MOS>` | `3.0` | 0.5.97 | MOS below which the column turns red. Config: `[quality] mos_bad` |
| `--rtt-warn-ms` | `<MS>` | `300.0` | 0.5.97 | Round trip at or above which the column turns yellow. The default is ITU-T G.114's 150 ms one-way guidance doubled. Config: `[quality] rtt_warn_ms` |
| `--rtt-bad-ms` | `<MS>` | `800.0` | 0.5.97 | Round trip at or above which the column turns red. The default is G.114's 400 ms one-way figure doubled. Config: `[quality] rtt_bad_ms` |

sipnab refuses, with exit `2`, a warn boundary above its matching bad
boundary:

```text
--jitter-warn-ms (60) is above --jitter-bad-ms (50), so no jitter could ever be a warning
```

It also refuses a boundary that is not a finite number of 0 or more, such as
`nan`.

**Examples**

- `sipnab -I lan-pbx.pcap --jitter-warn-ms 10 --jitter-bad-ms 20` — a LAN PBX, where the shipped 30 ms boundary hides a fault worth chasing
- `sipnab -I wifi-softphone.pcap --jitter-warn-ms 60 --jitter-bad-ms 120` — the other direction, for a Wi-Fi leg where the defaults paint every healthy call yellow
- `sipnab -I intl-trunk.pcap --loss-warn-pct 2 --loss-bad-pct 8` — an international trunk, where 1 percent loss is routine
- `sipnab -I strict-lan.pcap --loss-warn-pct 0 --loss-bad-pct 1` — the strict form: any loss at all takes a color
- `sipnab -I sat-trunk.pcap --rtt-warn-ms 700 --rtt-bad-ms 1200` — a satellite path, where G.114's terrestrial figures report every call as bad
- `sipnab -I campus.pcap --rtt-warn-ms 50 --rtt-bad-ms 150` — a campus network, where a 300 ms round trip is already an escalation
- `sipnab -I hd-codec.pcap --mos-warn 4.3 --mos-bad 3.8` — a wideband codec deployment, where 4.0 is not the good score it is on narrowband
- `sipnab -I gsm-gateway.pcap --mos-warn 3.6 --mos-bad 2.8` — a low-bitrate gateway, where nothing ever clears the shipped 4.0 warning
- `sipnab -I triage.pcap --jitter-warn-ms 15 --loss-warn-pct 0.5 --rtt-warn-ms 120 --mos-warn 4.2` — one strict pass across all four columns, for a first look at a network you have not seen before


## Security

| Flag | Value | Default | Since | Description |
|------|-------|---------|-------|-------------|
| `--kill-scanner` | -- | off | 0.3.0 | Detect SIP scanning (known UA signatures + behavioral rate/enumeration), alert on it, and send the kill response back to the scanner (the CLI matcher `-J`/`-j`). To detect without answering, use `--kill-scanner-detect-only`. Config: `[security] kill_scanner` |
| `--no-kill-scanner` | -- | off | 0.5.204 | Do not answer scanners even when `[security] kill_scanner = true`, so you can disarm, for one run, a response that a config file arms. The last of `--kill-scanner` / `--no-kill-scanner` typed wins. Config: `[security] kill_scanner` |
| `--kill-scanner-detect-only` | -- | off | 0.5.227 | Detect and report SIP scanners exactly as `--kill-scanner` does, and never answer them. sipnab starts no scanner-kill worker and sends nothing, on a live capture too. It builds the scanner detector by itself, so `--kill-scanner` is not needed; given together, detect-only wins. The run says `Scanner detection is detect-only` at startup and `scanner detection was detect-only` in its end-of-run summary, and `security_findings` reports `scanner_response: "detect_only"`. sipnab refuses it together with `-K`/`--kill-target` (exit 2), because `-K` asks sipnab to answer a named source. Config: `[security] kill_scanner_detect_only` |
| `--no-kill-scanner-detect-only` | -- | off | 0.5.227 | Answer scanners again even when `[security] kill_scanner_detect_only = true`, for one run. The last of `--kill-scanner-detect-only` / `--no-kill-scanner-detect-only` typed wins. Config: `[security] kill_scanner_detect_only` |
| `--kill-ua` | `<PATTERN>` | -- | 0.3.0 | Add a custom scanner User-Agent pattern (regex) to `--kill-scanner` detection. **Refused without it**: `--kill-scanner` or `--kill-scanner-detect-only` (or `[security] kill_scanner = true` or `kill_scanner_detect_only = true`) builds the detector that reads this pattern, so given alone it would feed nothing and the run would report no scanners — which is what a clean capture looks like. sipnab does not arm the detector for you, because on a live capture `--kill-scanner` also arms the response path. sipnab refuses an empty or blank pattern, which would match every User-Agent, and a pattern that is not a valid regular expression |
| `--kill-response` | `<CODE>` | `200` | 0.3.0 | SIP response code for the kill response (100-699). Config: `[security] kill_response` |
| `-K`, `--kill-target` | `<ADDR[:PORT-RANGE]>` | -- | 0.5.7 | Targeted kill: send the kill response to any SIP request whose source matches ADDR and an optional port range (`192.0.2.1:5060-5090`, `[::1]:5060`), regardless of UA/behavioral detection. Repeatable; spawns the kill worker on its own (no `--kill-scanner` needed). Refused (exit 2) together with `--kill-scanner-detect-only` or `[security] kill_scanner_detect_only = true` |
| `--kill-spoof` | `<MODE>` | `auto` | 0.5.12 | Source-address strategy for the kill response (Linux only; other platforms always `ephemeral`). `auto` forges the victim's ip:port via a raw socket when `CAP_NET_RAW` is available (so the reply appears to come from the targeted SIP port), falling back to an ephemeral source otherwise; `raw` requires the spoof and errors when it cannot open the raw socket; `ephemeral` never spoofs |
| `--kill-rate-limit` | `<N>` | `10` | 0.5.96 | Scanner-kill responses per second sipnab may put on the wire. There is no unlimited setting: sipnab rejects `0`. A per-destination cap of 3 per minute applies underneath, so raising this widens how many distinct hosts sipnab answers, never how hard it hits one. Config: `[security] kill_rate_limit` |
| `--sandbox` | `<MODE>` | `off` | 0.5.164 | Bound which files this process may reach, using Landlock. `best-effort` installs what the kernel supports and captures either way; `required` refuses to capture when no sandbox is in force. Reads and writes outside the input set, the output directory, the keylog and the crash directory come back `EACCES`. **Sockets are not bounded**: the ruleset governs the filesystem only. A denied open fails with `EACCES` and does not end the run, and a kernel without Landlock degrades to a warning unless `required` says otherwise |
| `--seccomp` | `<MODE>` | `off` | 0.5.165 | Record every system call (`log`), or refuse the ones outside a host-derived allowlist (`enforce`). `log` installs a seccomp filter whose only action is `SECCOMP_RET_LOG`. **It denies nothing and protects nothing**: use it to record which calls a run makes, as the input to an allowlist. `enforce` kills the process on a call outside the allowlist `SIPNAB_SECCOMP_ALLOWLIST` names, derived on the capture host with [`scripts/derive-seccomp-allowlist.sh`](https://github.com/NormB/sipnab/blob/main/scripts/derive-seccomp-allowlist.sh); when sipnab cannot install an enforcing filter (no list named, a list it cannot read, a kernel that refuses), it refuses to start, exit status 1. Where the records land depends on the host: `auditctl -s` prints a connected audit daemon's pid and the records are then in `ausearch -m SECCOMP`; a pid of 0 means no daemon and they are in `dmesg \| grep 'type=1326'`. Point it at a bounded offline run — a live capture emits one record per received packet and floods the log |
| `--fraud-detect` | -- | off | 0.3.0 | Enable fraud detection heuristics. Config: `[security] fraud_detect` |
| `--no-fraud-detect` | -- | off | 0.5.204 | Do not run fraud detection even when `[security] fraud_detect = true`. The last of `--fraud-detect` / `--no-fraud-detect` typed wins. Config: `[security] fraud_detect` |
| `--evidence-out` | `<PATH\|->` | off | 0.5.148 | Publish every security finding that names a source as JSON Lines, for a system that decides what to do with it. `-` is standard output, for a pipe, and `--mcp` refuses it; a path receives one appended line per finding, and sipnab opens it at startup, so a path it cannot write is an error before the first packet. sipnab takes no action on these lines: the system reading them decides. A finding carried by HEP publishes nothing without `--hep-allow-kill`, for the reason `--fail2ban` gives: the inner address is the sender's claim |
| `--fraud-destination` | `<ISO,...>` | off | 0.5.147 | Destination countries `--fraud-detect` reports an INVITE to, as ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 codes (`DO,VG,MA`). sipnab reads numbers through the common international prefixes (`+`, `00`, `011`) and resolves them by longest calling code, so `+1 809` is `DO`, not `US`; a number with no prefix is domestic and never matches. Every fraud finding also names the resolved destination. Absent: nothing changes. Config: `[security] fraud_destination` |
| `--business-hours` | `<START-END>` | -- | 0.5.96 | Business hours in whole UTC hours, for example `8-18`, or `22-6` for an overnight window. The off-hours fraud detection reports nothing until you set a window. Needs `--fraud-detect`. Config: `[security] business_hours` |
| `--fraud-short-call` | `<SECS>` | `3` | 0.5.96 | Measured duration below which `--fraud-detect` counts a completed call as short for wangiri detection. Three seconds is under a normal ring-no-answer on some carriers. Config: `[security] fraud_short_call_secs` |
| `--fraud-wangiri-calls` | `<N>` | `3` | 0.5.96 | Short calls to one destination prefix before `--fraud-detect` reports wangiri. Config: `[security] fraud_wangiri_calls` |
| `--fraud-sequential-calls` | `<N>` | `3` | 0.5.96 | Consecutive refused numbers before `--fraud-detect` reports sequential scanning. Config: `[security] fraud_sequential_calls` |
| `--fraud-volume-multiplier` | `<N>` | `5` | 0.5.96 | Multiple of a source's own baseline call rate that `--fraud-detect` reports as a volume spike. Config: `[security] fraud_volume_multiplier` |
| `--fraud-volume-min-calls` | `<N>` | `6` | 0.5.96 | Calls a source must place inside the volume window before `--fraud-detect` reports a spike at all. Config: `[security] fraud_volume_min_calls` |
| `--fraud-volume-window` | `<SECS>` | `60` | 0.5.100 | How much capture time one volume-spike window spans. The count and the baseline are both measured over it, so a steady source reads the same at any width; the width alone decides how concentrated a burst has to be, since a burst shorter than the window averages into the traffic beside it. Config: `[security] fraud_volume_window_secs` |
| `--fraud-wangiri-window` | `<SECS>` | `60` | 0.5.100 | How much capture time one wangiri window spans. The detector drops short calls older than this, so it decides how slowly a lure may arrive and still count as one pattern. No setting of `--fraud-wangiri-calls` reaches a lure paced wider than the window. Config: `[security] fraud_wangiri_window_secs` |
| `--scanner-behavioral-probes` | `<N>` | `10` | 0.5.98 | Probes from one source inside the scanner window, above which `--kill-scanner` reports a rate detection. Behind an SBC every source collapses to one address, so ordinary aggregated traffic clears ten in five seconds and the whole site reads as one scanner. Config: `[security] scanner_behavioral_probes` |
| `--scanner-enumeration-targets` | `<N>` | `5` | 0.5.98 | Distinct target extensions from one source inside the scanner window, above which `--kill-scanner` reports extension enumeration. Config: `[security] scanner_enumeration_targets` |
| `--scanner-rejected-probes` | `<N>` | `5` | 0.5.98 | Rejected probes inside the scanner window at which a source reads as probing rather than operating. This is the evidence gate: neither behavioral signal reports anything until a source clears this or `--scanner-unanswered-probes`, which is what separates an enumeration sweep from a trunk running keepalives at the same rate. Config: `[security] scanner_rejected_probes` |
| `--scanner-unanswered-probes` | `<N>` | `5` | 0.5.98 | Probes inside the scanner window that drew no response, at which a source reads as sweeping, provided they also outnumber the rest of what it sent. Config: `[security] scanner_unanswered_probes` |
| `--scanner-window` | `<SECS>` | `5` | 0.5.98 | How much capture time one scanner window spans. Every scanner count above is per window, so this is the binding constraint on a paced sweep rather than the counts: one probe every ten seconds never puts two inside the shipped five-second window, so the rate and the spread both stay at one however low the counts go. Config: `[security] scanner_window_secs` |
| `--scanner-established-factor` | `<N>` | `4` | 0.5.98 | How much more evidence `--kill-scanner` needs from a source that has completed a registration or a call. `1` judges a registered endpoint like any other source; raise it to report fewer of your own endpoints. Config: `[security] scanner_established_factor` |
| `--scanner-answer-grace` | `<MS>` | `500` | 0.5.98 | How long a probe may go without a response before `--kill-scanner` counts it as unanswered. The default is RFC 3261's Timer T1, the round-trip estimate at which SIP itself gives up waiting and retransmits. Raise it on a link whose round trip runs longer than that, where the default reports every probe still in flight as one nobody answered. Config: `[security] scanner_answer_grace_ms` |
| `--reg-flood` | -- | off | 0.3.0 | Detect registration floods: credentialed REGISTERs the registrar keeps refusing. sipnab reports a source when the REGISTERs it sent with `Authorization` that drew a `401`/`407` on the same transaction exceed `--reg-flood-threshold` inside one `--reg-flood-window` of capture time, one second by default. A REGISTER on its own is never evidence, so a re-REGISTER storm the registrar accepts after a restart is the customer's SBC and not a flood, and any `2xx` to a REGISTER clears the source's count |
| `--reg-flood-threshold` | `<N>` | `50` | 0.5.96 | Challenged failures from one source inside one `--reg-flood-window` before `--reg-flood` reports a flood: REGISTERs that carried credentials and drew a `401` or `407`. The default suits a carrier registrar; set it lower for a small PBX. Counted in capture time, so a file replays as the traffic it recorded rather than as fast as the disk reads it. Config: `[security] reg_flood_threshold` |
| `--reg-flood-window` | `<SECS>` | `1` | 0.5.189 | How much capture time one `--reg-flood` counting window spans, 1-3600 seconds. The threshold counts failures per window, so this decides how concentrated a credential-guessing run has to be: one refusal every two seconds never puts two inside the default one-second window, whatever the threshold. sipnab refuses `0` and anything past an hour. Config: `[security] reg_flood_window_secs` |
| `--reg-flood-transaction-timeout` | `<MS>` | `32000` | 0.5.189 | How long a credentialed REGISTER stays open to the `401`/`407` that answers it, 1000-600000 milliseconds. The default is [RFC 3261 Timer F](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3261.html#section-17.1.2.2), 64 times T1 at the default T1 of 500 ms. sipnab never counts a challenge that arrives later as a failure. Set it to 64 times the T1 your network runs, or to your registrar-side proxy's final-response timer when that is longer: `fr_timeout` in OpenSIPS (seconds, so multiply by 1000) or `fr_timer` in Kamailio (already milliseconds). See [Registration-flood timers](@/docs/troubleshooting.md#registration-flood-timers). Config: `[security] reg_flood_transaction_timeout_ms` |
| `--digest-leak` | -- | off | 0.3.0 | Detect digest credential leaks in SIP messages |
| `--allow-action` | `<TARGET:SURFACE[,SURFACE]>` | none | 0.5.196 | Enable an action that changes another system, from the named surfaces. **sipnab changes no external system by default**: it publishes what it saw to destinations you name and asks read-only questions, and an action, such as asking TFPS to ban a source, runs only when enabled here or under `[actions]` in the config file. Targets: `tfps`. Surfaces: `rest`, `mcp`. Repeatable, and added to what the config file enables. Enabling is one of two locks: a REST caller also needs a token minted with scope `actions` (`--token-scope actions`), and so does an MCP client over HTTP. A `full` token, or a static `--api-key`, reads everything and acts on nothing. Over MCP stdio the enabling is the only lock, because the client is a process you started. Refused, it answers `403` (REST) or a tool error (MCP) naming this flag, and `tfps_ctl` never runs. Enabled, sipnab records every action in the actions journal (see `--journal-dir`) before it asks TFPS, and refuses to start if it cannot use the journal. Every action also passes fixed rules and rate limits: some addresses are never banned (loopback, broadcast, multicast, `0.0.0.0`), every ban expires (an hour unless asked otherwise, 7 days at most), and there are at most 10 actions a minute for the server, 5 for one caller, and one per address a minute. `[action_limits]` in the config file tightens or loosens those, and nothing turns them off. sipnab lifts only bans it placed itself, and a token lifts only the bans it placed unless it holds scope `admin`. Config: `[actions] tfps` |
| `--journal-dir` | `<DIR>` | `/var/lib/sipnab/journal` | 0.5.196 | Where sipnab records the actions it takes on other systems, so a restart knows what it did: which bans are its own, what was in flight when it stopped, and how much of each rate limit is already spent. Needed whenever `--allow-action` enables anything: sipnab creates the directory (mode 0700) if it can, and refuses to start if it cannot use it, or if another sipnab is already using it. The packaged service gets `/var/lib/sipnab` from systemd's `StateDirectory=`. sipnab writes each record to disk before the action runs, and the files hold no token or request body. A file closes at 16 MiB, and sipnab deletes closed files more than 90 days old when the next one starts. A file that a root run of `--revert-actions` creates takes the directory's owner, so the service can still read it. Config: `[journal] dir` |
| `--journal-show` | -- | -- | 0.5.196 | Print what the actions journal says, then exit: the bans sipnab placed that are still in force, newest first, each with its action id, expiry and who asked; actions a crash left unfinished; bans TFPS shows that sipnab cannot prove it placed; how the last run ended; and the last hour's refusals. Only reads, so it works while another sipnab holds the journal |
| `--revert-actions` | `<all\|ACTION_ID>` | -- | 0.5.196 | Back out what sipnab did, then exit: `all` lifts every ban sipnab placed that is still in force, newest first; an action id from `--journal-show` lifts that one. Works with actions switched off, because after misuse the first thing to do is switch them off. sipnab records each unban as a revert. It reports a ban TFPS already dropped rather than unbanning it, and leaves alone a ban it cannot prove it placed. While another sipnab holds the journal it refuses: revert through that sipnab (`POST /v1/actions/revert` or the `actions_revert` MCP tool), or stop it first. Changing TFPS's blocks needs the privileges described in the [TFPS guide](@/docs/tfps-sipnab.md), so on the TFPS host run it as root. Exits `0` when it backed out everything you named or it had already ended, `1` when something remains, `2` when the revert could not run |
| `--tfps-ctl` | `<PATH>` | -- | 0.5.148 | Where the toll-fraud prevention system's `tfps_ctl` program is, for the `tfps_*` MCP tools and the `/v1/tfps/` REST routes. TFPS is optional peer software that condemns sources and enforces the decision in the firewall. sipnab reads its state; asking it to ban or unban a source is an action, refused unless [`--allow-action`](#security) enables it. Absent: sipnab looks for `tfps_ctl` on `PATH` only the moment a TFPS tool runs, and a machine without one answers `installed: false` rather than failing. Config: `[tfps] ctl`; the database goes in `[tfps] db` |
| `--recommend-block` | `<DIALECT>` | -- | 0.5.141 | Print a firewall rule for every source the detectors accused: `fail2ban`, `nftables`, `iptables` or `all`. **sipnab recommends and does not apply** — the rule is text on stdout, and nothing here reaches a firewall or holds a credential. Each block carries its evidence (how many findings named the address, which rules they tripped, and when) and its COUNTER-evidence beside it: a source that also completed a registration or a call is one a block would disconnect, so the address-specific dialects comment their commands out for it and the fail2ban dialect puts it in `ignoreip`. Needs a detector armed beside it; with none, nothing is ever accused and the empty output says which silence that is rather than reading as an all-clear. Requires `-N` |
| `--findings-history` | `<N>` | `1000` | 0.5.96 | Security findings kept in memory for later retrieval. `0` keeps none. Config: `[security] findings_history` |
| `--alert` | `<CHANNEL>` | -- | 0.3.0 | Repeatable alert channel (`syslog`, `json`, `exec`) or rule (`<name>:<threshold>/<window>[:<cooldown>]`). sipnab refuses a channel other than these three, and a rule naming a finding kind no detector reports, with exit `2`; the same value in `[security] alert` exits `1`, naming the key. Config: `[security] alert` |
| `--alert-exec` | `<CMD>` | -- | 0.3.0 | Execute this command when an alert fires. Config: `[security] alert_exec` |
| `--alert-json` | -- | off | 0.4.11 | Emit each security alert as a structured JSON line on stderr (in addition to the human `[ALERT]` line). Config: `[security] alert` |
| `--stir-shaken` | -- | off | 0.3.0 | Report STIR/SHAKEN Identity claims — decodes the PASSporT, does NOT verify the signature. With `--cores N` sipnab refuses it with exit 2, as it refuses the detection flags, because the parallel reader does not report them |
| `--run-provenance-file` | `<FILE>` | -- | 0.5.131 | Record the command that started this run, as one JSON line appended to FILE (`seq`, `ts`, `record`, `argv`, `cwd`, `uid`, `user`, `pid`, `started`, `version`, `features`, `capture`). Use it to trace a report, vCon container or exported pcap back to the capture, filter, port range and retention caps that produced it. `capture` is the same instance token the MCP and REST surfaces stamp on their answers, so a record joins to what that run produced. sipnab writes it once, at startup, before the config takes effect and before it opens any capture device; it reads the config file first, so `capture.node` is the node `--node-name` or `[capture] node_name` sets. Opened `O_APPEND` and never truncated, so successive runs accumulate; created mode `0600` when absent. The record replaces the value of a flag that takes a secret inline, such as `--hep-auth` or `--api-key`, with `[redacted]`. **A record sipnab cannot write stops the run.** Leave it off and nothing changes |
| `--tui-audit-file` | `<FILE>` | -- | 0.5.131 | Record what the operator did in the TUI, one JSON line per action appended to FILE (`seq`, `ts`, `record`, `action`, `target`, `format`, `caller`, `outcome`, `error`). Actions, not keystrokes: the capture opened, the capture swapped, a filter applied or cleared, an export and its destination, including one sipnab refused. **The search field is never recorded**, neither the query nor the fact that the operator typed one. Same writer and same file shape as `--mcp-audit-file`: append-only, never truncated, one sequence number per record so a gap is a lost record, created mode `0600`. A path sipnab cannot open stops the run before sipnab takes the terminal, and sipnab refuses `-N` rather than accepting it with nothing to record. **A write that fails mid-session does NOT stop the TUI**: the lost record leaves a permanent gap in the numbering, the status line says the trail is incomplete, and the closing `session_end` record and the exit message on standard error name the count. Leave it off and nothing changes. Feature: `tui` |

> **`--alert` accepts a channel or a threshold rule.** Channels are `syslog`, `json` or `exec`.
>
> - `--syslog` and `--alert-json` are the equivalent boolean forms. Naming the
>   channel here does the same thing.
> - A value containing `:` is instead parsed as an alert rule
>   (`<name>:<threshold>/<window>[:<cooldown>]`). The window needs an
>   `s`/`m`/`h` suffix.
>
> Rule names are `scanner`, `fraud`, `digest` and
> `reg-flood` (also `reg_flood`).
>
> - An unknown rule name exits 2 at startup.
> - A rule counts detector findings, not raw packets.
>
> An unknown channel exits 2 and names the valid ones:
>
> ```text
> --alert: Unknown alert channel 'bogus': expected one of syslog, json, exec, or a rule written name:threshold/window
> ```

**Examples**
- `sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --no-fraud-detect --report` — skip fraud detection for one run when your config file sets `[security] fraud_detect = true`
- `sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --fraud-detect --no-fraud-detect --report` — the last of the pair wins, so no fraud detector runs
- `sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --no-kill-scanner --report` — analyze without arming the scanner response that your config file's `[security] kill_scanner = true` would arm
- `sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --kill-scanner --no-kill-scanner --report` — the last of the pair wins, so sipnab arms no response
- `sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --kill-scanner-detect-only --report` — report the scanners in a capture; on a live interface the same flag still sends them nothing
- `sudo sipnab -N -d eth0 --kill-scanner-detect-only --fail2ban` — write fail2ban lines for the scanners a live interface sees, and send the scanners nothing
- `sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --no-kill-scanner-detect-only --report` — analyze without the detect-only setting that your config file's `[security] kill_scanner_detect_only = true` turns on
- `sudo sipnab -N -d eth0 --kill-scanner --no-kill-scanner-detect-only` — answer scanners for one run although your config file sets `[security] kill_scanner_detect_only = true`

- `sudo sipnab -d eth0 --kill-scanner --kill-ua 'friendly-scanner' --kill-response 486 --kill-spoof auto` — detect SIP scanners (plus a custom UA pattern) and reply 486 with the victim's spoofed source
- `sudo sipnab -d eth0 --kill-scanner --kill-target 192.0.2.66:5060-5090 --kill-ua 'sipvicious' --kill-response 480 --kill-spoof raw` — targeted kill of a scanning host across a port range, plus a second scanner UA, replying 480 via raw-socket spoof
- `sudo sipnab -d eth0 --kill-target 198.51.100.77:5060 --kill-spoof ephemeral` — kill requests from one more source port using a non-spoofed ephemeral reply
- `sudo sipnab -N -d eth0 --reg-flood --digest-leak --fraud-detect --stir-shaken --alert json --alert-json --alert-exec '/usr/local/bin/notify.sh'` — live security monitoring: registration floods, digest leaks, fraud, STIR/SHAKEN, with JSON alerts and an exec hook
- `sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --stir-shaken --digest-leak --alert-json` — offline audit of a pcap for digest leaks and STIR/SHAKEN attestation claims (as the originator presented them — sipnab checks no signature), emitting structured JSON alerts
- `sudo sipnab -N -d eth0 --reg-flood --reg-flood-threshold 10 --fraud-detect --business-hours 8-18 --fraud-short-call 1` — tune the detectors to a small PBX: ten REGISTERs a second is a brute force here, calls outside office hours are worth a line, and a one-second call is the only one short enough to be a lure
- `sudo sipnab -N -d eth0 --reg-flood --reg-flood-threshold 400 --fraud-detect --business-hours 22-6` — the carrier-registrar shape instead: only a genuine flood clears 400 REGISTERs a second, and the quiet window is overnight
- `sudo sipnab -N -d eth0 --reg-flood --reg-flood-threshold 20 --reg-flood-window 60` — a slow credential-guessing run: twenty refused credentialed REGISTERs from one source inside a minute is a flood, even when no single second holds more than one
- `sipnab -N -I registrar.pcap --reg-flood --reg-flood-transaction-timeout 64000` — a network whose phones run T1 at one second, so RFC 3261 Timer F is 64 seconds and a registrar challenge forty seconds after the REGISTER still answers an open transaction
- `sipnab -N -I trunk.pcap --fraud-detect --fraud-short-call 6 --fraud-wangiri-calls 5 --fraud-sequential-calls 6` — audit a wholesale trunk where short calls are ordinary, so a lure needs five of them and a dial-plan walk needs six consecutive dead numbers
- `sipnab -d eth0 -N --kill-scanner --evidence-out -` — publish findings on standard output for a reader to consume: sipnab says what it saw, and whatever consumes the stream decides what to do about it
- `sipnab -N -I trunk.pcap --kill-scanner --reg-flood --evidence-out findings.jsonl` — replay a capture and collect every source-naming finding in one file, to read before you wire anything to a response
- `sipnab -d eth0 -N --fraud-detect --fraud-destination DO,VG,MA` — an SBC that never dials the Dominican Republic, the British Virgin Islands or Morocco, three destinations where premium-rate fraud concentrates. The first INVITE to any of them alerts on sight
- `sipnab -N -I trunk.pcap --fraud-detect --fraud-destination CU,KP --json` — replay a trunk capture and write every INVITE to an embargoed destination as one JSON line, for the audit that asked whether any call ever went there
- `sipnab -N -I pbx.pcap --fraud-detect --fraud-wangiri-calls 2 --fraud-sequential-calls 2 --fraud-volume-multiplier 3 --fraud-volume-min-calls 4` — the sensitive form for a small PBX, where two short calls to one prefix and four calls in a minute are already unusual
- `sipnab -N -I trunk.pcap --fraud-detect --fraud-volume-multiplier 20 --fraud-volume-min-calls 200` — a busy carrier trunk, where a spike has to be twenty times its own baseline and 200 calls a minute before it means anything
- `sipnab -N -I trunk.pcap --fraud-detect --fraud-wangiri-window 900 --fraud-short-call 5` — hunt a paced lure: three short calls to one prefix over fifteen minutes, which the shipped sixty-second window forgets between calls
- `sipnab -N -I pbx.pcap --fraud-detect --fraud-volume-window 5 --fraud-volume-min-calls 20` — catch a burst shorter than a minute, which a sixty-second window averages into the ordinary traffic around it
- `sudo sipnab -N -d eth0 --fraud-detect --fraud-volume-window 300 --fraud-wangiri-window 300` — a low-volume site where five minutes is the shortest span that holds enough calls to say anything about either pattern
- `sipnab -N -I sbc.pcap --kill-scanner --scanner-behavioral-probes 200 --scanner-enumeration-targets 60` — an SBC that fronts a whole site behind one address, where ordinary aggregated traffic clears the shipped ten probes and five extensions within seconds
- `sipnab -N -I slow-sweep.pcap --kill-scanner --scanner-window 600 --scanner-enumeration-targets 8` — hunt a paced sweep across a ten-minute window: one probe every ten seconds never puts two inside the shipped five-second window, so widening the window is the only setting that reaches it
- `sudo sipnab -N -d eth0 --kill-scanner --scanner-window 60 --scanner-behavioral-probes 40 --scanner-rejected-probes 20` — a busy registrar that refuses every unauthenticated first attempt, so refusals only count as evidence once there are twenty of them in a minute
- `sipnab -N -I sat-trunk.pcap --kill-scanner --scanner-answer-grace 3000 --scanner-unanswered-probes 20` — a satellite trunk whose round trip runs well past RFC 3261's Timer T1, where the shipped 500 ms grace calls every probe still in flight unanswered
- `sudo sipnab -N -d eth0 --kill-scanner --scanner-established-factor 1 --scanner-rejected-probes 8` — judge a registered endpoint like any other source, for a site hunting compromised handsets rather than outside scanners
- `sipnab -N -I pbx.pcap --kill-scanner --scanner-answer-grace 1500 --scanner-established-factor 8 --scanner-unanswered-probes 10` — a small PBX on a slow access circuit, where a registered phone needs eight times the evidence and every probe gets a second and a half to draw a reply
- `sudo sipnab -N -d eth0 --kill-scanner --kill-rate-limit 2 --findings-history 20000` — answer scanners at a deliberately small two responses a second while keeping a long detection history for an agent to read back
- `sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --kill-scanner --recommend-block nftables` — read a capture you already have and print an `nft` rule per accused source, with the evidence and the counter-evidence in the same block. sipnab prints. You decide and run it
- `sipnab -N -I trunk.pcap --kill-scanner --reg-flood --digest-leak --recommend-block all --quiet > blocks.txt` — every dialect for every accused source on a trunk capture, with the packet echo suppressed so the file holds nothing but the recommendation. Read `blocks.txt` before running any of it: an address that also completed a call is one a block disconnects, and the block says so
- `sudo sipnab -N -d eth0 --kill-target 192.0.2.66 --kill-rate-limit 50 --findings-history 0` — a targeted response with a wider transmit budget and no findings retained in memory
- `sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --json --run-provenance-file /var/log/sipnab-runs.jsonl` — record the invocation beside the report, so a reader can trace the JSON above back to the capture, the filters and the build that produced it
- `sudo sipnab -N -d eth0 --portrange 5060-5090 --report --run-provenance-file /var/log/sipnab-runs.jsonl` — the case the record exists for: the port range decided what this run could see, and without the record a later reader cannot tell a narrow run from a complete one
- `sipnab -I capture.pcap --tui-audit-file /var/log/sipnab-tui.jsonl` — record which capture the analyst opened, what they filtered it down to and what they exported, for the review that opens with "who exported which calls"
- `sudo sipnab -d eth0 --tui-audit-file /var/log/sipnab-tui.jsonl --run-provenance-file /var/log/sipnab-runs.jsonl` — both halves on a live capture: one line saying how the session started, and one record per state-changing thing the operator then did
- `sipnab -N -d eth0 --mcp --tfps-ctl /usr/local/bin/tfps_ctl` — serve the MCP tools with TFPS named outright, so `tfps_status` and `tfps_banned` answer from that installation rather than whatever `PATH` finds
- `sipnab -N -I trunk.pcap --api 127.0.0.1:8080 --api-key "$SIPNAB_API_KEY" --tfps-ctl /opt/tfps/bin/tfps_ctl` — replay a capture behind the REST API and let `GET /v1/tfps/labels` fetch the verdict log the label harness scores it against
- `sudo sipnab -N -d eth0 --api 127.0.0.1:8080 --api-signing-key-file /etc/sipnab/api.key --allow-action tfps:rest` — let a REST caller holding a token minted with `--token-scope actions` ask TFPS to ban and unban through `POST /v1/tfps/ban` and `/unban`, and back a ban out through `POST /v1/actions/revert`. Every other credential still reads the TFPS routes and gets `401` on those three
- `sudo sipnab -N -d eth0 --mcp --allow-action tfps:mcp` — let the local agent this process serves over stdio call `tfps_ban`, `tfps_unban` and `actions_revert`. Without the flag the three tools refuse and name it, and the handshake tells the agent this server changes no external system
- `sudo sipnab -N -d eth0 --api 127.0.0.1:8080 --api-signing-key-file /etc/sipnab/api.key --allow-action tfps:rest --journal-dir /srv/sipnab/journal` — the same REST actions with the journal on a dedicated volume rather than under `/var/lib`
- `sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --mcp --allow-action tfps:mcp --journal-dir "$HOME/.local/state/sipnab/journal"` — try the MCP ban tools as an unprivileged user, with the journal in your home directory instead of the system one
- `sipnab --journal-show` — list the bans sipnab placed that are still in force, with the action ids `--revert-actions` takes
- `sipnab --journal-show --journal-dir /srv/sipnab/journal` — the same for a journal kept somewhere other than the default, while the sipnab that writes it keeps running
- `sudo systemctl stop sipnab && sudo sipnab --revert-actions all` — after a stolen token or a bad automation run: stop the service, then lift every ban sipnab placed, newest first. Run as root, because changing TFPS's blocks needs privileges the service gets from its unit
- `sudo sipnab --revert-actions a-r-68d9c1f2-4412-3 --tfps-ctl /opt/tfps/bin/tfps_ctl` — with the service stopped, lift one ban by the action id `--journal-show` printed, asking the TFPS installation named outright


## Event execution

| Flag | Value | Default | Since | Description |
|------|-------|---------|-------|-------------|
| `--on-dialog-exec` | `<CMD>` | -- | 0.3.0 | Execute command when a dialog state changes |
| `--on-quality-exec` | `<CMD>` | -- | 0.3.0 | Execute command when RTP quality drops below threshold |
| `--exec-rate-limit` | `<N>` | `10` | 0.3.0 | Maximum exec invocations per second (rate limit). `0` means no limit |
| `--exec-queue-depth` | `<N>` | `100` | 0.5.100 | Hook commands allowed to be running at once before sipnab drops `--on-dialog-exec` and `--on-quality-exec` events. The second ceiling above `--exec-rate-limit`, and the binding one for any hook that takes longer than a second: its slot is still occupied when the next second's budget arrives, so on a busy trunk this is what events actually meet. Config: `[limits] exec_queue_depth` |

**What a hook receives.** Every command gets the event as environment
variables.

- `--on-dialog-exec` sets `SIPNAB_CALL_ID`, `SIPNAB_FROM`, `SIPNAB_TO`,
  `SIPNAB_STATE`, `SIPNAB_METHOD` and `SIPNAB_JSON` (the whole dialog).
- `--on-quality-exec` sets `SIPNAB_SSRC`, `SIPNAB_MOS`, `SIPNAB_JITTER`,
  `SIPNAB_LOSS` and `SIPNAB_STREAM_JSON`. That last one is the stream object
  under its own name, never `SIPNAB_JSON`.
- `--alert-exec` hooks set `SIPNAB_SRC` (the source address), `SIPNAB_RULE` and
  `SIPNAB_DETAIL`.

**A hook inherits sipnab's whole environment, credentials included.**

- sipnab does not clear the environment before spawning.
- So a hook sees `SIPNAB_API_SIGNING_KEY`, `SIPNAB_MCP_TOKEN` and
  `SIPNAB_HEP_AUTH` if you set them there. [Authentication](@/docs/auth.md)
  recommends exactly that.
- A hook that calls back into the API uses those credentials.

It does mean a hook command is as trusted as the process.

- Do not pass one a string built from capture data.
- Do not run one you would not run by hand with your keys exported.

**Hooks cannot gain privileges.**

- sipnab sets `PR_SET_NO_NEW_PRIVS` at startup on Linux. It does so on every
  run, whether or not it is root.
- Every command it spawns inherits that flag.
- A hook may run anything you can already run.
- What it cannot do is get *more* than you have through a setuid or setgid
  helper. `sudo`, `pkexec` and `ping` start, then fail for want of the
  privilege they normally acquire.

A hook that needs to act privileged should ask something that already is,
rather than trying to become privileged itself. For example:

- a socket to a daemon,
- a `systemd` unit it triggers.

This applies to root runs and to unprivileged runs set up with
`sipnab --setup-caps`.

**Examples**

- `sudo sipnab -d eth0 --on-dialog-exec 'logger sipnab $SIPNAB_CALL_ID' --exec-rate-limit 5 --exec-queue-depth 20` — a slow syslog hook on a busy trunk, where twenty concurrent children is the ceiling events actually meet rather than the five-a-second budget
- `sipnab -N -I trunk.pcap --on-quality-exec 'curl -m 30 -X POST http://hook/quality' --exec-queue-depth 4` — a webhook that may take thirty seconds, held to four in flight so a stalled endpoint cannot fork the box flat


## Network listeners

| Flag | Value | Default | Since | Description |
|------|-------|---------|-------|-------------|
| `--metrics` | `<ADDR>` | -- | 0.3.0 | Prometheus metrics endpoint (e.g., `127.0.0.1:9090`). Serves in BOTH TUI and headless (`-N`) runs — headless is where a container or systemd unit uses it. sipnab **refuses** a non-loopback bind (e.g. `0.0.0.0:9090`) unless you also pass `--metrics-auth`/`--metrics-auth-file`, and the run then exits non-zero rather than carrying on without an endpoint — so in `sipnab -N -d eth0 --metrics 0.0.0.0:9090 && echo serving` the `echo` never runs, matching `--api`. Note a file run (`-I`) exits as soon as it finishes the capture, so there is little to scrape; the endpoint is for long-lived runs — a live device, `--hep-listen`, or a served API/MCP. Not served on the `--cores N` parallel offline path, which finishes and exits before a scrape could land; sipnab warns when you combine them. Feature: `metrics` |
| `--metrics-auth` | `<USER:PASS>` | -- | 0.3.0 | HTTP Basic auth credentials (`user:pass`) required by the metrics endpoint; requests must send `Authorization: Basic <base64>`. Prefer `--metrics-auth-file`. Feature: `metrics` |
| `--metrics-auth-file` | `<FILE>` | -- | 0.5.28 | Read the metrics Basic-auth `user:pass` from a file (contents trimmed), keeping the secret out of the process list. Takes precedence over `--metrics-auth`. Feature: `metrics` |
| `--metrics-tls-cert` | `<FILE>` | -- | 0.5.203 | Serve the metrics endpoint over HTTPS with this PEM certificate chain, the server's certificate first. Needs `--metrics-tls-key`; either alone stops sipnab at startup rather than serving plain HTTP on a port meant for HTTPS. The port then speaks HTTPS only: TLS 1.2 and 1.3, no client certificates; scrapers still authenticate with `--metrics-auth`. A file sipnab cannot read, or that holds no certificate, stops it at startup naming the file. Refused without `--metrics`. See [Metrics TLS](@/docs/metrics.md#metrics-tls). sipnab refuses an empty path with exit `2`, and an empty `[metrics] tls_cert` with exit `1`. Feature: `metrics`. Config: `[metrics] tls_cert` |
| `--metrics-tls-key` | `<FILE>` | -- | 0.5.203 | PEM private key for `--metrics-tls-cert`. sipnab **refuses a key any other user on the host can read** (`chmod 600` it; group-readable stays allowed), a file with no private key, and a key that does not belong to the certificate, each at startup and naming the file. Refused without `--metrics`. sipnab refuses an empty path with exit `2`, and an empty `[metrics] tls_key` with exit `1`. Feature: `metrics`. Config: `[metrics] tls_key` |

| `--api-tls-cert` | `<FILE>` | -- | 0.3.0 | Serve the REST API over HTTPS with this PEM certificate chain, the server's certificate first. A reverse proxy in front of a loopback bind remains an alternative. See [API TLS](@/docs/api.md#api-tls). sipnab refuses an empty path with exit `2`, and an empty `[api] tls_cert` with exit `1`. Feature: `api`. Config: `[api] tls_cert` |
| `--api-tls-key` | `<FILE>` | -- | 0.3.0 | PEM private key for `--api-tls-cert`. sipnab **refuses a key any other user on the host can read** (`chmod 600` it; group-readable stays allowed), a file with no private key, and a key that does not belong to the certificate, each at startup and naming the file. sipnab refuses an empty path with exit `2`, and an empty `[api] tls_key` with exit `1`. | `--api-max-conn` | `<N>` | `100` | 0.3.0 | Maximum API requests handled at once; sipnab answers 503 to a request past it. `0` means no limit. Feature: `api` |
| `--api-allowed-host` | `<HOST>` | -- | 0.5.198 | Additional `Host` header values the REST API accepts (repeatable), against DNS rebinding: a web page that points its own name at `127.0.0.1` and reads a loopback API with no key from your browser. Accepted by default: `localhost`, `127.0.0.1`, `::1` and the address `--api` binds, on any port, and any IP address when `--api` binds `0.0.0.0` or `::`. Add the name clients use, such as a reverse proxy's public name; `name:port` accepts that port only. Any other `Host` gets `403`, and a request with no `Host` gets `400`. `*` disables the check (not recommended). See [Which `Host` names the API answers](@/docs/api.md#which-host-names-the-api-answers). Config: `[api] allowed_hosts`, which the flag replaces Feature: `api` |

| `--api-signing-key-file` | `<FILE>` | -- | 0.4.3 | Read an API signing key from a file (contents trimmed); it becomes the minting key. Feature: `api` |

| `--api-token-ttl` | `<SECS>` | `3600` | 0.4.3 | Default TTL (seconds) when minting API tokens with `--mint-token`. Feature: `api` |
| `--api-max-rows` | `<N>` | `1000` | 0.5.100 | Rows one list-style REST response returns. The REST counterpart of `--mcp-max-rows`. Raise it for a batch consumer that reads every row of `/v1/dialogs`; lower it for a dashboard. A caller may always ask for less with `?limit=`, and nothing it sends asks for more than this. Config: `[limits] api_max_rows` Feature: `api` |
| `--api-rate-limit-per-peer` | `<N>` | `100` | 0.5.100 | REST requests one client IP may make per second; `0` disables the cap, the reading `--mcp-rate-limit-per-peer` and `--hep-rate-limit` also give it. The limiter counts by source address, so a dashboard polling `/v1/streams` on a short timer, or several collectors behind one NAT, share a single allowance. A refused request gets `503`, not `429`: the limiter runs before authentication and says nothing about the credential. Config: `[limits] api_rate_limit_per_peer` Feature: `api` |
| `--api-allow-relay-query` | -- | -- | 0.5.170 | Let REST clients query the relay named by `--rtpengine-control` through the six `GET /v1/relay/` routes (`stats`, `stats/names`, `stats/call/{call_id}`, `compare/{call_id}`, `holdings` and `holdings/{call_id}`), which transmit. The REST counterpart of `--mcp-allow-relay-query`, off for the same reason: every other REST answer comes from bytes sipnab already holds, and these put a packet on the network — at the address that flag names, never one a client chooses. Without a relay address (no `--rtpengine-control`), those routes answer `not_configured`. With one, they answer `not_permitted` when this flag is absent, and on a file-backed run even with the flag. Each response is HTTP 200 carrying an `outcome`, so a refusal is content, not a 4xx. Polling on an interval is not offered over REST at all. Feature: `api` |
| `--api-allow-vcon-fetch` | -- | off | 0.5.221 | Let REST clients read one vCon by uuid from the store the `[vcon_fetch]` keys configure, through [`GET /v1/vcon/fetch/:uuid`](@/docs/api.md#get-v1-vcon-fetch-uuid), which connects to that store. The REST counterpart of `--mcp-allow-vcon-fetch`, off for the same reason. The store, its kind, the credential and the decryption key come from `[vcon_fetch]` only, never from the request, and the answer holds no key. Without this flag the route answers `503` naming it; with it and no `[vcon_fetch] url`, `503` naming the keys. sipnab stops at startup when it cannot read the store's credential or key file. The container comes back in the answer, and sipnab writes no file. Feature: `api` and `vcon` |
| `--api-accept-archive-passwords` | -- | off | 0.5.187 | Accept the `Sipnab-Archive-Password` header on `GET /v1/captures/compare` from a client that is not on this host. Without `--api-tls-cert` sipnab serves plain HTTP, so the password crosses the network in the clear unless TLS terminates in front: making sure it does is your job when you pass this. Without it, only a loopback client may send one, and a remote one gets `403`, also when `--api-tls-cert` serves HTTPS. Feature: `api` |
| `--api-file-root` | `<DIR>` | -- | 0.5.177 | Directory of capture files `GET /v1/captures/compare` may diff. The REST counterpart of `--mcp-file-root`, off for the same reason: every other REST answer comes from bytes sipnab already holds, while this reads FILES a client names. It takes a bare FILENAME, never a path: sipnab rejects a separator, a `..`, an absolute prefix or a control character before touching the filesystem, and refuses a symlink that resolves out of the root at open, by the same check `-O` uses. Without this flag the compare route answers `503`. Naming one directory means the worst a client can do is name files inside it. Feature: `api` |
| `--metrics-max-conn` | `<N>` | `16` | 0.5.100 | Metrics scrapes served at once before further ones get `503`. Sixteen suits one Prometheus server; raise it when an HA pair, a federating parent, `remote_write` shards or sidecars scrape the same endpoint. A refused scrape leaves a gap in the series. Config: `[limits] metrics_max_conn` Feature: `metrics` |
| `-L`, `--hep-listen` | `<ADDR>` | -- | 0.3.0 | Listen for HEP (Homer Encapsulation Protocol) packets. **Combines with `-d <iface>`**: HEP then supplies signaling while the interface supplies the RTP a HEP feed cannot carry, and streams bind to dialogs by SDP media endpoint. With no BPF expression of your own, the interface gets a media-only default, since the mirror carries the signaling; an explicit expression such as `sipnab -N -d eth0 -L 127.0.0.1:9060 "udp portrange 10000-20000"` narrows it to your media ports. One interface and one listener only: `--multi-device` with `-L`, `-I` with `-L`, and `-O` alongside the pair are each refused with the reason. See [cookbook recipe "Take signaling from HEP and media off the wire, in one process"](@/docs/cookbook.md#take-signaling-from-hep-and-media-off-the-wire-in-one-process). The decrypted TLS and WebSocket legs OpenSIPS and Kamailio trace arrive with IP protocol 22, 50 or 6 and decode as TLS, WS or WSS, see [How `--hep-listen` reads the transport](#how-hep-listen-reads-the-transport). `--portrange` does not apply to HEP messages, so a proxy tracing SIP on 7060 needs no `--portrange 1-65535`. Each message takes the time its HEP packet carries; a HEP v3 packet without a `TS_SEC` chunk, and a HEP v1 packet, take the time sipnab received them. sipnab reads HEP v1 and v2 packets in the layout the `captagent` capture agent writes and Kamailio's `sipcapture` module reads: IPv4 or IPv6 addresses by the family byte, the transport by the IP protocol byte, and for v2 the time and capture ID in its time header. Feature: `hep` |
| `-H`, `--hep-send` | `<ADDR>` | -- | 0.3.0 | Send captured packets via HEP to a remote collector: SIP as protocol type 1, and RTCP as type 5 in the JSON form heplify sends, carrying the Call-ID of the call whose SDP set up that media. RTCP for a call whose SDP sipnab never saw is not sent, since Homer stores none of it. RTP is never forwarded. **On `-I <file>` this forwards the file's contents**: every SIP message sipnab reads out of the capture goes to `<ADDR>` as recorded, and every RTCP report of a call in it as JSON, redacted in no way. sipnab announces that at startup, naming the flag, the destination and the capture files, before it reads the first packet. See [What `--hep-send` sends](#what-hep-send-sends). **A headless run ends with one line saying what it exported**: packets sent, queued, replayed after an outage, dropped by reason (`queue_full`, `stopped`, `unsent_at_exit`), still queued, failed attempts by kind (`connect`, `tls_handshake`, `write`) and reconnects, at `warn` when anything failed or sipnab dropped a packet. Over UDP "sent" means handed to the kernel, and a collector that is down produces no failure; the line says so. `runtime_stats`, `GET /v1/runtime` (`hep_export`) and the Prometheus `sipnab_hep_export_*` series carry the same counts while it runs. Feature: `hep` |
| `--hep-send-transport` | `<udp\|tcp\|tls>` | `udp` | 0.5.150 | Transport `--hep-send` uses to reach the collector. Homer's collectors accept all three. HEP v3 carries its own total length, so a `tcp` or `tls` feed is packets laid end to end with no extra framing, and sipnab sets `TCP_NODELAY` because these are small packets whose value is timeliness. sipnab opens the first connection at startup: when the collector refuses it, or it does not complete within `--hep-send-timeout` (default 3 seconds), sipnab stops with exit `2` and names the error, such as `Failed to connect HEP sender to '127.0.0.1:9061' over TCP: Connection refused (os error 111)`. After that, a write that fails keeps its packet queued and drops the connection, and the sending thread dials again with backoff, never in a tight loop. Each dial gives up after `--hep-send-timeout` and counts as a `connect` failure, as a refused one does. See [When the `--hep-send` collector goes away](#when-the-hep-send-collector-goes-away). Refused without `--hep-send`, which is the side it governs. Feature: `hep` |
| `--hep-send-queue` | `<MIB>` | `64` | 0.5.226 | How many MiB of HEP packets `--hep-send` holds while the collector is unreachable, 1 to 4096. Sending runs on its own thread behind this queue, so a slow or dead collector never slows the capture, and sipnab replays the queue in capture order when the collector answers. At the bound sipnab drops the **oldest** packet and counts it as `queue_full`. A stop (SIGINT/SIGTERM) discards the queue and counts it as `stopped`: sipnab flushes nothing at shutdown. Refused without `--hep-send`; `[hep] send_queue_mib` on a run without `--hep-send` gets a startup warning naming it instead. Config: `[hep] send_queue_mib`. Feature: `hep` |
| `--hep-send-timeout` | `<SECS>` | `3` | 0.5.226 | Seconds one TCP dial or stalled write to the `--hep-send` collector may take before the collector counts as unreachable, 1 to 300. It also bounds the first connection at startup, which fails the run with exit `2`. A TLS handshake keeps its own 10-second bound. Retries back off from 0.1 s, doubling, to at most 5 s. A file read to its end waits for the queue to drain, and gives up after two timeouts plus 5 s with no delivery. Refused without `--hep-send`; `[hep] send_timeout_secs` on a run without `--hep-send` gets a startup warning naming it instead. Config: `[hep] send_timeout_secs`. Feature: `hep` |
| `--hep-listen-transport` | `<udp\|tcp\|tls>` | `udp` | 0.5.150 | Transport `--hep-listen` accepts. A `tcp` or `tls` listener serves several agents at once, one connection each, and reads every connection as HEP v3 packets delimited by the total length in each header. **HEP v1 and v2 are datagram-only**: they declare no total length, so nothing can delimit it on a stream. A peer that sends bytes that are not HEP v3 loses its connection, because a stream offers no point to resynchronize at. Refused without `--hep-listen`, which is the side it governs. Feature: `hep` |
| `--hep-tls-ca` | `<FILE>` | -- | 0.5.150 | Certificate authority (PEM) this sender checks the collector's certificate against under `--hep-send-transport tls`. A named CA **replaces** the trust store rather than joining it, so a private collector's issuer is the whole of what this sender accepts (`--hep-tls-extra-ca` adds a CA to the host's bundle instead); a file sipnab cannot read, or that holds no certificate, raises an error rather than an empty store. Omit it to use the host's CA bundle (`$SSL_CERT_FILE`, else `/etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt` and its equivalents). sipnab refuses it unless `--hep-send-transport tls` names the transport. Feature: `hep`. Config: `[hep] tls_ca` |
| `--hep-tls-extra-ca` | `<FILE>` | -- | 0.5.203 | Certificate authority (PEM) this sender trusts **in addition to** the host's CA bundle under `--hep-send-transport tls`: the sender accepts the collector's certificate when the host's bundle or this file issued it. Use it for a collector whose certificate comes from a private CA on a host whose public roots should still count; use `--hep-tls-ca` to trust only the named file. sipnab refuses the two flags together. The file must hold at least one certificate, and the host must have a CA bundle to add it to: on a host without one, sipnab refuses at startup and names `--hep-tls-ca`. sipnab refuses it unless `--hep-send-transport tls` names the transport. Feature: `hep`. Config: `[hep] tls_extra_ca` |
| `--hep-tls-cert` | `<FILE>` | -- | 0.5.150 | Server certificate chain (PEM, leaf first) a `--hep-listen-transport tls` listener presents to connecting agents. It must be an end-entity certificate: rustls refuses a CA certificate offered as a server certificate. sipnab refuses it unless `--hep-listen-transport tls` names the transport, and that transport requires it. Feature: `hep`. Config: `[hep] tls_cert` |
| `--hep-tls-key` | `<FILE>` | -- | 0.5.150 | Private key (PEM) for `--hep-tls-cert`. sipnab **refuses a key any other user on the host can read** — `chmod 600` it. Group-readable stays allowed, because `root:sipnab 0640` is how a key is normally handed to a service account. sipnab refuses it unless `--hep-listen-transport tls` names the transport, and that transport requires it. Feature: `hep`. Config: `[hep] tls_key` |
| `--hep-id` | `<ID>` | `1` | 0.5.8 | Capture-agent id (HEP `0x000c` chunk) stamped on packets sent via `--hep-send`. Refused without `--hep-send`, the side it governs, exit `2`. Feature: `hep` |
| `--hep-auth` | `<KEY>` | -- | 0.5.8 | Homer authenticate key (HEP `0x000e` chunk). On `--hep-send` sipnab stamps it on every outgoing packet; on `--hep-listen` it **enables receiver-side authentication** — incoming packets must carry a matching key, which sipnab compares in constant time, or it drops them. Also read from `SIPNAB_HEP_AUTH`; `--help` names the variable and never shows its value. **Security note:** the key travels in cleartext inside the HEP datagram, so it defeats blind/off-path spoofing but an on-path sniffer can capture and replay it. Over an untrusted path, tunnel HEP through WireGuard/IPsec/stunnel (the same posture as terminating API TLS in a reverse proxy) rather than relying on the key alone. Feature: `hep` |
| `--hep-auth-file` | `<FILE>` | -- | 0.5.28 | Read the HEP shared secret from a file (contents trimmed), keeping it out of the process list. Takes precedence over `--hep-auth`. Refused without `--hep-listen` or `--hep-send`, the two sides it governs, exit `2`. Feature: `hep` |
| `--hep-auth-mode` | `<plain\|hmac>` | `plain` | 0.5.28 | HEP auth mode. `plain` sends/expects the shared secret verbatim in the 0x000e chunk (Homer-compatible, but replayable by an on-path sniffer). `hmac` sends/expects a per-message token (timestamp + nonce + HMAC-SHA256 over the payload) that resists replay — **sipnab-to-sipnab only**; a stock Homer/Kamailio peer does not understand it. Refused without `--hep-listen` or `--hep-send`, the two sides it governs, exit `2`. Feature: `hep` |
| `--hep-hmac-window` | `<SECS>` | `30` | 0.5.100 | Seconds either side of now within which sipnab still honors a `--hep-auth-mode hmac` token's timestamp. When the agent's and the collector's clocks differ by more than this, sipnab refuses every packet as out of window and the listener admits nothing; `--hep-silence-warn` then names `hmac_timestamp_out_of_window`. A wider window keeps a packet captured on the path replayable for longer. Range 1-300. Refused without `--hep-listen`, the side that checks the window, exit `2`; a `[security] hep_hmac_window_secs` on a run without `--hep-listen` gets a startup warning naming it instead. Config: `[security] hep_hmac_window_secs`. Feature: `hep` |
| `--hep-silence-warn` | `<SECS>` | `30` | 0.5.185 | Seconds a `--hep-listen` listener may go without **admitting** a packet before it logs a warning; `0` turns the warning off. Only an admitted packet counts as traffic. When packets keep arriving and sipnab refuses every one, the warning says `no packets admitted` and names the refusal most of them met (`auth_mismatch`, `allowlist`, `hmac_timestamp_out_of_window` and so on) and a peer that sent them: the sender is reaching the port and sipnab is turning it away, which is a key, mode or allowlist problem rather than a network one. When nothing arrives at all the warning keeps its `no packets for` wording. Refused without `--hep-listen`, which is the side it governs. Feature: `hep` |
| `--hep-senders` | -- | off | 0.5.185 | At the end of a headless (`-N`) run, print who fed the `--hep-listen` listener: each sender, keyed by the capture id it claims and the address it sent from, with its packet count, when sipnab last heard from it, how long it has been idle and whether it went silent past `--hep-silence-warn`; then every address the listener refused, with counts by reason, and the refusal totals. The capture id is the sender's claim, never proven. With `--json`, the same as one JSON object on the last line of stdout, the shape `GET /v1/hep/senders` and the MCP `hep_senders` tool return. The roster covers this run only and nothing persists it. Refused without `--hep-listen`, which is the side it describes. Feature: `hep` |
| `-E`, `--hep-parse` | -- | off | 0.3.0 | Parse incoming HEP packets (enable HEP decoding): sipnab unwraps a HEP datagram on the wire or in a capture file and reads its message with the addresses the HEP chunks carry and the time the HEP packet carries, as `-L` does, not the time sipnab sniffed the wrapper. A HEP packet that carries no time (a HEP v3 packet without a `TS_SEC` chunk, or a HEP v1 packet) keeps the time sipnab sniffed the wrapper; a HEP v2 packet carries its time in its time header. Sniffing a HEP port that no process listens on loses messages from some senders: see the note under [`[capture]` in the configuration reference](@/docs/config.md#capture). The transport comes from the IP protocol chunk by the same rule `--hep-listen` uses, so a TLS, WS or WSS leg an OpenSIPS or Kamailio tracer sends reads the same from a file as from a socket, see [How `--hep-listen` reads the transport](#how-hep-listen-reads-the-transport). `--portrange` does not apply to the HEP messages it unwraps. It still gates SIP that sipnab captures directly. It applies wherever sipnab reads packets: a headless run, `--cores N`, the TUI's own capture, and a capture opened or re-scanned inside the TUI. `--no-hep-parse` turns it off again when the config file sets `[capture] hep_parse = true`. Config: `[capture] hep_parse`. Feature: `hep` |
| `--no-hep-parse` | -- | off | 0.5.204 | Do not unwrap HEP found in the capture, even when `[capture] hep_parse = true`. The last of `-E` / `--no-hep-parse` typed wins. Config: `[capture] hep_parse`. Feature: `hep` |
| `--hep-allow` | `<ADDR>` | -- | 0.3.0 | Allowed source addresses for HEP input (repeatable). Takes CIDR (`192.0.2.0/8`, `2001:db8::/32`) or a **bare address** (`192.0.2.40`), which means that host alone — `/32` for IPv4, `/128` for IPv6. A missing prefix always narrows, never widens: `192.0.2.0` is one host, not `192.0.2.0/8`. sipnab **refuses** a non-loopback `--hep-listen` bind unless you pass either this or `--hep-auth`/`--hep-auth-file`. Refused without `--hep-listen`, the side it governs, exit `2`; `-E` reads no allowlist. Feature: `hep` |
| `--hep-rate-limit` | `<N>` | `50000` | 0.3.0 | Maximum HEP packets per second (global ceiling across all senders); `0` disables the global ceiling, consistent with `off` on the per-peer knob. Refused without `--hep-listen`, the side it governs, exit `2`; a `[limits] hep_rate_limit` on a run without `--hep-listen` gets a startup warning naming it instead, because one config file serves runs with and without a listener. Feature: `hep`. Config: `[limits] hep_rate_limit` |
| `--hep-rate-limit-per-peer` | `<N\|auto\|off>` | `off` | 0.5.28 | Maximum HEP packets/second from any single source IP: a number, `off` (the default), or `auto`. Adds fairness so one flooding peer cannot exhaust the global `--hep-rate-limit`. `auto` divides the global ceiling evenly across the `--hep-allow` sources (stays off without an allowlist). The listener logs its active limiters at startup. Refused without `--hep-listen`, the side it governs, exit `2`. Feature: `hep` |
| `--hep-allow-kill` | -- | off | 0.5.28 | Allow scanner-kill to send active responses for packets received via HEP, and admit HEP-carried detections to the `--fail2ban` jail log. **Off by default**: a HEP sender asserts the inner src/dst, so absent `--hep-auth` an attacker could aim the kill at a victim of their choosing, or have the jail ban an address of their choosing. Only enable with authenticated, trusted HEP input. Feature: `hep` |
| `--syslog` | -- | off | 0.3.0 | Send alerts to syslog. Config: `[security] alert` |
| `--mint-token` | -- | off | 0.4.3 | Mint a signed bearer token from the first configured signing key (API or MCP), print it to stdout, and exit (no capture/servers). See [`auth.md`](@/docs/auth.md). |
| `--token-id` | `<ID>` | -- | 0.4.3 | Token id (`jti`) for `--mint-token`, used for revocation. Defaults to a generated id. |
| `--token-scope` | `<full\|metrics\|read\|actions\|admin\|audio>` | `full` | 0.5.59 | Scope for `--mint-token`. `metrics` reaches `GET /metrics` and returns `401` everywhere else — mint one for a scrape job rather than a credential that also reads `/v1/dialogs` and the message bodies underneath. `read` is the MCP counterpart: it reaches the tools annotated read-only and refuses every tool that writes or replaces state (`export_capture`, `open_capture`, `shutdown_server`, `tfps_ban` and the rest; `tools/list` marks each one with `readOnlyHint: false`). `actions` reaches everything `full` does plus the actions that change another system, such as TFPS ban and unban, where the server enabled them with [`--allow-action`](#security); a `full` token never reaches an action. A ban belongs to the caller that placed it, so an `actions` token lifts only its own bans; `admin` reaches everything `actions` does and also lifts a ban another caller placed. `audio` reaches the REST API's live call audio routes (`GET /v1/calls/live`, `GET /v1/calls/live/events` and `GET /v1/calls/{call_id}/audio`) and nothing else, and no other scope reaches them. A cross-surface mint fails at mint time, so sipnab refuses `metrics` and `audio` with MCP and `read` with the REST API rather than issuing them and then rejecting them. |

**Examples**
- `sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --no-hep-parse --report` — read HEP datagrams as plain UDP when your config file sets `[capture] hep_parse = true`
- `sipnab -N -I capture.pcap -E --no-hep-parse --report` — the last of the pair wins, so HEP is not unwrapped

- `sudo sipnab -d eth0 --api 127.0.0.1:8080 --api-signing-key-file /etc/sipnab/signing.key --api-revoked-file /etc/sipnab/revoked.txt --api-token-ttl 7200 --api-max-conn 200 --metrics 127.0.0.1:9090 --metrics-auth alice:s3cret` — live capture serving a signed-token REST API, a revocation list, and a Basic-auth'd Prometheus endpoint (loopback, so no TLS)
- `sudo sipnab -d eth0 --api 0.0.0.0:8080 --api-signing-key-file /etc/sipnab/signing.key --api-token-ttl 3600 --api-max-conn 100 --metrics 127.0.0.1:9090 --metrics-auth bob:hunter2` — public-facing API tuned to 100 connections and 1h token TTL, with its own auth'd metrics endpoint
- `sudo sipnab -N -d eth0 --api 127.0.0.1:8080 --api-key s3cret --api-max-rows 100000 --api-rate-limit-per-peer 0` — a batch consumer's API: one `GET /v1/dialogs?limit=100000` drains the whole store in a single page, and the per-peer cap is off so a scripted pager is not throttled against itself
- `sudo sipnab -N -d eth0 --api 127.0.0.1:8080 --api-key s3cret --api-max-rows 200 --api-rate-limit-per-peer 600` — the opposite, for a dashboard: short pages a browser can render, and six hundred requests a second per address, so a dozen browsers refreshing twice a second behind one office NAT share an allowance that fits them
- `sudo sipnab -N -d eth0 --api 127.0.0.1:8080 --api-key s3cret --rtpengine-control 127.0.0.1:22222 --api-allow-relay-query` — a live capture whose REST clients may also ask the relay: `GET /v1/relay/stats` returns its counters as one JSON object with an `outcome`, transmitting once per request. Off without this flag, when those routes answer `not_permitted`
- `sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --api 127.0.0.1:8080 --api-key s3cret --api-allow-relay-query --rtpengine-control 127.0.0.1:22222` — the relay routes still answer on a file run, but with `outcome: not_permitted`: a file-backed run holds no transmit permit, so no packet reaches the relay, and the addresses in a capture belong to third parties
- `sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --config sipnab.toml --api 127.0.0.1:8080 --api-key s3cret --api-allow-vcon-fetch` — REST clients may read one vCon by uuid with `GET /v1/vcon/fetch/:uuid` from the store `[vcon_fetch]` names; without the flag that route answers `503`
- `sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --config sipnab.toml --api 127.0.0.1:8080 --api-key s3cret --api-allow-vcon-fetch --mcp --mcp-transport http --mcp-allow-vcon-fetch` — both doors, each opted in by its own flag and reading the one store `[vcon_fetch]` names
- `sipnab -N -I today.pcap --api 127.0.0.1:8080 --api-key s3cret --api-file-root /srv/pcaps --archive-password-file /etc/sipnab/pcaps.pw` — the compare route opens password-protected ZIPs under `/srv/pcaps` with the operator's passwords, and a local client may add one per request in the `Sipnab-Archive-Password` header
- `sipnab -N -I today.pcap --api 0.0.0.0:8080 --api-key s3cret --api-file-root /srv/pcaps --api-accept-archive-passwords` — behind a TLS proxy on another host: remote clients may send `Sipnab-Archive-Password`, which without the flag get `403` because the password would cross the network in the clear
- `sipnab -N -I today.pcap --api 127.0.0.1:8080 --api-key s3cret --api-file-root /srv/pcaps --api-accept-archive-passwords --archive-password-file /etc/sipnab/pcaps.pw` — both at once: configured passwords first, then the request's
- `sudo sipnab -N -d eth0 --api 127.0.0.1:8080 --api-key s3cret --api-file-root /var/lib/sipnab/captures` — a live capture whose REST clients may also diff rotations: `GET /v1/captures/compare?a=yesterday.pcap&b=today.pcap` reads two files from that one directory and nothing outside it, ranking what moved. Off without the flag, when the route answers `503`
- `sudo sipnab -N -d eth0 --api 0.0.0.0:8443 --api-signing-key-file /etc/sipnab/signing.key --api-tls-cert /etc/sipnab/api.pem --api-tls-key /etc/sipnab/api.key` — a public-facing API over HTTPS with no reverse proxy: signed tokens, a certificate whose key is `chmod 600`, and no plain-HTTP warning at startup
- `sudo sipnab -N -d eth0 --api 127.0.0.1:8080 --api-key s3cret --api-allowed-host sipnab.example.com` — behind a reverse proxy that forwards `Host: sipnab.example.com` unchanged: sipnab serves that name, while a page that rebinds any other name to `127.0.0.1` gets `403`
- `sudo sipnab -N -d eth0 --api 0.0.0.0:8443 --api-signing-key-file /etc/sipnab/signing.key --api-tls-cert /etc/sipnab/api.pem --api-tls-key /etc/sipnab/api.key --api-allowed-host capture.example.com:8443` — a public-facing HTTPS API reached by name on port 8443 only: sipnab serves `Host: capture.example.com:8443` and refuses the same name on any other port. Clients reaching it by IP address need no entry on a wildcard bind
- `sipnab -N -I today.pcap --api 127.0.0.1:8443 --api-key s3cret --api-tls-cert api.pem --api-tls-key api.key` — HTTPS on loopback, for a client that insists on `https://` even on the same host; `api.pem` must name `127.0.0.1` for the client to accept it
- `sipnab -N -I today.pcap --api 127.0.0.1:8080 --api-key s3cret --api-file-root /srv/pcaps` — the compare route works on a file-backed run too: it diffs the two NAMED files under `/srv/pcaps`, never the loaded `today.pcap`, so a monitoring box can poll one sipnab for a rolling day-over-day comparison
- `sudo sipnab -N -d eth0 --metrics 127.0.0.1:9090 --metrics-max-conn 64` — an HA Prometheus pair, a federating parent, a `remote_write` shard and an alertmanager sidecar all scraping one sipnab: at sixteen slots a slow scrape turns the next one away with `503`, and the hole in the series reads as a capture that died
- `sudo sipnab -N -d eth0 --metrics 127.0.0.1:9090 --metrics-max-conn 2` — a single scraper on a small box, where two slots covers every client this endpoint has, and a third connection is something to turn away
- `sipnab -N -L 0.0.0.0:9060 --hep-parse --hep-auth-file /etc/sipnab/hep.key --hep-auth-mode hmac --hep-hmac-window 120` — a collector whose agents run on hardware with a drifting clock: two minutes of tolerance keeps them heard while someone repairs the NTP problem
- `sipnab -N -L 127.0.0.1:9060 --hep-parse --hep-auth-file /etc/sipnab/hep.key --hep-auth-mode hmac --hep-hmac-window 5` — the opposite, where every agent shares a local time source: five seconds narrows the replay window a captured packet stays valid in
- `sipnab -N -L 0.0.0.0:9060 --hep-parse --hep-auth-file /etc/sipnab/hep.key --hep-silence-warn 300` — a collector fed by PBXes that go quiet overnight: five minutes without an admitted packet before the listener warns, so a site with no calls overnight does not fill the journal
- `sipnab -N -L 127.0.0.1:9060 --hep-parse --hep-silence-warn 0` — a lab listener fed by hand, where long silences are normal and the warning would only be noise
- `sipnab -N -L 0.0.0.0:9060 --hep-parse --hep-auth-file /etc/sipnab/hep.key --duration 300 --hep-senders` — five minutes of a collector's feed, then the roster: which proxies sent and how much, which went silent, and which addresses the listener turned away and why
- `sipnab -N -L 127.0.0.1:9060 --hep-parse --hep-senders --count 5000 --json` — the same roster as one JSON object on the last line of stdout, after the per-message lines, for a script to pick up with `tail -1`
- `sudo sipnab -N -d eth0 --mcp --mcp-transport http --mcp-bind 127.0.0.1:8731 --mcp-token t0ken-alice --mcp-signing-key-file /etc/sipnab/mcp-signing.key --mcp-revoked-file /etc/sipnab/mcp-revoked.txt --mcp-token-ttl 1800` — loopback HTTP MCP server with a bearer token, file-loaded signing key, revocation denylist, and a 30-minute mint TTL
- `sudo sipnab -N -d eth0 --mcp --mcp-transport http --mcp-bind 0.0.0.0:8731 --mcp-token t0ken-bob --mcp-signing-key-file /etc/sipnab/mcp-signing.key --mcp-revoked-file /etc/sipnab/mcp-revoked.txt --mcp-allowed-host mcp.example.com` — non-loopback HTTP MCP server (token required) accepting an extra Host header for named clients
- `sudo sipnab -N -d eth0 --mcp --mcp-transport http --mcp-bind 0.0.0.0:8731 --mcp-token-file /etc/sipnab/mcp.token --mcp-allowed-host mcp.example.com --mcp-tls-cert /etc/sipnab/mcp.pem --mcp-tls-key /etc/sipnab/mcp.key` — a non-loopback MCP server serving HTTPS itself, with no nginx in front: the bearer token and every tool result cross the network encrypted
- `sipnab -N -I today.pcap --mcp --mcp-transport http --mcp-bind 127.0.0.1:8731 --mcp-tls-cert mcp.pem --mcp-tls-key mcp.key` — HTTPS on loopback, for an agent that insists on `https://` even on the same host; `mcp.pem` must name `127.0.0.1` for the agent to accept it
- `sudo sipnab -N -d eth0 --hep-send 192.0.2.10:9060 --hep-id 42 --hep-auth s3cr3t-homer-key` — forward captured packets to a Homer collector, stamping capture-agent id 42 and an authenticate key
- `sudo sipnab -N -d eth0 --hep-send 198.51.100.20:9060 --hep-id 7 --hep-auth homerkey2` — forward to a second collector under a different agent id and auth key
