- `sudo sipnab -N -d eth0 --hep-send 198.51.100.30:9060 --hep-auth-file /etc/sipnab/hep.key --hep-auth-mode hmac` — replay-resistant forwarding to another sipnab: HMAC-token auth over an untrusted path (both ends must set --hep-auth-mode hmac)
- `sipnab -N -I archive.pcap --hep-send 127.0.0.1:9060 --hep-id 9` — replay an archived capture into a collector on this host. sipnab warns at startup that the file's signaling leaves the machine, then forwards it
- `sipnab -N -L 0.0.0.0:9060 --hep-parse --hep-auth-file /etc/sipnab/hep.key --hep-auth-mode hmac` — the matching sipnab-to-sipnab HMAC collector: verifies the per-message token and rejects replays
- `sipnab -N -L 0.0.0.0:9060 --hep-parse --hep-allow 192.0.2.0/24 --hep-allow 198.51.100.20/32 --hep-rate-limit 20000` — run a HEP collector that parses incoming packets, only from two allowed CIDRs, capped at 20k pkts/sec
- `sipnab -N -L 0.0.0.0:9060 --hep-parse --hep-auth-file /etc/sipnab/hep.key --hep-rate-limit 40000 --hep-rate-limit-per-peer 5000` — authenticated HEP collector on a routable address: incoming packets must carry the shared secret, with a 5k/s per-peer fairness cap
- `sipnab -N -L 0.0.0.0:9060 --hep-parse --hep-auth-file /etc/sipnab/hep.key --hep-allow-kill --kill-scanner` — authenticated HEP collector that may also actively kill scanners seen in the HEP stream (only safe because the feed carries authentication)
- `sipnab -N -L 0.0.0.0:9060 --hep-parse --hep-auth s3cr3t-homer-key --hep-rate-limit-per-peer 2000 --hep-allow-kill --kill-target 198.51.100.7` — inline HEP secret (visible in the process list. Prefer --hep-auth-file.) with a tight per-peer cap for a busy multi-proxy fleet
- `sudo sipnab -N -d eth0 --hep-send 192.0.2.10:9061 --hep-send-transport tcp --hep-id 42` — forward to a collector that speaks HEP over TCP, so a busy collector orders and keeps the feed instead of losing datagrams
- `sipnab -N -I archive.pcap --hep-send 127.0.0.1:9061 --hep-send-transport tcp` — replay an archived capture into a local TCP collector. The stream is packets laid end to end, framed by each HEP v3 header's total length
- `sudo sipnab -N -d eth0 --hep-send collector.example.com:9063 --hep-send-transport tls --hep-tls-ca /etc/sipnab/collector-ca.pem` — encrypted forwarding across a path you do not control, verifying the collector against your own issuer
- `sudo sipnab -N -d eth0 --hep-send homer.example.net:9063 --hep-send-transport tls --hep-tls-ca /etc/pki/tls/certs/homer-ca.pem --hep-auth-file /etc/sipnab/hep.key` — the same, with the Homer authenticate key inside the session as well as the session around it
- `sudo sipnab -N -d eth0 --hep-send collector.example.com:9063 --hep-send-transport tls --hep-tls-extra-ca /etc/sipnab/collector-ca.pem` — encrypted forwarding to a collector whose certificate comes from a private CA, while the host's public roots still count: the sender accepts a certificate from either
- `sudo sipnab -N -d eth0 --hep-send homer.example.net:9063 --hep-send-transport tls --hep-tls-extra-ca /etc/sipnab/homer-ca.pem --hep-auth-file /etc/sipnab/hep.key` — the same with the Homer authenticate key inside the session; compare `--hep-tls-ca`, which would trust only `homer-ca.pem`
- `sudo sipnab -N -d eth0 --hep-send 192.0.2.10:9061 --hep-send-transport tcp --hep-send-queue 512` — a busy SBC whose collector restarts for maintenance: eight times the default queue rides out an outage eight times as long before the oldest packets go
- `sudo sipnab -N -d eth0 --hep-send 192.0.2.10:9061 --hep-send-transport tcp --hep-send-queue 16 --hep-send-timeout 2` — a small box on the collector's LAN: a 16 MiB ceiling on the memory an outage can take, and a collector that does not answer a dial within two seconds counts as down
- `sudo sipnab -N -d eth0 --hep-send collector.example.com:9063 --hep-send-transport tls --hep-tls-ca /etc/sipnab/collector-ca.pem --hep-send-timeout 15` — a collector across a slow WAN, where a dial can take longer than the default three seconds
- `sipnab -N -L 0.0.0.0:9061 --hep-listen-transport tcp --hep-parse --hep-auth-file /etc/sipnab/hep.key` — an authenticated TCP HEP collector: several proxies connect at once and sipnab reads each connection as a stream of HEP v3 packets
- `sipnab -N -L 127.0.0.1:9061 --hep-listen-transport tcp --hep-parse` — the loopback version, for an agent mirroring to a collector on the same host over a connection rather than datagrams
- `sipnab -N -L 0.0.0.0:9063 --hep-listen-transport tls --hep-tls-cert /etc/sipnab/collector.pem --hep-tls-key /etc/sipnab/collector.key --hep-parse --hep-auth-file /etc/sipnab/hep.key` — a TLS HEP collector: agents reach it over an encrypted stream and still prove who they are with the shared secret
- `sipnab -N -L 0.0.0.0:9063 --hep-listen-transport tls --hep-tls-cert /etc/sipnab/collector.pem --hep-tls-key /etc/sipnab/collector.key --hep-parse --hep-allow 192.0.2.0/24` — the same listener bounded by source address instead: TLS encrypts the path, and `--hep-allow` is still what says which addresses may speak on it
- `sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --metrics 127.0.0.1:9090 --metrics-auth-file /etc/sipnab/metrics.cred` — loopback metrics endpoint reading its Basic-auth credential from a file (keeps user:pass out of the process list)
- `sudo sipnab -d eth0 --metrics 0.0.0.0:9090 --metrics-auth-file /etc/sipnab/metrics.cred` — routable metrics endpoint (non-loopback requires auth) using a file-backed credential. Terminate TLS at a reverse proxy
- `sudo sipnab -N -d eth0 --metrics 0.0.0.0:9090 --metrics-auth-file /etc/sipnab/metrics.cred --metrics-tls-cert /etc/sipnab/metrics.pem --metrics-tls-key /etc/sipnab/metrics.key` — the same routable endpoint serving HTTPS itself, so the Basic credential crosses the network encrypted with no reverse proxy; Prometheus scrapes it with `scheme: https` and the issuing CA in `tls_config`
- `sipnab -N -L 127.0.0.1:9060 --hep-parse --metrics 127.0.0.1:9443 --metrics-tls-cert metrics.pem --metrics-tls-key metrics.key` — HTTPS on loopback, for a scraper on the same host that only speaks `https://`; `metrics.pem` must name `127.0.0.1` for the scraper to accept it
- `sipnab --mint-token --token-id alice-2026 --api-signing-key-file /etc/sipnab/signing.key --api-token-ttl 3600` — mint a signed bearer token with a fixed id (for later revocation) and a 1-hour TTL, then exit
- `sipnab --mint-token --token-scope metrics --token-id prom-scraper --api-signing-key-file /etc/sipnab/signing.key --api-token-ttl 86400` — mint a scrape-only token for Prometheus: it reaches `/metrics`, and every `/v1/` route refuses it
- `sipnab --mint-token --token-scope full --token-id ops-oncall --api-signing-key-file /etc/sipnab/signing.key` — the default scope, stated explicitly: full access to the REST API surface

### What `--hep-send` sends

`--hep-send <ADDR>` forwards every SIP message sipnab reads to the collector
at `<ADDR>`, byte for byte as the capture holds it. It also forwards **the RTCP
reports of every call whose SDP it read**.

On a live capture that matches what the flag sounds like. Traffic passes the
interface, and a copy reaches Homer.

Each datagram's IP protocol chunk carries the transport the message arrived on:

- 17 for UDP,
- 6 for TCP, TLS and WebSocket,
- 132 for SCTP.

A collector filtering by transport finds a TCP trunk under TCP.

RTCP travels as HEP protocol type 5. That is what lets a remote collector
report media quality (loss, jitter, MOS) rather than only whether calls
connect.

Each RTCP report goes in the form heplify sends:

- sipnab decodes the report to JSON.
- The Call-ID of the call it belongs to goes in the correlation-ID chunk
  (`0x0011`).
- sipnab finds the call from the SDP that set up the media: the RTP port, the
  port above it, or an `a=rtcp` port.

Homer's collector keeps an RTCP report only under a Call-ID. So a report whose
call sipnab never saw the SDP of is not sent, as heplify and captagent do not
send it. Capture the signaling as well as the media to let the reports
through.

SIP goes without a correlation-ID chunk, as heplify sends it. The collector
still derives the call from `X-CID` or `Call-ID` itself.

**RTP is never forwarded.**

- RTCP is a control channel that [RFC 3550 section 6.2](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3550.html#section-6.2)
  holds to a small fraction of session bandwidth.
- So it carries the quality summary at a rate a WAN link and a UDP feed can
  absorb.
- The media itself is the opposite on both counts.
- Forwarding it would make this a call recorder pointed at the collector.

On `-I <file>` the same sentence carries a sharper meaning.

- The messages sipnab reads come out of the capture file.
- So that file's signaling leaves the machine:
  - request lines,
  - headers,
  - URIs,
  - any message bodies it holds.
- sipnab redacts nothing. It drops nothing beyond what `--portrange` and the
  matching flags already exclude.
- Testing a HEP pipeline against a customer capture therefore ships that
  customer's signaling to whatever `<ADDR>` names.

sipnab announces this before it reads the first packet. For
`sipnab -N -I customer.pcap --hep-send collector.example:9060 --no-cli-print`
the warning reads:

```text
WARN sipnab::app::bootstrap: --hep-send collector.example:9060 forwards every SIP message this run reads, and the RTCP reports of the calls in it, to that address, and this run is reading a capture FILE (customer.pcap). The signaling in those captures leaves this machine: request lines, headers, URIs, and any message bodies they hold. The RTCP carries the media quality summary alongside it — SSRCs, loss, jitter, the endpoints reporting them and the Call-ID they belong to — but not the audio, which is never forwarded. sipnab redacts nothing. Point --hep-send at a collector you control, or drop it to analyze the captures without forwarding them.
```

That line is a warning rather than a refusal, because you chose the
destination. Replaying an archive into your own collector stays a supported
workflow. Two habits keep it uneventful:

- Name a collector you control.
  - sipnab never takes the destination from the capture.
  - The address always comes from your command line or your config file.
- Read the startup warning before you walk away. It names the flag, the
  destination, and the capture files.

The scanner-kill path works the other way round and refuses to run offline.

- It aims at addresses recorded *inside* the capture.
- Those belong to third parties who have nothing to do with your analysis.
- So `-I file` grants it nothing at all. See [Security](#security).

### When the `--hep-send` collector goes away

Sending runs on its own thread, behind a queue. The capture hands each HEP
packet to the queue and moves on, so a collector that is slow, unreachable or
accepting connections without reading never slows the capture or costs it a
packet.

sipnab still makes the first connection at startup. A collector that refuses
it, or does not answer within `--hep-send-timeout`, stops the run with exit
`2`, as does a TLS collector whose certificate sipnab refuses.

While the collector is unreachable after that:

- **Packets queue**, up to `--hep-send-queue` MiB (default 64). At that bound
  sipnab drops the **oldest** packet and counts it as `queue_full`. Dropping the
  oldest puts the gap at the start of the outage, so the replay runs straight
  into the live feed. Dropping the newest would cut the calls still in
  progress, which are the ones you look for after an outage.
- **The sender redials** with backoff: 0.1 s after the first failure, doubling
  to at most 5 s. Each dial and each stalled write gives up after
  `--hep-send-timeout` seconds (default 3). A TLS handshake gives up after 10
  seconds.
- **When the collector answers, sipnab replays the queue in capture order**,
  then the live feed continues. The `replayed` count grows by one per packet.

**Delivery is at-least-once across a reconnect** for every packet sipnab still
holds. sipnab sends a packet whose write failed partway again, whole, on the
new connection, so a collector that kept the first fragment can see that packet
twice. Packets the kernel had already accepted are out of sipnab's hands: a
collector that vanishes without closing its connection (power, network) can
take the unsent contents of the socket's send buffer with it, and no error
names them. A collector that you stop and restart closes its connections, and
sipnab checks for that before every write, so that case loses nothing.

**Over UDP, sipnab cannot see an outage.** sipnab sends each datagram from
an unconnected UDP socket, so a collector that is down, or a host that answers
with ICMP port unreachable, produces no failure, and sipnab has nothing to hold
or replay. Use `--hep-send-transport tcp` or `tls` when an outage must not lose
signaling.

**A stop discards the queue.** On SIGINT or SIGTERM sipnab sends nothing it
still holds: captured SIP carries credentials, numbers and media keys, and data
that outlives a stop is data you believed gone. The `stopped` count says how
many packets it discarded. The end of the input is not a stop. A file read to
its end, `-c` or `--duration` delivers what the queue holds, and gives up only
after two `--hep-send-timeout` periods plus 5 s pass with no delivery. It counts
what it gave up as `unsent_at_exit`.

The end-of-run line states every count. For a run whose collector restarted
once:

```text
HEP export to 192.0.2.10:9061 over tcp: 1840 packet(s) sent, 1840 queued, 212
replayed after an outage, none dropped, 0 still queued, 14 failed attempt(s)
(connect 14), 1 reconnect(s); sent means written to the connection: a write
that fails is counted, the packet stays queued, and the sender dials again with
backoff
```

`failed attempt(s)` counts attempts, not lost packets: a failed attempt keeps
its packet. Losses are the `dropped` count. `queued` always equals `sent` plus
`dropped` plus `still queued`. The same counts appear in `runtime_stats` and
`GET /v1/runtime` (`hep_export`) and as the Prometheus `sipnab_hep_export_*`
series.

### How `--hep-listen` reads the transport

A HEP packet names the transport of the message it carries in its IP protocol
chunk (`0x0002`).

- The [HEP3 specification](https://github.com/sipcapture/hep/blob/83451db00e99f43b24dc68a391c0a7b2bb749b02/docs/HEP3_Network_Protocol_Specification_REV_37.pdf)
  defines that chunk as the IP protocol ID.
- sipnab reads 17 as UDP, 6 as TCP and 132 as SCTP.

OpenSIPS and Kamailio also send a decrypted TLS or WebSocket message over HEP.

- Its payload is plain SIP.
- No IP protocol number means TLS or WebSocket. So both proxies put a fake
  number in the chunk.
- Neither number tells WS from WSS.
- Kamailio's does not even tell TLS from WebSocket.
- So sipnab reads the number first. It lets the message's top Via narrow it to
  WS or WSS:

| Number | Sender | What the sender means | sipnab reports |
|---|---|---|---|
| 22 (`IPPROTO_IDP`) | OpenSIPS `tracer` | TLS | TLS |
| 22 (`IPPROTO_IDP`) | Kamailio `siptrace` | TLS, WS or WSS | TLS, or WS or WSS as the top Via says |
| 50 (`IPPROTO_ESP`) | OpenSIPS `tracer` | WS or WSS | WS, or WSS as the top Via says |
| 6 (TCP) | Kamailio `siptrace`, for a message it sends | TCP, or WS on a TCP connection | TCP, or WS or WSS as the top Via says |

The last row exists because of how Kamailio traces a message it sends.

- It uses the protocol of the socket it sends from.
- A WebSocket connection's socket is a TCP one.
- So a reply to a WS client arrives as 6, and only its Via says WebSocket.
- The Via only ever narrows to WS or WSS.
- A Via naming UDP never turns a TCP leg into UDP.

The top Via names the transport of the hop a message travels on.

- [RFC 3261 section 18.2.2](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3261.html#section-18.2.2)
  has a response travel back over the transport its Via names.
- [RFC 7118 section 5.1](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7118.html#section-5.1) defines
  `WS` and `WSS` as Via transports.

The `transport` field of each `--json` message carries the name. So
`jq 'select(.transport == "WSS")'` picks these legs out of a run that also
captures the wire.

A WebSocket leg captured from the wire itself reports:

- WS when it is plain,
- WSS when sipnab decrypted it with `--keylog`.

`--hep-parse` reads a HEP datagram it finds on the wire or in a capture file by
the same rule. A datagram whose number names no transport counts in the NOT
DECODED line by that number, as a listener does.

sipnab applies all of this to HEP input only. On a frame read from an interface
or a file, as before:

- 50 is a real IPsec ESP packet,
- sipnab refuses 22,
- 6 is TCP whatever the payload says.

Any other number a HEP sender puts in the chunk stays in the NOT DECODED line,
by number.

## MCP server

Run sipnab as a Model Context Protocol server so an AI agent can drive it.

- See [MCP Server](@/docs/mcp.md) for the full guide.
- [Network Listeners](#network-listeners) lists the `--mint-token` /
  `--token-id` pair that issues MCP bearer tokens. It serves the REST API too.

| Flag | Value | Default | Since | Description |
|------|-------|---------|-------|-------------|
| `--mcp` | -- | off | 0.3.2 | Run sipnab as an MCP server. With the default stdio transport, stdout carries the JSON-RPC wire, so `--mcp` implies `-N`/`--no-tui` and rejects every flag that writes its answer to stdout, such as `--json` and `--report`. With `--mcp-transport http` the TUI stays up and the server answers beside it, reading the capture the TUI shows; add `-N` for a headless server. See [Query a capture over MCP while the TUI is open](@/docs/mcp.md#query-a-capture-over-mcp-while-the-tui-is-open). Feature: `mcp` (or `mcp-http` for HTTP transport). See [`mcp.md`](@/docs/mcp.md). |
| `--mcp-transport` | `stdio\|http` | `stdio` | 0.3.2 | MCP transport: `stdio` (default) or `http` (requires the `mcp-http` feature). Feature: `mcp` |
| `--mcp-bind` | `<ADDR>` | -- (defaults to `127.0.0.1:8731` at runtime when `--mcp-transport http` appears without an explicit bind) | 0.3.2 | HTTP MCP bind address. A non-loopback address needs a credential: a bearer token (`--mcp-token`, `--mcp-token-file` or `$SIPNAB_MCP_TOKEN`) or a signing key (`--mcp-signing-key`, `--mcp-signing-key-file` or `$SIPNAB_MCP_SIGNING_KEY`). Without one, sipnab refuses to start, with exit `2`. Feature: `mcp-http` |
| `--mcp-token` | `<TOKEN>` | -- | 0.3.2 | Bearer token for HTTP MCP. A non-loopback bind needs this or a signing key (`--mcp-signing-key`). Precedence: explicit flag, token file, then `$SIPNAB_MCP_TOKEN`. Feature: `mcp-http` |
| `--mcp-token-file` | `<FILE>` | -- | 0.3.2 | Read bearer token from file (preferred over env in systemd units). Feature: `mcp-http` |
| `--mcp-tls-cert` | `<FILE>` | -- | 0.5.203 | Serve MCP over HTTP with HTTPS, using this PEM certificate chain, the server's certificate first. Needs `--mcp-tls-key`; either alone stops sipnab at startup rather than serving plain HTTP on a port meant for HTTPS. The port then speaks HTTPS only: TLS 1.2 and 1.3, ALPN `http/1.1`, no client certificates; clients still authenticate with the bearer token. A file sipnab cannot read, or that holds no certificate, stops it at startup naming the file. sipnab refuses it without `--mcp --mcp-transport http`. See [MCP TLS](@/docs/mcp-deploy.md#mcp-tls). sipnab refuses an empty path with exit `2`, and an empty `[mcp] tls_cert` with exit `1`. Feature: `mcp-http`. Config: `[mcp] tls_cert` |
| `--mcp-tls-key` | `<FILE>` | -- | 0.5.203 | PEM private key for `--mcp-tls-cert`. sipnab **refuses a key any other user on the host can read** (`chmod 600` it; group-readable stays allowed), a file with no private key, and a key that does not belong to the certificate, each at startup and naming the file. sipnab refuses an empty path with exit `2`, and an empty `[mcp] tls_key` with exit `1`. Feature: `mcp-http`. Config: `[mcp] tls_key` |
| `--mcp-signing-key` | `<KEY>` | -- | 0.4.3 | HMAC signing key for MCP bearer tokens, taken as raw bytes (any string — not hex-decoded). Repeatable: the first mints, verification accepts every one. Also reads `$SIPNAB_MCP_SIGNING_KEY`; `--help` names the variable and never shows its value. See [`auth.md`](@/docs/auth.md). Feature: `mcp-http` |
| `--mcp-signing-key-file` | `<FILE>` | -- | 0.4.3 | Read an MCP signing key from a file (contents trimmed); it becomes the minting key. Feature: `mcp-http` |
| `--mcp-revoked-file` | `<FILE>` | -- | 0.4.3 | MCP revocation denylist (one token `id` per line; reloaded on mtime change). Feature: `mcp-http` |
| `--mcp-token-ttl` | `<SECS>` | `3600` | 0.4.3 | Default TTL (seconds) when minting MCP tokens with `--mint-token`. Feature: `mcp-http` |
| `--mcp-audit-file` | `<FILE>` | -- | 0.5.130 | Append every MCP tool call to this file, one JSON record per line (`seq`, `ts`, `tool`, `id`, `caller`, `outcome`, `elapsed_ms`, `args`, `error`). The same facts go to the normal log under the `mcp_audit` target, where `--quiet` and `SIPNAB_LOG` can hide them; this file keeps every record whatever the log level. Opened `O_APPEND` and never truncated, so restarts and a second sipnab on the same path add to it; created mode `0600` when absent. The `seq` counter starts at 1 each run, so a gap within a run is a missing record. **sipnab refuses a call whose record it cannot write, rather than answering it**, so no result leaves the server that is not in the file; a path sipnab cannot open stops the run at startup. Records reach the kernel rather than an `fsync`. Leave it off and nothing changes. Feature: `mcp` |
| `--mcp-max-concurrent` | `<N>` | `100` | 0.5.84 | Maximum tool calls the MCP server runs at once (`0` = unlimited). sipnab refuses a call that cannot take a slot immediately, with a retry-shortly error, rather than queueing it. The default matches `--api-max-conn`. Applies to both stdio and HTTP servers, though a network-exposed HTTP server is the case it matters for. Feature: `mcp` |
| `--mcp-tools` | `<LIST>` | `full` | 0.5.130 | Which tools the MCP server registers: a comma-separated list of bundles (`core`, `signaling`, `captures`, `security`, `media`, `relay`, `tfps`, `server`, `vcon`, `tls`), single tool names, names from `[mcp.bundles]`, or `full`. Every registered tool's name, description and schema goes to the client on `tools/list` and stays in the model's context for the whole session, so fewer tools means a smaller context. `core` holds nine tools that still answer a whole call end to end: `capture_status`, `list_dialogs`, `get_dialog`, `triage_call`, `rtp_stats`, `find_problems`, `aggregate_dialogs`, `search_messages`, `get_capture_report`. [Choosing which tools load](@/docs/mcp-tools.md#choosing-which-tools-load) lists every bundle and its size. An unknown or empty name refuses the run, exit 2 (exit 1 when it came from `[mcp] tools`). sipnab removes the tools you did not choose from the router rather than hiding them, so a call to one of them fails as an unknown tool. The handshake names the tools sipnab loaded and the bundles it left out. Replaces `[mcp] tools`. Feature: `mcp`. Config: `[mcp] tools` |
| `--mcp-output-schemas` | `[=BOOL]` | off | 0.5.197 | Send each tool's output schema on `tools/list`. Off by default: MCP makes output schemas optional, and they more than double the size of the `tools/list` answer. Responses carry the same JSON, as text and as `structuredContent`, either way; only a client that validates responses against a schema needs them. `--mcp-output-schemas=false` turns them off over a config that turns them on. Config: `[mcp] output_schemas`. Feature: `mcp` |
| `--one-way-delay` | `<MS>` | -- | 0.5.93 | One-way network path delay, in milliseconds — the single MOS input a passive tap cannot measure directly. Declared here it beats an RTCP-reported round trip, which an unauthenticated packet can move, and that in turn beats the round trip sipnab derives from a sender-report echo carried in a receiver report; with none of the three, sipnab assumes 100 ms and says so. Config: `[media] one_way_delay_ms` |
| `--mcp-max-rows` | `<N>` | `1000` | 0.5.93 | Maximum rows in one list-style MCP response. The consumer decides the right value: a small-context agent wants fewer, a batch client wants more. Config: `[limits] mcp_max_rows`. Do not mistake this for `-l`/`--limit`, which bounds dialogs tracked over the run. At least 1: sipnab refuses `0` |
| `--mcp-max-body-bytes` | `<N>` | `4096` | 0.5.97 | Maximum bytes of SIP body or matched snippet in one MCP response. `--mcp-max-rows` bounds how many rows an answer carries; this bounds how wide one row may be, and a caller can ask for fewer rows but cannot widen one. An SDP body with a dozen codecs and ICE candidates passes the default, and the agent reading the clipped half cannot tell a truncated answer from a short one. Config: `[limits] mcp_max_body_bytes` |
| `--mcp-max-response-bytes` | `<N>` | `1048576` | 0.5.212 | Maximum bytes of ONE whole paged MCP response: the JSON page, the provenance note and the completeness fields. `--mcp-max-rows` bounds how many rows a page carries and `--mcp-max-body-bytes` how wide one body in a row can be; this bounds the page as a whole. Past it the tool drops whole rows from the end of the page, never part of one, and answers `truncated_by: "bytes"` with a `next_cursor` to the rest. A page always keeps at least one row. A caller narrows it per call with `max_response_bytes` and cannot exceed it. Config: `[limits] mcp_max_response_bytes`. At least 1: sipnab refuses `0` |
| `--mcp-max-wait-seconds` | `<N>` | `60` | 0.5.141 | Longest ONE `await_condition` MCP call may wait, in seconds. `--mcp-max-rows` and `--mcp-max-body-bytes` bound how much an answer carries; this bounds how long a caller may hold one of `--mcp-max-concurrent` slots while it waits for a condition on a live capture. sipnab clamps a larger request to it and says so in the response. It also bounds `wait_seconds` on `find_in_captures` and `find_in_captures_status`, how long one of those calls waits for a background sweep before it answers with the running job. Config: `[limits] mcp_max_wait_seconds` |
| `--mcp-max-findings` | `<N>` | `1000` | 0.5.100 | Findings the MCP `save_findings` tool accepts before refusing further writes. Past it sipnab refuses the write and says so, and drops nothing to make room. Raise it for a long agent session on a large capture. Config: `[limits] mcp_max_findings` |
| `--mcp-sweep-max-files` | `<N>` | `20` | 0.5.207 | Files one MCP `find_in_captures` sweep may open, from `1` to `4294967295`. It is the ceiling on the tool's per-call `max_files`: sipnab clamps a larger request to it, and `0` or no request means this value. A rotated spool of forty files needs `40` here before one sweep can reach the oldest file. The response reports the limits applied and `files_examined`, `files_total` and `complete`. Config: `[limits] mcp_sweep_max_files` |
| `--mcp-sweep-deadline-ms` | `<MS>` | `30000` | 0.5.207 | Milliseconds one MCP `find_in_captures` sweep may spend, from `1` to `43200000` (twelve hours). It is the ceiling on the tool's per-call `deadline_ms`, applied the same way as `--mcp-sweep-max-files`. The sweep runs as a background job on its own thread and checks it before each file and before each packet. Config: `[limits] mcp_sweep_deadline_ms` |
| `--mcp-sweep-max-running` | `<N>` | `4` | 0.5.208 | MCP `find_in_captures` sweeps one server runs at once, from `1` to `64`. Each running sweep is an operating system thread reading capture files. sipnab refuses a start past this many with a message that reports the bound and names this flag, rather than queueing it. Config: `[limits] mcp_sweep_max_running` |
| `--mcp-sweep-max-held-results` | `<N>` | `16` | 0.5.208 | Finished MCP `find_in_captures` results one server holds for collection, from `1` to `256`. Past this many, sipnab drops the result of the earliest-started sweep first. Config: `[limits] mcp_sweep_max_held_results` |
| `--mcp-sweep-result-retention-secs` | `<SECS>` | `600` | 0.5.208 | Seconds a finished MCP `find_in_captures` result waits for its poll, from `1` to `43200` (twelve hours), counted from the moment the sweep finished. After it, the job id is unknown. Config: `[limits] mcp_sweep_result_retention_secs` |
| `--mcp-sampling-budget` | `<PER_HOUR>` | off | 0.5.130 | Requests per hour sipnab may ask the CLIENT's model to narrate. Off unless set. A client that did not advertise the sampling capability is never asked and gets structured evidence instead. Requests dedupe by finding signature before they spend from this budget, so a rule a scanner trips five hundred times costs one narration. `0` means none, not unlimited. sipnab forwards named fields only -- control characters stripped, length clamped, under a system prompt stating every value is untrusted observation -- and never raw message text. Feature: `mcp` |
| `--mcp-rate-limit-per-peer` | `<N>` | `100` | 0.5.87 | Maximum tool calls one peer may make per second (`0` = unlimited). `--mcp-max-concurrent` caps calls *in flight*; this caps their *arrival rate*. A call over the cap gets the same retry-shortly error, never a queue slot. A peer is the source IP over HTTP (the address, not the socket, so reconnecting mints no fresh allowance) and the pipe itself over stdio. Shares its per-peer accounting with `--hep-rate-limit-per-peer`. Feature: `mcp` |
| `--mcp-allowed-host` | `<HOST>` | -- | 0.3.2 | Additional `Host` header values the HTTP MCP server accepts (repeatable). DNS-rebind protection accepts `localhost`, `127.0.0.1`, `::1` and the address `--mcp-bind` binds, on any port, and any IP address when it binds `0.0.0.0` or `::`: the same rule as [`--api-allowed-host`](#network-listeners). Add the public hostname when clients connect by that name. Use `*` to disable host checking entirely (not recommended; pair the resulting open binding with a network-level source-IP allowlist). Feature: `mcp-http` |
| `--mcp-resource-url` | `<URL>` | -- | 0.5.141 | Public URL clients reach this MCP server at, published as the OAuth 2.0 protected-resource identifier ([RFC 9728](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9728.html)). Setting it turns on discovery: the `401` challenge gains a `resource_metadata` parameter and sipnab serves the metadata document unauthenticated at the path [RFC 9728 section 3.1](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9728.html#section-3.1) derives from this value, so `https://sipnab.example.com/mcp` publishes at `/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource/mcp`. Leave it unset and the challenge still appears — only the metadata half is off. sipnab does not derive it from the request: behind a TLS-terminating proxy that would name `http://` for a resource the client reached over `https://`, which [RFC 9728 section 3.3](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9728.html#section-3.3) makes a conformant client discard. Discovery only: sipnab issues and validates no OAuth tokens, so the document advertises no `authorization_servers`, and the bearer tokens it accepts are still its own. Must be absolute, `http` or `https`, with no userinfo, query or fragment; a rejected value is a startup error. Feature: `mcp-http` |
| `--mcp-file-root` | `<DIR>` | -- | 0.5.70 | Directory the MCP file tools (`export_capture`, `export_audio`, `list_captures`) may read and write. Without it those tools refuse to run. They take a bare FILENAME, never a path — an agent cannot escape this directory. Feature: `mcp` |
| `--mcp-evidence-ring` | `<MIB>` | -- | 0.5.168 | Retain this many MiB of raw frames so a provenance pointer into a LIVE capture resolves. A reader can seek a capture file again and needs none of this; a device or a HEP listener offers no second read, because sipnab holds parsed messages and not frames. The ring keeps frames only from a source nothing can read twice. A pointer it cannot answer names which kind of miss it hit — the ring dropped that frame, the ring has not reached that ordinal, or the ring keeps nothing for that source — because only one of those means "use a bigger ring". A frame it does answer carries the label `retained` rather than resolved: those bytes come from this process's own buffer, and no second reader can confirm them. Feature: `mcp` |
| `--mcp-allow-shutdown` | -- | off | 0.5.70 | Permit the `shutdown_server` MCP tool to stop this process. Off by default, so an agent cannot stop a stock server. Even enabled, the tool dry-runs unless told otherwise and refuses to discard an unsaved live capture. sipnab refuses it with the TUI up, because the TUI would stay on screen after the tool stopped the run; add `-N`. Feature: `mcp` |
| `--mcp-allow-open-capture` | -- | off | 0.5.74 | Permit the `open_capture` MCP tool to load a different capture from `--mcp-file-root`, discarding every dialog and stream held. Off by default, so a stock server keeps the capture the command line named. The tool refuses while the source is live or still filling the stores, loads in the background, and mints a new capture identity every later answer carries. sipnab refuses it with the TUI up, because the tool would replace the capture the operator is reading; add `-N`. Feature: `mcp` |
| `--mcp-allow-relay-query` | -- | off | 0.5.139 | Permit the `query_relay` MCP tool to ask the configured relay what calls it holds right now. Off by default because this tool **transmits**: every other MCP tool answers from bytes sipnab already has, and this one puts a packet on the network at the address `--rtpengine-control` names. That address comes from the flag and from nowhere else, never from a tool argument. Without `--rtpengine-control`, or on a run reading a file, the tool refuses and names which of the two is missing. sipnab refuses it with the TUI up, because the TUI's relay statistics view holds the run's one transmit permit; add `-N`. Feature: `mcp` |
| `--mcp-allow-tls-capture` | -- | off | 0.5.102 | Let an agent install kernel uprobes and read TLS plaintext ([`start_tls_capture`](@/docs/mcp-tools-tls.md#start-tls-capture), `stop_tls_capture`). **The most consequential opt-in on this surface**: it lets an agent read the plaintext of TLS sessions belonging to processes it does not own, needs the server to still be root, and creates kernel state that outlives a crash. `list_tls_libraries` stays available without it, so an agent can always report what a capture WOULD see. sipnab refuses it with the TUI up, because the capture would write into the stores the operator is reading; add `-N`. Feature: `mcp` |
| `--mcp-allow-vcon-fetch` | -- | off | 0.5.221 | Permit the [`fetch_vcon`](@/docs/mcp-tools-vcon.md#fetch-vcon) MCP tool to read one vCon by uuid from the store the `[vcon_fetch]` keys configure. Off by default because this tool **connects** to that store: every other vCon tool answers from bytes sipnab already has. The store, its kind, the credential and the decryption key come from `[vcon_fetch]` only, never from a tool argument; the tool takes a uuid and nothing else, and its answer holds no key. Without `[vcon_fetch] url` the tool refuses and names the keys. sipnab stops at startup when it cannot read the store's credential or key file. The container comes back in the answer, and sipnab writes no file. Feature: `mcp` and `vcon` |
| `--mcp-allow-save-findings` | -- | off | 0.5.81 | Permit the `save_findings` MCP tool to record an agent's conclusion. Off by default. A finding goes to sipnab's log and nowhere else: no tool reads it back, it appears in no query result, and no analysis consumes it, so it cannot return as evidence in a later answer. Clipped at 500 characters of summary and bounded at 1000 findings per process, both reported rather than silent. sipnab refuses it with the TUI up, because a TUI run logs only errors and nobody would see the finding; add `-N`. Feature: `mcp` |
| `--retain-audio` | -- | off | 0.5.84 | Retain RTP audio payload in memory, so sipnab can look at the audio itself. Two things read it back: the `export_audio` MCP tool, which decodes a WAV, and the amplitude measurement in the media diagnosis, which reports dead-air spans and hard-clip runs on `--call-report` and `--json-dialogs`. Off by default, because call audio is content. Works with or without `--mcp`. Keeps whole calls, from the first frame. Costs a per-packet payload clone, bounded by one budget across every stream, `[limits] max_audio_bytes` (default 1 GiB, which holds 67 concurrent ten-minute G.711 calls; see [Audio retention budget](@/docs/config.md#audio-retention-budget)). At the budget sipnab releases the oldest stream's earliest frames first, and that call's export and vCon say PARTIAL with the count. `[limits] max_audio_frames` caps each stream as well when set. Without it `export_audio` refuses and names this flag, and the amplitude object is absent — both describe what the run kept, never whether the call carried audio. `--cores` honors this flag |

## TLS / decryption

| Flag | Value | Default | Since | Description |
|------|-------|---------|-------|-------------|
| `-k`, `--tls-key` | `<FILE>` | -- | 0.3.0 | RSA private key (PEM) for TLS 1.2 RSA-key-exchange decryption. Non-PFS RSA only; ECDHE/DHE handshakes need `--keylog`. Feature: `tls` |
| `--keylog` | `<FILE>` | -- | 0.3.0 | TLS key log file (NSS `SSLKEYLOGFILE` format). Accepts a **FIFO** here and reads it as a live stream, so a producer can feed secrets in without writing them to disk. sipnab opens the file **before** it drops privileges, so a keylog only the proxy's user can read still loads when sipnab runs as root and drops to `nobody`, and `--keylog-watch` keeps reading what the producer appends through that open file. A producer that replaces the file after the drop needs it reachable by the user sipnab dropped to. When sipnab cannot read the keylog it refuses the run with exit `1`, as it does for `--tls-key` and `--dtls-keylog`, and the error names the reason, such as `Failed to load --keylog /run/keys.log: Loading keylog from /run/keys.log: Failed to read keylog file: /run/keys.log: No such file or directory (os error 2)`. Feature: `tls` |
| `--keylog-fd` | `<N>` | -- | 0.5.101 | Read NSS keylog lines from an already-open descriptor, for a privileged producer that hands secrets over a pipe rather than a file. **Implies `--keylog-watch`**, and conflicts with `--keylog` — pass one, never both. sipnab **cannot start that producer itself**: it sets `PR_SET_NO_NEW_PRIVS` at startup and every child inherits it, so a child can never acquire the `CAP_BPF` an eBPF extractor needs. Start it from a supervisor and pass the read end here. Feature: `tls` |
| `--keylog-watch` | -- | off | 0.3.0 | Watch the key log for new entries (live decryption). Feature: `tls` |
| `--tls-lockon-window` | `<RECORDS>` | 1048576 | 0.5.115 | How far into an established TLS connection a capture may start and still be readable. No TLS version puts the record number on the wire, so a capture that joined a running connection searches for it, widening only as records fail to open — raising this costs nothing on a connection captured from its handshake, because the search stops at the first candidate that authenticates. Raise it for a carrier trunk held open for days; lower it where key material for unrelated connections is common. At least 1: `0` would turn the search off, so sipnab refuses it with exit 2. Feature: `tls` |
| `--dtls-keylog` | `<FILE>` | -- | 0.3.0 | DTLS key log (NSS `SSLKEYLOGFILE`); extracts SRTP keys from DTLS-SRTP handshakes ([RFC 5764](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5764.html) exporter, AES-CM profiles). sipnab does not treat a record declaring more than 2^14 + 2048 bytes as DTLS (the ciphertext limit TLS sets and DTLS inherits). Feature: `tls` |
| `--srtp-keys` | `<FILE>` | -- | 0.3.0 | SRTP master-keys file for media decryption (AES-CM, [RFC 3711](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3711.html)); also honors SDES `a=crypto` keys from SDP. Feature: `tls` |
| `--pcap-export-mode` | `<MODE>` | `raw` | 0.3.0 | `raw` writes original packets without TLS keys. `encrypted+dsb` explicitly embeds TLS keys in PCAP-NG for Wireshark. `decrypted` writes what sipnab decrypted as plaintext, and no keys: SIP from TLS and WSS as plain TCP frames and SRTP as plain RTP, on the captured addresses, ports and times, with everything else as captured. The file can hold readable signaling and listenable audio. Frames wait up to 5 s of capture time for a late decryption, and a stop discards what is still waiting. The TUI's live `-O` rewrites SRTP only, because the TUI does not decrypt TLS |
| `--allow-coredump` | -- | off | 0.3.0 | Allow core dumps (do not call `prctl` to disable them) |
| `--uprobe-tls` | -- | off | 0.5.102 | Read SIP plaintext straight out of the TLS libraries this host is running, using kernel uprobes. **No certificate, no private key, no keylog and no restart** of the process it observes. Probes **every** mapped TLS library rather than one, because an ordinary host runs OpenSSL and wolfSSL together. Needs root (or `CAP_SYS_ADMIN` + `CAP_PERFMON`) and a mounted `tracefs`. Linux only. **Read [the walkthrough](@/docs/uprobe-walkthrough.md) before using this**: it reads the plaintext of every SIP session on the host, and states what that means. Feature: `native` |
| `--uprobe-library` | `<PATH>` | discovered | 0.5.102 | Probe this library instead of discovering them; repeatable. Bypasses discovery, so it also reaches a library nothing has mapped **yet**. For a process inside a container, give the path as sipnab sees it: `/proc/<pid>/root/usr/lib/libssl.so.3`. Feature: `native` |
| `--uprobe-symbol` | `<NAME>` | per flavor | 0.5.102 | Write symbol to probe. Defaults to the one the library's flavor exports — `SSL_write` for OpenSSL, `wolfSSL_write` for wolfSSL — so you need it only for a library sipnab cannot classify by name. Feature: `native` |
| `--uprobe-flavor` | `<NAME>` | all | 0.5.102 | Probe only these flavors (`openssl`, `wolfssl`); repeatable. Feature: `native`. Also accepts the spelling `--uprobe-flavour` |
| `--uprobe-list` | -- | off | 0.5.102 | List the TLS libraries sipnab would probe, then exit **without installing anything in the kernel**. Run this first: it answers the question that decides whether the capture is worth starting. Exits `1` when nothing is visible, so a health check does not read "no TLS library" as success. With `--uprobe-library` it lists the named libraries and the symbol it would probe in each, instead of discovering them; a path that names no file shows as `(MISSING)` and the command exits `1`, and a library whose flavor its name does not tell, given without `--uprobe-symbol`, exits `2`. Feature: `native` |
| `--uprobe-backend` | `<NAME>` | `tracefs` | 0.5.102 | Which machinery reads the plaintext. `tracefs` works on any Linux with tracefs mounted and sees **no socket**, so its dialogs name a process rather than a peer. `bpf` pairs each write with its `tcp_sendmsg` and so recovers the **real addresses** — but needs a sipnab built with `--features bpf` and a kernel with `CONFIG_DEBUG_INFO_BTF` (BTF is the BPF Type Format, which tells sipnab where the socket's fields sit on *this* kernel). sipnab refuses `bpf` without those rather than quietly downgrading: the addresses are the only reason to ask for it. Feature: `native` |

**Examples**

- `sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --mcp --mcp-file-root /var/spool/sipnab-exports` — let an agent save captures and audio, confined to one directory
- `sudo sipnab -N -d eth0 --mcp --mcp-file-root /var/spool/sipnab-exports --mcp-allow-shutdown` — a live capture an agent may export from and stop
- `sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --mcp --mcp-sampling-budget 20` — let sipnab ask the connected client's model to characterize an alert in a sentence, at most twenty times an hour. No API key in the config and no weights in the binary: the client already has a model, and this borrows it
- `sipnab -d eth0 -N --mcp --mcp-sampling-budget 0` — sampling explicitly refused rather than left unset, which is what to write when a policy forbids sending observations to a model at all. The difference from omitting the flag is that this states the decision
- `sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --mcp --mcp-allow-shutdown` — a replay session an agent may end when it has finished. Nothing to lose, since the file is already on disk
- `sipnab -N -I first.pcap --mcp --mcp-transport http --mcp-file-root /var/spool/sipnab-captures --mcp-allow-open-capture` — a long-lived service an agent may move through a corpus with, one capture at a time
- `sudo sipnab -N -d eth0 --mcp --mcp-evidence-ring 256` — a live capture an agent can quote FROM. Without it sipnab refuses every pointer into `eth0`: it holds parsed messages and not frames, so nothing remains to seek to. 256 MiB buys a window. Outside it the refusal reports that the ring dropped the frame rather than that the frame never existed
- `sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --mcp --mcp-evidence-ring 64` — the ring has no effect on a file run: a reader can open a capture file again, so the ring keeps nothing and never spends the 64 MiB. It holds frames only from a source nothing can read twice
- `sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --mcp --mcp-file-root /var/spool/sipnab-captures --mcp-allow-open-capture --mcp-allow-shutdown` — the same, plus the ability to end the session. Each permission needs its own flag
- `sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --config sipnab.toml --mcp --mcp-allow-vcon-fetch` — let an agent read a vCon by uuid with `fetch_vcon` from the store the config file's `[vcon_fetch]` section names; the agent gives the uuid and never a URL or key
- `sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --config sipnab.toml --mcp --mcp-transport http --mcp-allow-vcon-fetch --mcp-tools vcon` — the same over HTTP, with only the `vcon` bundle loaded, so the agent can fetch a stored call and run `analyze_vcon` on it
- `sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --mcp --mcp-allow-save-findings` — let an agent write its conclusions into the log while it works through a capture. Read them back with `journalctl -u sipnab`, never through a tool
- `sudo sipnab -N -d eth0 --mcp --mcp-transport http --mcp-allow-save-findings` — a live triage session whose findings survive in the journal after the agent disconnects, without granting it any other write
- `sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --mcp --mcp-file-root /var/spool/sipnab-exports --retain-audio` — hold call audio in memory so an agent can `export_audio` a WAV of a problem call
- `sudo sipnab -N -d eth0 "portrange 5060-5061 or portrange 10000-20000" --mcp --retain-audio --mcp-file-root /var/spool/sipnab-exports` — live capture with media in scope AND retained. Without `--retain-audio` the same run measures quality but keeps no payload to export
- `sipnab -N -I dead-air.pcap --retain-audio --call-report <call-id> --json` — no MCP server involved: retain the samples so the media diagnosis can measure them, and read `diagnosis.amplitude` for dead-air spans and clip runs with the thresholds that produced them
- `sudo sipnab -N -d eth0 --mcp --mcp-transport http --mcp-bind 127.0.0.1:8731 --mcp-max-concurrent 8` — a network-facing MCP server that runs at most eight tool calls at once and refuses the ninth with a retry-shortly error rather than queueing it
- `sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --mcp --mcp-max-concurrent 0` — a stdio replay for one trusted agent with no concurrency cap (`0` = unlimited)
- `sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --mcp --mcp-tools core` — a small-context agent: nine tools instead of the whole surface, so the schema block sipnab sends it before it asks anything is a fraction of the size
- `sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --mcp --mcp-tools core,relay,get_sdp_timeline` — a small-context agent that also chases relay-side media: the core set, the relay bundle and one signaling tool, rather than every bundle
- `sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --mcp --mcp-output-schemas` — the whole surface with its output schemas, for a client that validates each response against the tool's declared shape
- `sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --mcp --config sipnab.toml --mcp-output-schemas=false` — a host config that turns output schemas on, overridden for one client that does not validate responses
- `sudo sipnab -N -d eth0 --mcp --mcp-transport http --mcp-tools full` — the default written out, for a service definition that should say what it offers rather than leave it to whatever the next release registers
- `sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --mcp --quiet --mcp-audit-file /var/log/sipnab-mcp.jsonl` — record every tool call to a file that survives `--quiet`, for the question asked after the fact rather than at the console
- `sipnab -N -I sat-trunk.pcap --one-way-delay 280` — score MOS for a satellite trunk, where the real one-way delay is 280 ms. Without it sipnab falls back to the trunk's own RTCP and, on a capture carrying none, to an assumed 100 ms that reports roughly a full point too high, because G.107's delay penalty has a knee at 177.3 ms the assumption never crosses
- `sipnab -N -I lan.pcap --one-way-delay 5` — a LAN capture, where assuming 100 ms understates the score. The declared figure also beats any round trip the far end reports or sipnab derives from RTCP, since no packet on the wire can rewrite a config value
- `sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --mcp --mcp-max-rows 50` — cap every list-style MCP response at fifty rows, for an agent whose context window a thousand-row page would swamp. A caller asking for more gets fifty
- `sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --mcp --mcp-max-rows 5000` — raise the ceiling above the 1000 default for a batch client that pipes whole pages to a file, where the round trips cost more than the bytes
- `sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --mcp --mcp-max-body-bytes 65536` — let an agent read a whole `INVITE` with a long SDP body rather than the first 4096 bytes of it, on a capture whose bodies are what the investigation is about
- `sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --mcp --mcp-max-rows 20 --mcp-max-body-bytes 512` — a small-context agent: few rows, and each one short, so a page of hits fits the window it has to reason in
- `sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --mcp --mcp-max-response-bytes 65536` — no answer larger than 64 KiB, however many rows the caller asks for or however long their bodies run; a page that would pass it ends early with `truncated_by: "bytes"` and a cursor to the rest
- `sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --mcp --mcp-max-rows 5000 --mcp-max-response-bytes 4194304` — a batch client allowed five thousand rows per page, with each answer still held to 4 MiB, so a page of long SIP messages ends early with a cursor rather than growing without a bound
- `sudo sipnab -N -d eth0 --mcp --mcp-max-wait-seconds 300` — let an agent sit on a live capture for up to five minutes per `await_condition` call, on a box watching for a fault that reproduces slowly
- `sudo sipnab -N -d eth0 --mcp --mcp-max-wait-seconds 5` — hold every wait to five seconds, for a host where MCP slots are scarce and a stalled agent must not occupy one
- `sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --mcp --mcp-file-root /var/spool/sipnab --mcp-sweep-max-files 40` — let one `find_in_captures` call sweep a spool that rotates forty files, so the sweep reaches a call in the oldest file
- `sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --mcp --mcp-file-root /var/spool/sipnab --mcp-sweep-max-files 40 --mcp-sweep-deadline-ms 120000` — the same spool of large files, with two minutes for the sweep to read them
- `sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --mcp --mcp-file-root /var/spool/sipnab --mcp-sweep-deadline-ms 5000` — end every sweep after five seconds, for a host where MCP slots are scarce and one sweep must not hold a slot for longer
- `sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --mcp --mcp-file-root /var/spool/sipnab --mcp-sweep-max-running 1` — run one sweep at a time, for a host whose capture spool sits on a single slow disk that two concurrent sweeps would share
- `sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --mcp --mcp-file-root /var/spool/sipnab --mcp-sweep-max-running 8 --mcp-sweep-max-held-results 32` — let an agent run eight sweeps side by side on a spool spread over several disks, and hold four uncollected results per running sweep, the ratio the defaults carry
- `sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --mcp --mcp-file-root /var/spool/sipnab --mcp-sweep-max-held-results 4` — hold at most four uncollected results, for a host where memory is scarce and agents poll each sweep they start
- `sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --mcp --mcp-file-root /var/spool/sipnab --mcp-sweep-result-retention-secs 3600` — keep a finished result for an hour, for an agent that starts long sweeps and returns to them later in the session
- `sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --mcp --mcp-file-root /var/spool/sipnab --mcp-sweep-result-retention-secs 60` — drop a result one minute after its sweep finished, for a scripted client that polls at once and never returns to a job it abandoned
- `sudo sipnab -N -d eth0 --mcp --mcp-transport http --mcp-rate-limit-per-peer 20` — a network-facing MCP server where any one client may make twenty tool calls a second. sipnab answers the twenty-first that second with a retry-shortly error instead of serving it
- `sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --mcp --mcp-max-concurrent 8 --mcp-rate-limit-per-peer 0` — bound how many calls run at once but put no cap on the arrival rate (`0` = unlimited), for a scripted client that sweeps a capture as fast as it can
- `sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --tls-key /etc/sipnab/tls-rsa.key --keylog /etc/sipnab/keys.log --allow-coredump` — decrypt TLS 1.2 RSA-key-exchange SIP from a pcap using an RSA private key, with core dumps left enabled
- `sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --srtp-keys /etc/sipnab/srtp.keys --dtls-keylog /etc/sipnab/dtls.log` — decrypt SRTP media in an offline pcap from an SRTP master-keys file plus DTLS-SRTP handshake keys
- `sudo sipnab -d eth0 --tls-key /etc/sipnab/tls-rsa.key --srtp-keys /etc/sipnab/srtp.keys --keylog /etc/sipnab/keys.log --keylog-watch --allow-coredump` — live decrypt both SIP (RSA key) and SRTP media, watching the key log for new PFS session keys
- `sudo sh -c 'ecapture tls -m keylog --keylogfile=/dev/stdout | sipnab -N -d eth0 --keylog-fd 0'` — read SIP over TLS with **no certificate and no restart of the SIP daemon**: an eBPF extractor pulls session secrets out of the running daemon's OpenSSL. It pipes them straight in, so nothing is ever written to disk. sipnab cannot launch the extractor itself, because every child inherits `PR_SET_NO_NEW_PRIVS` and so can never acquire `CAP_BPF`
- `sudo sipnab -N -d eth0 --keylog-fd 3 --user sipnab 3< /run/sip.keys` — take the secrets on descriptor 3 opened by the shell, then drop to an unprivileged user for the capture itself. The pipe is already open, so nothing has to be reachable from `/run` afterwards
- `sudo mkfifo -m 600 /run/sip.keys && sudo sipnab -N -d eth0 --keylog /run/sip.keys --keylog-watch` — the same idea through a named pipe rather than a descriptor, for a producer started separately by systemd. sipnab opens the FIFO while still privileged. It does so before it drops to an unprivileged user and can no longer reach `/run`
- `sudo sipnab -N -d eth0 --keylog /run/sip.keys --keylog-watch --tls-lockon-window 8388608` — read a carrier trunk that has been up for days without restarting it. The record counter is not on the wire, so a capture joining an established connection has to find it. The default reaches about a day of a trunk at ten records a second, and this raises the ceiling to roughly a week
- `sipnab -N -I trunk.pcap --keylog keys.log --tls-lockon-window 4096` — narrow the search when reading a capture whose key log holds secrets for many unrelated connections, so a session that can never match gives up sooner instead of spending the run's trial budget
- `sudo sipnab --uprobe-list` — **run this first.** Report which TLS libraries processes on this host are actually mapping, and exit without installing a single probe. Answers the only question that matters before starting: is the daemon you care about using a library sipnab can read?
- `sudo sipnab --uprobe-list --uprobe-flavor wolfssl` — the same listing narrowed to one flavor, so the output says what *this* command would probe rather than what merely exists
- `sudo sipnab -N --uprobe-tls` — read SIP over TLS with **no certificate, no key and no restart of the SIP daemon**. sipnab probes every mapped TLS library, so one command covers a host running OpenSSL for one daemon and wolfSSL for another
- `sudo sipnab -N --uprobe-tls --uprobe-flavor openssl` — probe only the OpenSSL side on a mixed host, when the wolfSSL processes are something else entirely and their plaintext is not yours to read
- `sudo sipnab -N --uprobe-tls --uprobe-library /usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libssl.so.3` — skip discovery and probe one named library, which is how you attach to a daemon that has not started yet: discovery can only see what is already mapped
- `sudo sipnab -N --uprobe-tls --uprobe-library /proc/$(docker inspect -f '{{.State.Pid}}' opensips)/root/usr/lib/libssl.so.3` — probe the OpenSSL **inside a container**. The path a container process sees names a different file from sipnab's namespace, so the probe must go through `/proc/<pid>/root` or it silently attaches to the host's copy and captures nothing
- `sudo sipnab -N --uprobe-tls --uprobe-library /opt/vendor/libtls-custom.so --uprobe-symbol vendor_write` — probe a library sipnab cannot classify by name. Without `--uprobe-symbol` it refuses rather than guessing which function to attach to
- `sudo sipnab -N --uprobe-tls --uprobe-library /usr/lib/libssl.so.3 --uprobe-symbol SSL_write_ex` — probe OpenSSL 3's newer write entry point instead of the default `SSL_write`, for a daemon built against it. The argument positions match, so the probe shape does not change
- `sudo sipnab -N --uprobe-tls --json` — the same capture as JSON. Dialogs from this source carry `uprobe:<comm>/<pid>` as their interface and **unspecified addresses with port 0**, because a uprobe sees the bytes an application handed its TLS library and nothing about the socket beneath. sipnab names the process rather than inventing a peer
- `sudo sipnab -N --uprobe-tls --uprobe-backend bpf --portrange 0-65535` — read SIP over TLS **with the peer addresses**: each dialog names the real source and destination address and port of its connection. Widen `--portrange`, because a TLS trunk on 5061 is the exception and the port a uprobe reports is whatever the socket used
- `sudo sipnab -N --uprobe-tls --uprobe-backend tracefs` — the default, spelled out. Use it on a kernel without BTF, where the `bpf` backend cannot run at all. Dialogs then name the process instead of a peer
- `sudo sipnab -N -I done.pcap --mcp --mcp-allow-tls-capture` — let an agent decide, mid-investigation, that the answer is in traffic it cannot see, and start reading TLS plaintext itself. Finish the file source first: sipnab's stores have one writer, and a uprobe capture is a live one
- `sudo sipnab -N -I done.pcap --mcp --mcp-allow-tls-capture --mcp-allow-save-findings` — the same, plus somewhere for the agent to record what it concluded. Without `--mcp-allow-tls-capture` the agent can still call `list_tls_libraries` and report what a capture would have seen


## Privilege

| Flag | Value | Default | Since | Description |
|------|-------|---------|-------|-------------|
| `--user` | `<USER>` | -- | 0.3.0 | Drop privileges to this user after opening capture devices. **Only takes effect when the process is root** — see the note below. Config: `[privilege] user` |
| `--no-priv-drop` | -- | off | 0.3.0 | Do not drop privileges after opening capture devices. Config: `[privilege] no_priv_drop` |
| `--priv-drop` | -- | off | 0.5.204 | Drop privileges even when `[privilege] no_priv_drop = true`. The last of `--no-priv-drop` / `--priv-drop` typed wins. Config: `[privilege] no_priv_drop` |
| `--chroot` | `<DIR>` | -- | 0.3.0 | Chroot to this directory after initialization. It applies to `-I` file runs too, and needs root privileges: as an ordinary user the run exits `1`, and `--chroot /tmp` fails with `Failed to chroot: chroot(/tmp) failed: Operation not permitted (os error 1)`. Config: `[privilege] chroot` |
| `--setup-caps` | -- | off | 0.4.3 | Grant this binary the Linux capabilities for live capture (`cap_net_raw,cap_net_admin+ep` via `setcap`) so it runs without `sudo`, then exit. Re-invokes through `sudo` when not already root. Linux only. |

**`--user` does nothing unless the process is root.**

- sipnab skips the drop when the effective user is not root, and says so only
  at `debug` level.
- So after the recommended install (`--setup-caps`, then run without `sudo`),
  sipnab accepts `--user` and does nothing with it. An unprivileged process has
  nothing to drop.

The platforms also differ.

- On Linux, root plus `--user` drops to that user.
- On macOS, sipnab skips the drop even as root unless you pass `--user`.
  Dropping to `nobody` strands the process without a per-user login session.
  That crashes CoreAudio the moment anything touches it.

**Examples**
- `sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --priv-drop --report` — drop privileges as usual when your config file sets `[privilege] no_priv_drop = true`
- `sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --no-priv-drop --priv-drop --report` — the last of the pair wins, so sipnab drops privileges

- `sudo sipnab -d eth0 --user sipnab` — live capture that drops root to the sipnab service user once the capture device is open
- `sudo sipnab -d eth0 --user nobody --chroot /var/empty` — long-running monitor that drops to nobody and confines itself to an empty chroot
- `sudo sipnab -d eth0 --chroot /var/empty --no-priv-drop` — chrooted capture that keeps root privileges for the whole run
- `sudo sipnab --setup-caps` — grant the binary the capture capabilities (cap_net_raw,cap_net_admin) so future runs work without sudo, then exit


## Resource limits

| Flag | Value | Default | Since | Description |
|------|-------|---------|-------|-------------|
| `--max-capture-sources` | `<N>` | `65536` | 0.5.197 | Distinct capture sources sipnab remembers by name: input files, the device, HEP senders, traced processes. A packet from a new source past the limit is still analyzed but carries no `frame` pointer, so `--show-frame` cannot reach its bytes; sipnab counts it (`sipnab_capture_sources_refused_total`) and warns once. sipnab refuses to start, exit 2, when the limit cannot hold the input files or device plus `[limits] max_tracked_peers` HEP senders. Accepts 1 and up. Config: `[limits] max_capture_sources` |
| `--max-reassembly` | `<N>` | `10000` | 0.3.0 | Maximum concurrent TCP/TLS reassembly sessions. At least 1: sipnab refuses `0`. Config: `[limits] max_reassembly` |
| `--reassembly-ttl` | `<SECS>` | `30` | 0.5.100 | Seconds sipnab holds an incomplete IP datagram or half-read TCP stream before a sweep drops it. `--max-reassembly` bounds how MANY entries sipnab holds; this bounds how long. A persistent SIP/TCP or SIP/TLS trunk can stay quiet for longer than 30 seconds, and when sipnab drops its half-read stream the next segment starts mid-message and the sender's valid message reports as malformed. Raise it on such a trunk; `--max-reassembly` caps the extra state either way. Config: `[limits] reassembly_ttl_secs` |
| `--lint-max-per-rule` | `<N>` | `25` | 0.5.96 | Findings one lint rule may report for one dialog. A dialog that retransmits an `INVITE` eleven times trips a message rule eleven times and every one of them is true, so this decides whether the other rules stay readable underneath. Needs `--lint`. Config: `[limits] lint_max_per_rule` |
| `--lint-suppress-file` | `<FILE>` | discovered | 0.5.130 | Read lint suppressions from this file instead of discovering one. Without it sipnab looks for a `.sipnablint` beside the capture and then in each parent directory up to the nearest one holding a `.git`, the same file the MCP lint tools read. A named file sipnab cannot open fails hard rather than falling back to a full-catalog run. sipnab names whatever applies on stderr, with a count of what it silenced. Needs `--lint` |
| `--lint-no-suppress` | -- | off | 0.5.130 | Ignore any `.sipnablint`, including one named by `--lint-suppress-file`. It wins over both the explicit file and discovery, so it overrides a wrapper script that always passes a suppression file. Needs `--lint` |
| `--cores` | `<N>` | `1` | 0.4.14 | CPU cores for offline pcap reconstruction (`-I`). At least 1: sipnab refuses `0`. 1 = single-threaded; >1 shards by host pair for multi-core throughput and prints the whole-capture views (`--report`, `--json-dialogs`, `--analyze`, `--call-report`). A run that asks for none of them exits 2 before reading. A flag it does not carry out, such as `--json`, `--hexdump`, a matcher, a key file, an exec hook, a server or `--sandbox`, exits 2 naming it. Started as root it opens every input file first, then drops to `--user` (or `nobody`) as the single-core read does, so a root-only capture still reads. At any core count sipnab reads a plain uncompressed `.pcap` by mapping it, which is where most of the multi-core gain comes from; pcapng, gzip, a non-regular file, or any run with a BPF filter reads through libpcap instead. Set `SIPNAB_NO_MMAP=1` to force the libpcap path everywhere — an escape hatch for a filesystem where mapping misbehaves, such as some network or FUSE mounts. Results are identical either way, except that libpcap reads a nanosecond-resolution pcap's timestamps to the microsecond. With `--retain-audio` each worker gets an equal share of `[limits] max_audio_bytes`, so the run as a whole stays inside the budget |
| `--max-metadata-file-bytes` | `<BYTES>` | `2147483648` | 0.5.97 | Bytes of pcapng sipnab reads into memory for embedded names and TLS secrets. A `tcpdump -C` or `dumpcap -b` ring member passes 2 GiB on a host with the RAM to spare, and the refusal is fatal. **A memory-exhaustion guard on untrusted input:** raising it to N lets ONE file claim N bytes of this host's RAM, roughly 2N while `--strip-secrets` writes its copy, on nothing but a file size and before sipnab can tell the file is a capture at all. Raise it for captures you produced. Config: `[limits] max_metadata_file_bytes` |
| `--max-gunzip-bytes` | `<BYTES>` | `1073741824` | 0.5.97 | Bytes sipnab may inflate out of one gzip-compressed input: a `-I capture.pcap.gz`, every gzip layer of an archive summed across the layers of one input, the embedded names and TLS secrets it reads out of a `.pcapng.gz`, the copy `--strip-secrets` rewrites, and the whole capture in the browser build. **A gzip-bomb guard:** inflation stops one byte past the ceiling, so raising it to N lets a few kilobytes of input claim N bytes of RAM or disk. Raise it for archives you compressed yourself. Config: `[limits] max_gunzip_bytes` |
| `--max-tcp-buffer` | `<BYTES>` | `65536` | 0.5.99 | Bytes one SIP/TCP direction may buffer before sipnab flushes it. **The only limit here that destroys data rather than truncating a report.** TCP sets no such ceiling and neither does RFC 3261: on a carrier trunk a message carrying ISUP encapsulation, a long `Record-Route` set or a fat SDP offer passes 64 KiB legitimately, and sipnab then flushes the buffer mid-message — both halves parse as malformed, the cut destroys the framing for every message behind it, and the peer that sent a valid message is the one sipnab reports as broken. Raising it to N lets one TCP direction hold N bytes. The floor is one SIP header line (8192), below which no message survives, and sipnab refuses a smaller value by name. Config: `[limits] max_tcp_buffer` |

**Examples**

- `sudo sipnab -d eth0 --max-reassembly 50000` — live capture on a busy TCP/TLS trunk with a raised reassembly-session ceiling
- `sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --cores 4 --max-reassembly 2000 --report` — offline reconstruction sharded across 4 cores, with a tight reassembly bound for an untrusted capture
- `sipnab -N -I calls.pcap --lint --lint-max-per-rule 3 --no-cli-print` — keep the lint output to three repeats of any one rule, so a capture full of retransmissions still shows what else it trips
- `sipnab -N -I calls.pcap --lint --lint-max-per-rule 500 --no-cli-print` — the opposite: every repeat, for counting how often one rule actually fires
- `sipnab -N -I calls.pcap --lint --lint-fail-on error --no-cli-print` — honors the `.sipnablint` sitting beside `calls.pcap`, and names it on stderr with a count of what it silenced. A short finding list always says why it is short
- `sipnab -N -I calls.pcap --lint --lint-suppress-file ci.sipnablint --no-cli-print` — a suppression list of the pipeline's own, for a CI job whose tolerances differ from the tree's
- `sipnab -N -I calls.pcap --lint --lint-no-suppress --no-cli-print` — the full catalog, ignoring every suppression file, for auditing what the project has agreed to live with
- `sipnab -N -I ring-00042.pcapng --max-metadata-file-bytes 8589934592 --report` — read the embedded names and TLS secrets out of an 8 GiB ring member you captured yourself, which the shipped ceiling refuses outright
- `sipnab -N -I ring-00042.pcapng --max-metadata-file-bytes 8589934592 --strip-secrets sanitized.pcapng` — the same file, sanitized for handover. The copy costs roughly twice the ceiling in memory, so raise it only for a file you trust
- `sipnab -N -L 0.0.0.0:9060 --hep-allow 192.0.2.0/24 --config collector.toml --max-capture-sources 100000` — a HEP collector whose `collector.toml` sets `[limits] max_tracked_peers = 100000` for a large agent fleet: at the shipped 65536 sipnab refuses to start, exit 2, because the table could not hold every sender the listener may admit
- `sipnab -N -I a.pcap -I b.pcap --max-capture-sources 2 --report` — the smallest table two input files can run with; one less and sipnab refuses to start, naming the setting
- `sipnab -N -I archive.pcapng.gz --max-gunzip-bytes 8589934592 --strip-secrets sanitized.pcapng` — sanitize an 8 GiB pcapng you compressed yourself, without spending the disk that decompressing it by hand would need
- `sipnab -N -I from-customer.pcapng.gz --max-gunzip-bytes 268435456 --report` — the opposite, for a file that arrived from outside: a quarter-gigabyte ceiling on the embedded names and secrets sipnab reads out of it, so a gzip bomb wearing a capture's name cannot take the box down
- `sipnab -N -I isup-trunk.pcap --max-tcp-buffer 1048576 --json-dialogs --no-cli-print` — a carrier trunk whose SIP/TCP messages carry encapsulated ISUP bodies past 64 KiB: at the shipped ceiling sipnab cuts each one in half and reports it malformed, and at 1 MiB the same bytes produce the call
- `sudo sipnab -d eth0 --max-tcp-buffer 262144` — watch a live SBC that answers with long `Record-Route` sets, holding a quarter-megabyte per TCP direction so a large response frames whole instead of arriving as two malformed fragments
- `sudo sipnab -N -d eth0 --reassembly-ttl 600 --max-reassembly 50000` — a persistent SIP/TLS trunk to a carrier that goes quiet overnight: ten minutes of patience keeps the half-read stream, so the first segment of the morning continues a message rather than landing in the middle of one
- `sipnab -N -I untrusted.pcap --reassembly-ttl 5 --max-reassembly 2000` — the opposite, for a capture from outside: a five-second wait drops a half-sent stream almost at once, so a peer that opens streams and never finishes them cannot hold state
- `sipnab -N -I calls.pcap --mcp --mcp-allow-save-findings --mcp-max-findings 20000` — a long agent session over a large capture, where a thousand annotations is a session doing its job and the journal on this box can take twenty
- `sipnab -N -I calls.pcap --mcp --mcp-allow-save-findings --mcp-max-findings 25` — a scripted agent run on a box with a small journal: twenty-five annotations, then sipnab refuses further writes and says so rather than filling the disk


## vCon forwarder

`--vcon-forward` runs sipnab as the process that delivers an
`--export-vcon-dir` spool to a vCon store.

- It captures nothing.
- sipnab refuses it beside any capture source, listener or export flag.
- The other flags in this section need it, except `--vcon-spool-status`. That
  flag reads a spool's state and runs on its own.
- Each flag but `--vcon-forward`, `--vcon-forward-once`, `--vcon-forward-auth`
  and `--vcon-spool-status` has a `[vcon_forward]` key in the config file. The
  flag overrides the key.
- Needs the `vcon` Cargo feature.
- More: [Deliver the spool to a store](@/docs/vcon.md#deliver-the-spool-to-a-store).

| Flag | Value | Default | Since | Description |
|------|-------|---------|-------|-------------|
| `--vcon-forward` | `<SPOOL_DIR>` | -- | 0.5.205 | Deliver each container in this spool to `--vcon-forward-url`, byte for byte, and move it out of the spool by the store's answer: `2xx` to `--vcon-forward-done`, another `4xx` to `--vcon-forward-failed` beside a `<name>.error.json` record, `5xx`, a timeout or no connection left in place and retried after `--vcon-forward-backoff-first` (2 s), doubling to at most `--vcon-forward-backoff-cap` (5 minutes). A `401` or `403` refuses the credentials or the client for every container, so the forwarder stops instead: it sends nothing more, moves no file, logs the status and the first 200 bytes of the answer, and exits `3`, in either mode. Skips dot-prefixed names and names that do not end in `.json`. A container sipnab rewrites under the same name goes again. A `2xx` means the store accepted the container, not that it stored it. Needs a URL and a credential, each from its flag or its `[vcon_forward]` key; without one sipnab refuses the run with exit `2`, naming both |
| `--vcon-forward-kind` | `<KIND>` | `generic` | 0.5.206 | The kind of store: `generic`, `vcon-store` or `conserver`. A kind supplies the ingest path when the URL names no path and the header when the credential is a bare key; an explicit setting overrides each. No kind changes the container sent. `generic` supplies nothing. The table: [Choose the store kind](@/docs/vcon.md#choose-the-store-kind). Config: `[vcon_forward] kind` |
| `--vcon-forward-url` | `<URL>` | -- | 0.5.205 | Where the forwarder POSTs each container, `http://` or `https://`, with its path and query. With a `--vcon-forward-kind` other than `generic`, a URL with no path is the store's base URL and the kind adds its ingest path. sipnab refuses credentials in the URL: they belong in the auth file. Plain `http://` to a host other than loopback logs a warning. Config: `[vcon_forward] url` |
| `--vcon-forward-auth` | `<HEADER>` | -- | 0.5.206 | The credential itself, also read from `SIPNAB_VCON_FORWARD_AUTH`, as the auth file would hold it: one `Header-Name: value` line, or the bare key with a `--vcon-forward-kind` other than `generic`. A flag's value is visible in the process list to other users of the host: prefer the environment variable or `--vcon-forward-auth-file`. Refused when empty, beside `--vcon-forward-auth-file`, and beside `[vcon_forward] auth_file`. `--help` names the variable and never shows its value. The value never appears in a log line, an error or a failure record. A capture run ignores the variable |
| `--vcon-forward-auth-file` | `<FILE>` | -- | 0.5.205 | File holding one line, `Header-Name: value`, sent with every request: `Authorization: Bearer <token>`, or `x-conserver-api-token: <key>`. With a `--vcon-forward-kind` other than `generic` it may hold the bare key instead. Refused when other users can read it (`chmod 600` it), by the rule sipnab applies to its other secret files. A file sipnab cannot read, or one that holds no credential, stops the forwarder with exit 2. The same file named by `[vcon_forward] auth_file` exits 1. The value never appears in a log line, an error or a failure record. Config: `[vcon_forward] auth_file` |
| `--vcon-forward-done` | `<DIR>` | `<SPOOL_DIR>/delivered` | 0.5.205 | Where a delivered container goes, under its own name. Created mode `0700` if missing. Must be on the spool's file system. Config: `[vcon_forward] done` |
| `--vcon-forward-failed` | `<DIR>` | `<SPOOL_DIR>/failed` | 0.5.205 | Where a refused container goes, beside `<name>.error.json`: the status, the method and URL, and the first `--vcon-forward-max-error-body` bytes (8 KiB) of the store's answer with the auth value removed, or the forwarder's own reason. Created mode `0700` if missing. Must be on the spool's file system. Config: `[vcon_forward] failed` |
| `--vcon-forward-replace-url` | `<TEMPLATE>` | -- | 0.5.205 | When the POST answers `409`, PUT the same bytes to this URL with `{uuid}` replaced by the container's `uuid`. Without it a `409` is a refusal like any other `4xx`. Config: `[vcon_forward] replace_url` |
| `--vcon-forward-once` | -- | off | 0.5.205 | Make one pass and exit: `0` when the store accepted every container or the spool held none, `1` when the store refused one or one is still waiting, `2` when sipnab refuses the settings, `3` when the store answered `401` or `403`. A config file sipnab cannot read, or one that holds a `[vcon_forward]` number or `kind` outside its range or list, an empty path, or a `url` or `replace_url` sipnab refuses, exits `1` before the pass, as any run does; the same refusal of `--vcon-forward-url` or `--vcon-forward-replace-url` exits `2`. Without it the forwarder passes over the spool every `--vcon-forward-interval` seconds until SIGTERM or SIGINT, and sends nothing after the signal |
| `--vcon-forward-interval` | `<SECS>` | `5` | 0.5.205 | Seconds between passes, 1 to 3600. Config: `[vcon_forward] interval` |
| `--vcon-forward-timeout` | `<SECS>` | `30` | 0.5.205 | Seconds to wait to connect, and for each read and write, before the store counts as unreachable and the container waits for a retry, 1 to 600. It also bounds each SCITT registration: polling a `202`'s `Location` for the receipt ends within it. Config: `[vcon_forward] timeout` |
| `--vcon-forward-ca` | `<FILE>` | host bundle | 0.5.205 | Trust only the CA certificates in this PEM file for an `https://` store. Without it the forwarder trusts the host's CA bundle. Config: `[vcon_forward] ca` |
| `--vcon-forward-extra-ca` | `<FILE>` | -- | 0.5.219 | Trust the CA certificates in this PEM file for an `https://` store **in addition to** the host's CA bundle: the forwarder accepts the store's certificate when the host's bundle or this file issued it. Use `--vcon-forward-ca` instead to trust only the named file; the forwarder refuses the two together. Either flag replaces both `[vcon_forward] ca` and `[vcon_forward] extra_ca`. Config: `[vcon_forward] extra_ca` |
| `--vcon-forward-backoff-first` | `<SECS>` | `2` | 0.5.206 | Seconds a container waits after its first failed try (a `5xx`, a timeout or no connection); each failed try doubles the wait, up to `--vcon-forward-backoff-cap`. 1 to 4294967295, and no longer than the cap. Config: `[vcon_forward] backoff_first` |
| `--vcon-forward-backoff-cap` | `<SECS>` | `300` | 0.5.206 | The longest a container waits between tries, 1 to 4294967295, and no shorter than `--vcon-forward-backoff-first`. Config: `[vcon_forward] backoff_cap` |
| `--vcon-forward-max-response-head` | `<BYTES>` | `65536` | 0.5.206 | The most bytes of a store's status line and headers read, 1 to 4294967295. The forwarder treats an answer with more as no answer, and the container waits for a retry. Config: `[vcon_forward] max_response_head` |
| `--vcon-forward-max-error-body` | `<BYTES>` | `8192` | 0.5.206 | The most bytes of a store's answer to a refused container that its `<name>.error.json` record keeps, 1 to 4294967295. Config: `[vcon_forward] max_error_body` |
| `--vcon-forward-scitt-url` | `<URL>` | -- | 0.5.219 | Register SCITT lifecycle statements (draft-howe-vcon-lifecycle-01) with the transparency service at this base URL. For each delivered container, `vcon_created` when sipnab wrote it once and `vcon_sent` every time, each a COSE_Sign1 Signed Statement POSTed to `<URL>/entries`.
